News.title: Crete wildfires live: Rethymno in flames amid mass evacuations on Greek islands
News.content:
Flames are tearing across Greek Islands, forcing the evacuation of entire villages on Crete, Paros and Andros as wildfires continue to sweep across Europe

Raging wildfires have taken hold across several Greek islands, forcing villages to be evacuated as firefighters struggle to contain the flames.

Wildfires in the Rethymno region of the south of Crete are burning "out of control on all fronts", with firefighting aircraft unable to be deployed due to strong winds. Thousands of people, including tourists, were evacuated overnight. Urgent evacuation orders have also been issued for parts of Paros and Andros.

Three firefighters have died in Greece, with two becoming trapped in a vehicle while tackling the flames in Rethymno. Meanwhile, Europe's emergency response chief warned that the entire continent could be engulfed as wildfires rage in France, Spain and Portugal.

"Italy will face risk at the beginning of August, and we will need to see what will happen with the Iberian Peninsula, because if [it is] there as well, we will have all Europe on fire," Maria Zuber, head of the EU's Emergency Response Co-ordination Centre, said yesterday.

News.title: Brit rugby player dies after alleged attack left him brain dead on Turkey holiday
News.content:
Brit rugby player dies after alleged attack left him brain dead on Turkey holiday

Scot James, 34, who played for Maesteg Celtic RFC, was on holiday with family in Turkey when he was declared brain dead on July 11 after an alleged attack

View Image Scot James was on holiday in Turkey when he was allegedly attacked earlier this month

A British rugby player has died after an alleged attack while on a family holiday in Turkey earlier this month left him brain dead.

‌



Scot James, 34, was declared brain dead in Turkey on July 11 after what his family have described as an assault.

‌



He was brought back to the UK last Friday via air ambulance and passed away on Sunday at The Royal Glamorgan hospital in Wales.

‌



Scot, who played for Maesteg Celtic RFC, was described as a "loving father, son, grandson and partner" and an "all-round loveable man" in tributes on social media.

A GoFundMe was initially set up to raise money for the family as they extended their stay in Turkey to remain with Scot, Wales Online reports.

"Peacefully yesterday with all his loved ones around him my beloved brother Scot passed away," wrote his sister Hannah in an update on the GoFundMe page.

‌



"Scot was sadly declared brain dead in Turkey on Saturday 11th July 2026. For 13 days Scot’s family stayed in Turkey to be at Scot’s side as Scot was still on life support as the laws in Turkey are different to ours and they won’t just switch the life support off.

"On Friday 24th July Scot was flown home via air ambulance to the UK with my mother by his side where he was taken to ICU in The Royal Glamorgan hospital. We as a family got to spend and cherish his last few days with Scot and be by his bedside.

"But sadly yesterday afternoon 26/07 Scot decided it was his time to go and us as a family was there to hold his hand while his life support was turned off and while he sadly passed away.

‌



"I’m giving you this update as initially this was set up to help cover the cost of the family staying out in Turkey etc. But as I’ve explained the circumstances have changed and now Scot has passed away.

"So I’m giving this one final push now with this sad news as we was all hoping that the outcome would have been different, but sadly our Scot have passed away due to him having seizures in which it left him brain dead due to his injuries. [SIC]"

The Foreign Office confirmed it is working with local authorities following Scot's death.

‌



An FCDO spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British national who died following an incident in Turkey and are in contact with the local authorities.”

His local rugby club, which hosted a football tournament to raise funds in recent weeks, paid tribute to Scot on social media.

"We are deeply saddened to share the heart-breaking news that our former player, Scot James, sadly passed away yesterday," said Maesteg Celtics RFC on Facebook.

Article continues below

"Everyone at the club is devastated by this news, and our thoughts go out to his family and friends at this difficult time.

"Scot will be remembered as an outstanding player and a great character and friend by everyone who had the pleasure of sharing the field with him."

The Mirror has approached the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Turkish Police Foreign Relations Office for comment.

News.title: Sizewell B: The 30-year-old Suffolk nuclear power plant 3 miles from wildfire
News.content:
Sizewell B: The 30-year-old Suffolk nuclear power plant 3 miles from wildfire

Sizewell B is one of the UK's major nuclear sites, and is located within a few miles of the active Dunwich wildfire - so emergency services are paying it special attention

View 5 Images Smoke has been rising from the vicinity of Sizewell B in Suffolk (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

A massive wildfire is raging within just a few miles of a major UK nuclear site - Sizewell B - after growing to the size of 140 football pitches.

‌



Although firefighters have tackled the devastating Dunwich fire in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, for nearly 24 hours, it has grown to the size of 100 hectares - or 247 acres. Suffolk Fire and Rescue is believed to have deployed 18 engines to the area, and plan to continue tackling the blaze for another at least 36 hours as it edges ever closer to Suffolk's spawling nuclear complex.

‌



Pillars of smoke have been seen rising behind Sizewell B this morning, with officials scrambling to reassure the general public as operators EDF confirm they are "closely monitoring the situation".

‌



View 5 Images Firefighters at the scene of a wildfire at Dunwich Heath (Image: Suffolk County Council/PA Wire)

The UK's youngest power plant

Sizewell B is the UK's youngest nuclear power plant, having been opened just over 30 years ago on Valentine's Day 1995, around eight years after construction began. Sizewell uses a pressurised water reactor , the most common type of reactor which combines liquid and steam to generate electricity.

According to EDF, the power it generates is enough to power every home in Suffolk for nearly 200 years, and meets approximately three percent of the UK's total electricity demands.

‌



At its current rate that power is enough to deliver electricity to around 2.5 million homes. As part of a "golden age of nuclear", it will remain active for another few decades. An extension agreed last year will see it remain operative until 2055 after the Government postponed an initially agreed date of 2035 by 20 years.

View 5 Images Sizewell B is a nuclear power station on the Suffolk coast (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Is Sizewell B on alert?

The fire at Dunwich has been declared a "major incident", and it is raging around three miles away from Sizewell B and its neoughbouring in-development power station, Sizewell C.

‌



It had been reported earlier that the fire was headed directly towards the complex after a change of wind, and that plant bosses had placed the plant on "high alert". This has however since been denied by EDF, which said the site remains safe, and its position on the fire's danger "unchanged".

A spokesperson for the firm said: “We are continuing to monitor the situation, but the fire at Dunwich Heath is not currently affecting operations at Sizewell B power station."

View 5 Images The fire on Dunwich Heath near Sizewell, reportedly pictured at 3.30am (Image: X/KOBCOB2)

‌



Will the Dunwich fire reach Sizewell B?

Power plant bosses have been keen to stress that the fire currently poses no risk to Sizewell B, which operates from a base on the Suffolk coast. It is not getting bigger, Suffolk Fire and Rescue Chief fire officer Jon Lacey said today during a briefing at Westleton Village Hall this afternoon, and is moving inland rather than out to the coast.

Asked about the danger to Sizewell B and C, Mr Lacey said: "We're not expecting the wind direction to change to send the fire to Sizewell C or B.

"B is the main concern, but the big building site is also a priority for us. The terrain and land between us and the fire and Sizewell B and C means it's not a significant fire spread concern. At the moment Sizewell B and C are being monitored and we're in consultation with them, but we are not worried about the fire spreading in that direction.

‌



"It's a difficult fire because they're so wide spread and the resources are so wide spread. It is definitely one of the more challenging incidents we've had here in Suffolk."

View 5 Images Smoke has been rising near the Sizewell C construction site (Image: @X)

Is there an emergency plan for Sizewell B and C?

Sizewell B is understood to have a detailed emergency plan that prepares workers in the event of a range of scenarios, including a potential fire at the site. Sizewell C is nearby, and currently an active construction site. A spokesperson for the site has confirmed that the site is "closely monitoring" the wildfire's development.

Article continues below

A spokesperson for Sizewell C said the construction site was also “closely monitoring” the growing blaze, adding that it “currently poses low risk to Sizewell C, given its distance from site and watercourses in between”.

The spokesperson added particular attention is being paid to smoke production and the state of the road network, adding: "Sizewell C sites and offices continue to operate as normal, but we are continuously assessing the impacts of smoke and the effects on the road network to ensure that our people remain safe and emergency services have priority."

News.title: Suffolk fire live: Nuclear plant monitors ‘unprecedented’ wildfire destroying rare bird habitat
News.content:
A wildfire is raging in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk where evacuations have been ordered - the blaze is close to three nuclear plant sites, and has burned an area the size of 140 football pitches

Hundreds of people were evacuated overnight after a wildfire erupted in Dunwich Heath, Suffolk, with firefighters still battling to bring it under control today.

Temperatures have soared into the 30s in southern England, doing little to help the huge emegrency response. The fire has now burned an area the size of 140 football pitches, posing a risk to holiday parks and the UK's largest nuclear power plant. Some 200 caravans were evacuated, with holidaymakers woken up by banging on their doors.

EDF says it is "continuing to monitor the situation" at the Sizewell B power plant, while staff at Sizewell C - a planned nuclear power station located 10 miles from the fire - say there is a "low risk".

There is also concern for wildlife in the area, after nature reserve RSPB Minsmere announcing its closure this morning. RSPB Suffolk area manager Adam Rowlands said the land was home to rare wildlife including nightjars - and it could take "more than a decade" for the habitat to recover.

The fire spread across Dunwich Heath due to a change in wind conditions overnight, and there are fears more changes could worsen the situation. Chief Fire Officer Jon Lacey said it was a "very dynamic and fast-paced incident", adding: "I wouldn't say the fire is surrounded and we're on top of it because it moves faster than we're able to deal with it."

Have you been affected by the fire at Dunwich Heath? Get in touch with us at livenews@reachplc.com

News.title: Palestine Action's ban as 'terror group' goes to Supreme Court as 77 arrested in London
News.content:
Palestine Action's ban as 'terror group' goes to Supreme Court as 77 arrested in London

Palestine Action’s legal challenge against the ban on the organisation as a terror group will now go to the Supreme Court

View 4 Images Police vehicles parked near Westminster Magistrates' Court, London, as Palestine Action and Defend Our Juries protest outside today (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire)

Palestine Action’s co-founder can take her case to the Supreme Court after Court of Appeal judges ruled the group’s ban was lawful.

The update in the legal challenge came after police arrested 77 people at a protest outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court in central London for expressing support for the protest group.

In June, five Court of Appeal judges said the ban on the organisation as a terror group was a “justified and proportionate” interference on freedom of expression rights.

This overturned the judgment of three judges at the High Court who ruled in February that the then-home secretary Yvette Cooper’s decision to ban Palestine Action was unlawful, after a legal challenge from the group’s co-founder Huda Ammori.

After the judgment, Ms Ammori said she intended to take the case to the Supreme Court, and the European Court of Human Rights if necessary.

View 4 Images Police officers gather outside the Westminster Magistrates Court (Image: AP Photo/Alberto Pezzali)

She launched her bid to take the case to the UK’s highest court earlier this month and in a decision published on Thursday, Lord Sales, Lord Leggatt and Lady Simler granted permission for her appeal.

The case is to be expedited, court records show, with a hearing expected between October and December.

Justices granted the green light to challenge the ban on the basis that Ms Cooper had incorrectly applied her own policy, but refused a bid to challenge the decision based on interference with freedom of speech and freedom of association rights.

After the decision, Ms Ammori referenced the arrests and said: “This further evidences our case that the proscription of Palestine Action has become a vehicle for a far broader crackdown on expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people.

View 4 Images Protesters outside the Royal Courts of Justice (Image: PA)

“This unprecedented attack on free speech and the right to protest in this country is already having a chilling effect at a time when speaking out about Israel’s crimes could not be more urgent.”

Hundreds gathered outside the magistrates’ court where more than 2,000 cases related to supporting the group had been due to be heard on Thursday. But their cases had been adjourned to October, earlier this week.

Protesters shouting “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action” were detained by police, while demonstrators shouted “shame on you” and “under what power?”.

View 4 Images Police arrested 77 people at the protest (Image: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Article continues below

The Metropolitan Police said in a statement: “Officers have arrested 77 people. The majority of arrests have been for expressing support for a proscribed organisation.

“Four people have been arrested for encouraging or assisting a criminal offence. Police officers remain at the scene and continue to make arrests.”

Court officials confirmed that all cases relating to Palestine Action have been adjourned until October 26, to await the outcome of the Supreme Court appeal over the proscription of the group as a terrorism organisation.

News.title: Huge 7ft 4in man dies aged 33 after complications with growing too tall
News.content:
Huge 7ft 4in man dies aged 33 after complications with growing too tall

Sulemana Abdul Samed had began growing drastically in his early 20s as his tongue became swollen, which later led to his whole body growing and his spine curving

View 3 Images A shocked nurse previously told him "You've grown taller than the scale." (Image: BBC)

A man who never stopped growing has died aged 33 after complications linked to his rare condition

‌



Sulemana Abdul Samed, who measured 7ft 4in but was believed to have grown even taller before his death, died on Monday after sores on his legs became infected. Known across Ghana by his nickname Awuche, he became the local celebrity whose extraordinary height put his hometown of Gambaga on the map.

‌



Sulemana Abdul Kudus, a relative, said: “Everyone knew how generous and kind he was. From when he died until now, a lot of people are still coming to the house to find out what exactly happened.”

‌



Samed’s life changed dramatically in his early 20s after he suddenly began growing at an extraordinary rate. He had been working in a butcher’s shop in the capital, Accra, and saving to attend driving school when he woke one morning to find his tongue had swollen and he could no longer breathe properly.

View 3 Images Samed was restricted from doing many things due to his height (Image: TWITTER)

Britain showcases cutting-edge tech to protect nation underwater amid Putin threat READ MORE :

Over the following days, he realised the rest of his body was also continuing to grow. As his height increased, his spine began to curve and he was eventually forced to give up his dream of becoming a driver as well as his love of football.

‌



In an interview in 2023, he said: “I was planning to go to driving school, but even when I shift the seat back, I can’t hold the steering wheel… I can’t stretch my leg because my knee will knock the wheel.

“I used to play football like every other young man, I was athletic but now I cannot even walk short distances.”

Doctors later diagnosed Samed with Marfan syndrome, a genetic condition affecting the body’s connective tissue. The NHS said the condition affects around one in 5,000 people in the UK and can cause people to be unusually tall with long limbs, fingers and toes, as well as serious heart problems.

‌



He died in hospital in the northern city of Tamale after being admitted when sores on his legs became infected. Relatives said the sores were not directly caused by his syndrome but were likely a complication.

View 3 Images The brother of Ghana’s president, John Mahama, offering to pay his medical bills after he struggled to access treatment. (Image: TWITTER)

Kudus told the BBC: “Anywhere he found himself in the country and they asked him, he would say he is from Gambaga and people knew that was where the tallest man was from. It gave the community identity, and he was popular as well.”

Article continues below

His fame even led to the brother of Ghana’s president, John Mahama, offering to pay his medical bills after he struggled to access treatment.

Samed’s height also sparked speculation that he could challenge for the title of the world’s tallest man when a hospital once recorded him at 9ft 6in - a measurement that would have made him the tallest person in recorded history. It later emerged the figure had only been an estimate because staff did not have equipment capable of measuring him accurately. Journalists who later visited his home measured him at 7ft 4in.

According to Guinness World Records, the world’s tallest living man is Sultan Kosen, from Turkey, at 8ft 3in. The tallest person ever recorded was American Robert Wadlow, who reached 8ft 11in before dying aged 22 in 1940.

News.title: 'Best solar eclipse' in nearly 30 years hits UK in August - here's how to spot it
News.content:
'Best solar eclipse' in nearly 30 years hits UK in August - here's how to spot it

The UK is set to witness the 'best solar eclipse' in 27 years in just a couple of weeks' time, and here's everything you need to know about how to make sure you don't miss it

View Image The UK will be able to see a partial eclipse in August (stock photo) (Image: Thomas Roell via Getty Images)

Mark your calendars, as something spectacular is heading our way. Skygazers across the UK are in for a treat this summer, with experts hailing an upcoming solar eclipse as the finest we've had in nearly three decades.

‌



A solar eclipse happens when the moon moves between the Earth and the sun, casting a shadow that blocks out sunlight either partially or completely. These events aren't necessarily as rare as you might think - somewhere on Earth, they occur two to five times a year, with total solar eclipses happening roughly every 18 months globally. However, seeing one from your own back garden is a very different matter.

‌



That's because a total solar eclipse only passes over the same spot on Earth once every 360 to 410 years. So if you get to witness even one in your lifetime without travelling the world in pursuit of them, consider yourself truly lucky.

‌



The last time the UK experienced a total eclipse was back in August 1999 - and even then, only Cornwall and pockets of Devon were treated to the full blackout. Everyone else had to make do with a partial view.

Now, the next golden opportunity is almost upon us. On 12 August this year, the UK will experience a deep partial solar eclipse, with the moon set to blot out a stunning 90% of the sun. It won't be a total eclipse, as we'll have to wait until 2090 for that, but it will be the most impressive eclipse British skies have seen in 27 years.

How to spot the partial solar eclipse

Daisy Dobrijevic, Skywatching Editor at Space.com, has shared a handy guide on Instagram to help Brits get the most out of the event. According to Daisy, the eclipse will get underway at approximately 6pm BST, building to its dramatic peak, when the sun will be at its most obscured, at around 7pm BST. Things will wrap up by about 8pm BST, though she points out that exact timings will vary slightly depending on where you are in the country.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

One key thing to bear in mind is that because the eclipse falls in the evening, the sun will be sitting low in the sky as it unfolds. That means you'll need an unobstructed view towards the west to stand the best chance of catching it.

As Daisy puts it: "Because it happens in the evening, the sun will be low to the west, so try to find somewhere with a clear view of the western horizon."

‌



She also had a very important safety reminder. Even when the moon is covering the vast majority of the sun, the remaining light is still powerful enough to cause lasting damage to your eyes. Certified solar eclipse glasses are an absolute must - not just for a quick peek, but for the entire duration of the event.

"Remember, you'll need certified solar eclipse glasses for the entire eclipse," Daisy stressed. "It's never safe to look directly at the sun without proper eye protection. Hopefully, we'll all get clear skies."

How to watch an eclipse safely

If you're going to watch the eclipse in person, you must make sure you have special eclipse glasses that will block out the sun's harmful rays and allow you to look at the eclipse safely. Regular sunglasses are not safe to use, as they don't have adequate UV protection for looking directly at the sun.

‌



According to Royal Museums Greenwich, you must have glasses that have safety certification 'ISO 12312-2' or 'ISO 12312-2:2015' printed somewhere on them. Be careful if you are reusing old glasses, as they may not be safe, especially if the lenses are scratched or creased.

If you don't fancy travelling to find somewhere to watch the eclipse in person, you can also watch the Royal Observatory's live stream on 12th August, which will be broadcasting a free, live feed of the eclipse from London.

This will be the deepest partial eclipse visible from the UK and Ireland since the total eclipse of 1999. If you happen to be travelling to Greenland, Iceland or northern Spain around that time, you're in for an even bigger spectacle - those regions will experience full totality.

Article continues below

Even for those of us watching from home, the effects will be noticeable. Royal Museums Greenwich says the partial eclipse will trigger a drop in temperature and a dimming of the light, though don't expect the sky to go fully dark.

As they explain on their website: "At the maximum, enough of the Sun will be covered to make a noticeable difference in the temperature and light levels. However, unlike with a total eclipse, the sky will not become dark - it will feel more like a cloudy day or close to dusk or dawn."

So dust off those eclipse glasses, scout out a spot with a clear western horizon, and get ready - 12th August could be one of the most memorable evenings of the year.

News.title: Parents warned over coin battery dangers - 5 tips to keep your child safe
News.content:
Parents warned over coin battery dangers - 5 tips to keep your child safe

A new survey has found that many parents are unaware of the potential dangers of coin batteries in everyday household items, and are only alerted to the risks after their child has already come into contact with them

Rachel Riley speaks to primary school children about battery safety

Parents are failing to spot everyday household hazards, including toys containing coin batteries, according to new research. A poll of 1,000 mothers and fathers of children aged 0-5 years old revealed that 51% consider themselves 'very aware' of potential dangers in the home. Yet nearly half (45%) admitted they only recognise a safety risk after their child has already encountered it.

‌



Fewer than half (49%) acknowledge that toys containing coin batteries could pose a threat to their child. Even fewer are aware of the risks posed by batteries in common household items such as car key fobs (33%), TV remotes and bathroom scales (30%).

‌



With children due to spend more time at home during the summer holidays, Energizer is urging parents to swap out coin batteries in household devices for its new Ultimate Child Shield batteries.

‌



The batteries feature child-resistant packaging, a bitter coating to deter swallowing, and a blue dye that is released upon contact with saliva. They are also the world's only coin lithium battery specifically engineered to prevent ingestion burns if accidentally swallowed.

View 2 Images Rachel Riley joins Energizer to help families spot hidden coin battery risks (Image: PinPep)

To promote its 'Summer Safety Swap' campaign, the brand teamed up with broadcaster, mathematician and mum Rachel Riley, who visited a primary school to educate young children about the hidden dangers of coin batteries.

‌



Rachel said: "As parents, we all want to do everything we can to keep our children safe, so it's reassuring to see innovations that can help reduce everyday risks. "The summer holidays mean children naturally spend more time at home exploring and playing, and with so much going on, it's easy for everyday hazards to be overlooked.

"Many of us don't realise just how many everyday household items may contain coin batteries, which is why taking a few simple steps before the holidays can make such a difference.

"By checking for loose batteries, storing them safely and making simple swaps where possible, families can help make their homes even safer while children are busy exploring."

‌



View 2 Images She spoke to a group of primary children about the potential dangers (Image: PinPep)

The research indicated parents are already taking proactive measures to childproof their homes by storing knives, scissors and sharp tools safely (64%), moving hot drinks, pans and kettles away from edges (61%) and putting tablets out of reach (61%)..

Almost a quarter (23%) review the safety of their home every day. Still, 21% admitted they wouldn't know how to respond if their child swallowed a coin battery.

‌



One in ten said they would try to remove it themselves, another one in ten would turn to AI for advice. The OnePoll.com study found 55% felt there isn't enough information about hidden dangers around the home.

Paediatric doctor Radhika Thakrar's practical tips for making simple safety swaps this summer:

1. Look beyond the toy box

Coin batteries can be found in many everyday household items, including slim remote controls, key fobs, digital scales, lights and musical greetings cards. Take time to identify which devices in your home contain them and consider switching to batteries with additional child-safety features.

‌



2. Check that battery compartments are secure

Inspect battery-powered devices for loose backs, missing screws or damaged compartments. Batteries should not be accessible without the use of a tool or a secure opening mechanism. Stop using any device if its battery compartment cannot be properly secured.

3. Store loose batteries safely

Keep new, spare and used batteries in a secure place that is high up, locked away and completely out of children’s sight and reach. Avoid leaving batteries loose in drawers, bags, on worktops or beside devices waiting to be replaced.

4. Dispose of used batteries promptly

Used or “flat” batteries can still pose a danger. Keep them securely out of reach until they can be taken to an appropriate battery recycling point, rather than placing them in household bins or leaving them lying around the home.

Article continues below

5. Know what to do in an emergency

If you think a child may have swallowed a coin battery, do not wait for symptoms, attempt to remove it yourself or rely on online advice. Take them straight to A&E and tell medical staff that a battery may have been swallowed.

News.title: European nations to boycott World Cup if Fifa goes ahead with investment plan
News.content:
European football's 55 member associations have voted to boycott World Cups if the sport's governing body proceeds with a plan to sell stakes in its competitions to private investors.

The decision was made at an emergency meeting called to discuss the proposal announced earlier this week by Fifa, which oversees world football.

Uefa, which governs European football, had already made its opposition clear by releasing two damning statements - and that strength of feeling has been reaffirmed.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," it said on Thursday.

"It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale."

Uefa's boycott would cover all Fifa competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups and Club World Cup, and be triggered if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's proposals are voted through by member associations.

The first time this stance will be tested at a senior tournament is in October, when the Women's World Cup play-offs are due to be held.

News.title: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'
News.content:
A drought has been extended across the whole of Wales with the country on course for its driest July on record in 190 years.

Declaring the drought, the country's environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate".

The decision has been made in response to record-low river levels, dry soils, widespread wildfires and mounting impacts on wildlife, farming and forestry.

NRW had already announced a drought across the north and parts of mid Wales last week.

The nationwide announcement made on Thursday will trigger more monitoring of rivers and stronger advice for the public on use of water.

The declaration of a drought does not mean there is currently a threat to water supplies for homes and businesses, with Welsh water companies saying reservoir levels are holding up after a wet start to the year.

NRW said figures had shown Wales had received 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, with most rivers in the country "exceptionally low".

Groundwater levels are also falling in Wales, with some lower than expected for the time of year.

The environmental body said its teams were dealing with reports of "wide-reaching impacts to the environment", and that "conditions across Wales' natural environment have continued to deteriorate".

This includes drying riverbeds, fish in distress, an accumulation of algae, wildfire risk and concern from farmers about crop growth, grazing conditions and water availability for livestock.

News.title: Bank holds interest rates but says it is ready to raise them if Iran war escalates
News.content:
The Bank of England has kept interest rates unchanged for the fifth meeting in a row but has indicated it could raise them if the Iran war escalates.

It expects inflation - the rate at which prices rise - to pick up due to volatile oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East conflict, although the peak will be slightly lower than previously thought.

While major uncertainties remain because of the war, the Bank predicts the UK economy will grow this year by more than previously forecast.

The Bank voted to hold interest rates at 3.75% at its latest meeting. It said any change in borrowing costs would depend on how long the energy shock will last and how severe it is.

Three members of the Bank's nine-member rate-setting committee voted for a hike, one more than the previous meeting.

Speaking at a news conference, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said: "If the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period... it's likely that we will have to tighten policy to counter inflationary pressures in the UK economy."

However, Bailey said the Bank was not currently moving towards raising interest rates.

"Please do not leave this room thinking that the Bank of England is edging towards a hike, because frankly, there's nothing in what I said, and I think any of us have said along those lines," he told reporters.

If the Iran war continues and oil prices hover around $100 a barrel, then a rate rise seems likely. But many in the markets expect tensions to subside in the coming weeks, ahead of crucial elections across the US in the autumn.

News.title: Watch: Giant iceberg turns over near  Greenland's coast
News.content:
A massive iceberg was seen turning over off the coast of Greenland, near Ilulissat.

Video captured by an eyewitness showed the moment the iceberg turned over, creating waves close to the coastal city.

Ilulissat is home to the Unesco listed Ilulissat Icefjord and is located on the west coast of the island.

News.title: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures reveal
News.content:
There has been a large rise in the number of offenders being recalled to prisons in England and Wales having been released on licence, new government figures show.

There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.

The figures follow government schemes to release a number of offenders early in an effort to ease prison overcrowding.

The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said offenders released on licence face strict conditions "and can be hauled back to prison if they break these rules".

Cassia Rowland, from the Institute for Government think tank, said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.

"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.

News.title: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year
News.content:
Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.

One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, local officials said, with a one-year-old child among those hurt.

Seven hours later, three people were found dead aboard a small boat after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.

French officials confirmed their deaths as the Home Office reported that Wednesday saw the highest number of crossings in a single day this year, with nine boats reaching the UK.

Local authorities in France said the first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.

The man is thought to have been in his 30s or 40s, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.

Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.

Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.

The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.

Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people aboard. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.

A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, speaking separately about small boat crossings on Thursday, said the UK had made "significant progress" on reducing the number of arrivals.

But, asked by reporters about US President Donald Trump's remark that the UK had a "huge immigration problem", Burnham said there was much still to do "to get those numbers right down".

News.title: Greek police probe 'foul play' in death of woman found in suitcase
News.content:
Greek police have said they are trying to determine whether foul play was involved in the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, reportedly by a homeless man.

She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found and is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus two weeks before her death.

A spokesperson for police in Greece told the BBC: "We are awaiting the results of the toxicology tests to determine the cause of death and ascertain whether foul play was involved, as this was not clarified by the initial examination of the body."

News.title: Zendaya and Tom Holland's decade-long Spider-Man romance in pictures
News.content:
Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the film's casting and initial production.

The film showed British actor Holland as Peter Parker balancing high school life with being a superhero - Spider-Man - for the first time.

It also introduced US actress Zendaya as MJ, his awkward but intellectual classmate.

The on-screen chemistry was clear from the start and the film received good reviews but the pair denied rumours of a romance, insisting they were just close friends while promoting the movie.

They even took to Twitter [now X] to make light of the rumours. She posted: "Wait wait ... my favourite is when it says we go on vacations together HA! I haven't been on a vacation in years! hbu @TomHolland1996 ???"

Holland responded: "Does the press tour count?"

News.title: Missing child, 5, dies after being found in water
News.content:
A missing five-year-old child has died after being found in a body of water.

West Mercia Police said officers had responded to reports of a missing child in Badsey, Worcestershire, on Wednesday evening.

The child was found unresponsive in the water and a short time later was pronounced dead.

The force said they were believed to have drowned and called it "an incredibly tragic incident", adding there was no third-party involvement in the death.

Officers said they would not be identifying the child's sex out of respect for the family.

West Midlands Ambulance Service said they were called at 18:50 BST, sending an ambulance, two paramedic officers and the Midlands Air Ambulance Critical Care Car to the scene.

A spokesperson said: "On arrival we discovered one patient, a young child.

"Ambulance staff and police worked quickly to treat the patient, but sadly, it became apparent nothing could be done to save them and they were confirmed dead at the scene."

News.title: Olivia Dean nominated and  Lily Allen snubbed in Mercury Prize list
News.content:
Olivia Dean's campaign to collect every major music award in existence continues, with a nomination for this year's Mercury Prize.

The star is among the favourites to win the Â£25,000 prize, which recognises outstanding albums, after her second record, The Art of Loving, won album of the year at both the Brits and the Mobo Awards.

Sir Paul McCartney also receives his first ever Mercury nomination, aged 84, for the nostalgia-laden The Boys of Dungeon Lane, while Suede, Jade, Raye and Nia Archives are also in contention.

But there was a surprise omission for Lily Allen, whose scathing break-up album, West End Girl, was one of the biggest critical and commercial successes of the last 12 months.

News.title: England on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates
News.content:
England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.

Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.

Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".

Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.

"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."

He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.

Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.

News.title: Suspected Kinahan gang leader faces extradition
News.content:
Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan is to be extradited back to Ireland, BBC News NI understands.

He was arrested in Dubai under a warrant issued by the Irish courts in April but has fought attempts to extradite him.

However, his appeals have been unsuccessful and he is due to be flown back to Ireland within weeks.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) now expect authorities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to sign his extradition which will formally commence the extradition process.

GardaÃ­ expect this will take place very quickly.

Bringing the suspected gang leader back to Ireland will now be the subject of a major security operation between the gardaÃ­ and the Irish Defence Forces.

The US government imposed sanctions on him in April 2022 after he and other members of his family were identified as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.

Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton.

However, Kinahan is now expected to face the Irish courts in the coming weeks and has previously been named as the head of the drug cartel.

The Irish authorities are expected to prosecute him for his involvement in leading an organised crime group.

An extradition agreement is in place between the UAE and Ireland and it was used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the organised crime group.

He was sentenced to 24 years in prison last month for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

News.title: Dad pays tribute to son who died after sea rescue
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy who died a week after being rescued from the sea "never failed to bring happiness" to others, his father has told the BBC.

Musa Ahmed and five relatives got into difficulty in the water in West Mersea on 22 July, having travelled to the Essex seaside from east London.

His 15-year-old cousin, Sameeha Rahman, and her mother Shelina, 41, drowned at the scene.

Shahin Ahmed said his son was "a unique and happy personality, a sphere of joy" in a tribute after his death on Tuesday evening.

"Everyone who knew him had a unique relationship with him. He made every person feel special and never failed to bring happiness," Ahmed said.

"He was everyone's favourite and he made everyone feel like his favourite."

Ahmed also referred to Islam and said Musa "embodied" traits of the Prophet Muhammad.

News.title: Jenrick urges Burnham to rule out tax rises to fund social care
News.content:
Reform UK's Robert Jenrick has urged PM Andy Burnham to rule out future tax rises to fund his plans to fix adult social care in England.

Burnham has said he wants to look at existing budgets before considering tax rises but he has not ruled them out, adding that "difficult decisions" lay ahead with funding options to be set out in a review being published next year.

Jenrick said any reforms should be paid for by cutting foreign aid and benefit payments for migrants, urging the prime minister to rule out what he called a universal "death tax".

Burnham was health secretary in a Gordon Brown government which proposed a compulsory levy which people could defer until after they had died.

The idea was labelled a "death tax" by the Conservative Party.

Burnham has not mentioned introducing an adult social care levy in this form.

He told reporters on Wednesday that proposals he put forward in 2009 were intended to stop people having to sell their home in order to pay for their care.

The new prime minister has said fixing the social care system was a top priority and he has speeded up a review of the system by Baroness Casey, which will now be published next summer.

He said the review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding that there needed to be a system in place that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

He said he would immediately start to examine, with Chancellor John Healey, how to boost the pay and training of care workers, something he said would be "fully funded" from existing budgets.

On paying for the wider shake-up of the system, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets "before we talk about tax rises".

Speaking at a press conference earlier today, Jenrick said: "He won't, he can't, he will not rule out a death tax."

The former Tory minister, who is now Reform's Treasury spokesman, called on Burnham to "rule out this tax, end the uncertainty, end the worry today".

He said he agreed with Burnham that care workers were "scandalously underpaid" and said a Reform government would stop visas for overseas workers in order to employ more British citizens.

And he said Reform would find the money to fix social care by cutting waste and raiding the foreign aid budget.

"I could not look the British taxpayer in the eye and impose a tax - another tax - before I had stopped sending taxpayers' money to rich countries overseas," he said.

The Conservatives have also called on the prime minister to rule out tax rises and further borrowing to pay for social care.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch wrote to Burnham earlier this week that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

Jenrick's speech comes a day after Burnham held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to secure cross-party support for any changes. Badenoch was unavailable.

Reform and the Green Party were not invited for talks. Both parties expressed disappointment at this.

Jenrick said he was "not surprised" Reform leader Nigel Farage had not been asked to attend.

"Andy Burnham knows that Nigel will never go along with the betrayal of people who've paid in all their lives," he said.

He insisted that Reform were serious about health and social care, despite not having a health spokesperson.

"We are absolutely at the coalface of this, trying to do our utmost to support people in difficult times. Don't tell us we don't care about this issue. We really do."

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, but it has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

News.title: Mum and boyfriend jailed for girl's  murder
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A mum and her new boyfriend have been jailed for life for the "sadistic" abuse and murder of her two-year-old daughter.

Isabelle Welsh was a "happy and thriving" child before her mother, Alexandra Walker, invited Harrison Simpson into their lives in Thornaby, Stockton, in June 2025, Teesside Crown Court heard.

A judge said Isabelle was the victim of a campaign of violent and sexual abuse at the hands of those meant to love, care for and protect her.

Simpson, 22, and Walker, 26, were both found guilty of murder and child cruelty, with Simpson also convicted of sexual abuse of a child. Simpson must serve a minimum of 28 and a half years and Walker 22 years.

Ms Justice Norton said both were "equally and jointly responsible" for Isabelle's murder and the campaign of cruelty she endured, with the couple putting up a "wall of silence, lies and obfuscation" about the last weeks of her life.

News.title: ScotRail apology as passengers unable to book tickets in app launch chaos
News.content:
ScotRail has apologised for the chaotic launch of its new app, which has left hundreds of passengers unable to book train tickets.

The operator replaced its existing system, provided by Trainline, with an updated ticketing platform for travellers on Thursday morning.

Complaints on ScotRail's social media channels saw a series of issues with passengers being forced to reset account passwords and journeys not appearing in booking searches.

ScotRail said it was working to fix "intermittent technical issues" and said passengers should continue using their old phone app until resolved.

Many people attempting to catch morning trains were frustrated by the processes involved before they could buy tickets.

Passengers on social media branded the roll-out a "shambles" and a "nonsense".

Uefa will boycott all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its major tournaments to external investors are voted through, it was announced on Thursday.

A Uefa statement, following an emergency meeting, said: “Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

open image in gallery Spain won the last Fifa Women’s World Cup in 2023 but, as it stands, will boycott the 2027 event ( Getty )

Uefa were left dismayed that Infantino has given Fifa’s member associations just 53 days to decide their position and are outraged by Infantino promising a $40m (£30m) windfall to nations who back the proposals, or have the one-off payment withdrawn. Uefa previously said that Infantino’s plans to sell off stakes in Fifa’s major tournaments to private investors, including members of Donald Trump’s family, “crossed a line”.

Here’s everything you need to know.

What have Uefa agreed?

An emergency virtual meeting on Thursday was held between all 55 national associations which are members of Uefa, European football’s governing body.

In a lengthy statement, Uefa confirmed that “no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive” – adding “unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.”

It added: “Nobody should be in any doubt: UEFA and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.”

What tournaments will it cover?

It will cover all Fifa-sanctioned tournaments covering national teams. As it stands, the boycott will not cover club teams, meaning the planned 2029 Fifa Club World Cup would not be affected.

As such, the first senior tournament would be the 2027 Fifa Women’s World Cup, taking place between 24 June and 25 July, in Brazil next year.

Europe have 11 guaranteed slots in the 32-team competition. Spain are the defending champions, while England were finalists last time out in Australia.

England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland all have scheduled play-off qualifiers in October, which are organised by Uefa. Whether these matches specifically will go ahead, therefore, is yet to be confirmed.

open image in gallery England are European champions but would boycott next year’s Fifa World Cup as it stands ( Getty )

The next men’s World Cup takes place in 2030 in Spain, Portugal and Morocco – with opening games in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.

The next Fifa tournament at any age group is the 2026 Fifa Under-20 Women’s World Cup, which starts on 5 September in Poland. Six European teams, including England, were set to compete.

The 2026 Fifa Under-17 World Cup, for which England did not qualify, starts on 19 November in Qatar.

What have the FA said?

Following the Uefa statement, an FA spokeswoman said: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view.

“We oppose FIFA’s plans - the FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will."

What happens now?

First, let’s see how all the other confederations respond - and whether they also agree to a boycott.

Asia (AFC) and North America (CONCACAF) have all voiced their opposition and disapproval of the plans in the last few days. The South American and African federations, however, have been quiet so far.

Really though, it’s now over to Fifa.

Will Infantino and his executives plough on undeterred with their plans? Or will they modify, amend or abandon their proposals, given the uproar across Europe?

Uefa has announced that it will stage a full boycott of Fifa competitions, including the World Cup, if Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its tournaments to private investors are voted through.

The drastic action, which follows an emergency Uefa meeting on Thursday, was “unanimously” agreed among all 55 of Uefa’s member associations. A statement confirmed that “no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive”.

open image in gallery Donald Trump, President of the United States, and FIFA President Gianni Infantino with the World Cup trophy (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

Uefa carries significant leverage as a World Cup without major nations such as champions Spain, France, England and Germany would compromise Infantino’s designs on extracting as much revenue from the global showpiece as possible. Six of the eight quarter-finalists from this summer’s World Cup were European.

It would also harm next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, with Spain the reigning winners and European champions England also bringing considerable commercial interest in the tournament. England, runners-up at the 2023 World Cup, face two-legged qualification play-offs in October, as do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

A spokeswoman for the English FA echoed the Uefa sentiment, saying: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

Meanwhile, the majority of the 2030 World Cup will be staged in Europe, with Spain and Portugal sharing hosting rights along with Morocco, following games in South America hosted by Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay to commemorate the tournament’s centenary year.

On Tuesday, Fifa revealed plans to create a new $20bn subsidiary, 20 per cent owned by private investors, to manage the commercial rights and delivery of the World Cup and other major tournaments. Thrive Eternal, led Joshua Kushner, the brother of US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, are set to lead the new investment.

“This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football,” Uefa said. “The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever. “Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure.”

open image in gallery Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin has gone to war with Fifa president Gianni Infantino ( Reuters )

In a letter to the member associations, Infantino promised that national federations would benefit from an increase of its ‘Fifa Forward’ funding from around $8m to $20m for the upcoming four-year cycle between 2027 and 2031 if the new FFE subsidiary is created.

Additionally, the letter states that a “one-off” payment of another $20m would be made available for member associations who vote for Infantino’s proposals on 19 September. Member associations are then warned that their funding for the 2027-2031 cycle would only stand at $10m if the vote does not pass, meaning they would miss out on $30m. “This says everything you need to know about this plan,” Uefa said in a statement on Wednesday. “Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends.”

Many of the world’s smaller countries, especially those outside of Europe, are more dependent on funding from Fifa to run their national teams, develop long-term grassroots projects and and invest in infrastructure, like pitches, academies and stadiums. Before this year’s World Cup, Infantino claimed that “without Fifa, there would be no football in 150 countries in the world”

Uefa’s confirmation that it would stage a boycott comes ahead of a vote between Fifa’s 211 member associations on 19 September. Infantino’s proposals only require a majority vote of above 50 per cent from as well as backing from the Fifa Council, which means Uefa still requires more support to win the vote.

Uefa’s statement in full

“Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

“It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

“But our opposition goes far beyond process.

“The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure. From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.

“This model has no place in world football. Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return. Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

“Europe’s position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.

“Nobody should be in any doubt: Uefa and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.

“There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments.

“Some things are simply too important to sell. The Fifa World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

If you live in Philly and want to know information about your tap water quality, start with the latest consumer confidence report, which is required to be produced annually by every community water system in the country. Most people never read them, but the reports provide essential information about drinking water quality.

Like other large water systems, the Philadelphia Water Department publishes this information online, including the most recent 2025 drinking water quality report. The report provides an overview of Philly’s drinking water from source to tap. It reports that levels of approximately 100 regulated contaminants all meet federal standards.

As an interdisciplinary scientist and engineer, I study drinking water infrastructure and how science gets translated into policy and decision-making.

While the Philadelphia Water Department report is a good place to start, knowing what it tells you and where there may be gaps requires some background on how drinking water is regulated.

open image in gallery While the Philadelphia Water Department report is a good place to start, knowing what it tells you and where there may be gaps requires some background on how drinking water is regulated ( Getty Images )

How drinking water gets regulated

In the U.S., drinking water is regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act, which set limits for just over 20 contaminants when it became law in 1974.

Subsequent amendments and regulatory processes have brought the total to about 100. That’s still a small number compared to the approximately 700 disinfection byproducts, the tens of thousands of chemicals in commercial use in the U.S. today, or other contaminants of emerging concern.

While not all of these compounds end up in drinking water in amounts that can harm public health, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s regulatory process is designed to be reactive, not proactive.

Before setting a limit, the EPA must demonstrate that a contaminant may cause adverse health effects, that it occurs at levels that are a public health concern, and that regulation would meaningfully reduce risk.

This process is repeated contaminant by contaminant, though a single glass of tap water may contain dozens of trace contaminants at once. The EPA has recently moved partly toward regulating mixtures of contaminants. The 2024 federal PFAS rule set individual limits for six PFAS compounds and also regulated four of them as a mixture. However, proposed changes to the 2024 federal PFAS rule include rescinding the mixture provision.

Goals versus limits

Federal drinking water standards involve two numbers for each contaminant. The maximum contaminant level goal, or MCLG, is the concentration at which the contaminant is believed to pose no significant risk to health in people who drink that water every day for 70 years.

For chemicals classified as possible human carcinogens, MCLGs are typically set at a level where drinking the water daily for 70 years would cause one additional cancer case per 1 million people above the background rate.

However, MCLGs are nonenforceable. Enforceable drinking water limits, also called maximum contaminant levels, or MCLs, are often higher than MCLGs because they take cost and feasibility into account.

Levels of forever chemicals

Two forever chemicals, PFOA and PFOS, deserve attention first. Both are types of perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. PFAS are a family of synthetic chemicals widely used in consumer products. They persist in the environment and accumulate in the body.

The 2025 report from the Philadelphia Water Department shows Philly’s highest reported levels of PFOA at 6.1 parts per trillion, or ppt, and PFOS at 4.6 ppt. Both are above the new federal limit of 4 ppt.

But Philly remains in compliance. Meeting the federal limit is not required until 2029, and the EPA has proposed extending that deadline to 2031.

The levels are well below Pennsylvania’s limits of 14 ppt for PFOA and 18 ppt for PFOS.

Encouragingly, the Philadelphia Water Department is expanding its capacity to remove PFAS systemwide using powdered activated carbon. Small-scale tests have shown that powdered activated carbon can be effective for removing PFOA and PFOS, though effectiveness in real treatment conditions depends on dosing, contact time and other factors.

Lead, disinfectants and sodium

Lead in drinking water comes from lead leaching into the water from service lines leading from the water main to your house or from plumbing inside your home. Lead can cause serious health problems, and it accumulates in the body.

As required by the Lead and Copper Rule, the Philadelphia Water Department’s treatment includes corrosion control that forms a protective coating on the inside of pipes. This reduces the amount of lead that leaches into drinking water from lead service lines. Homes built before a 1986 federal ban on lead pipes and solder carry the most risk, as do homes with lead service lines. More recent brass fixtures could legally contain small amounts of lead until 2014.

The Philadelphia Water Department is required to collect samples from homes in Philly with lead service lines every three years. Testing in 2025 showed 90% of sampled homes were at or below 2 parts per billion, or ppb. That’s well under the 15 ppb EPA action level. But testing results ranged from 0 to 21 ppb, meaning some homes with lead service lines had measurable lead in their water.

The maximum contaminant level goal for lead is zero because no safe level of childhood lead exposure has been determined.

Chemical disinfection keeps water safe across Philly’s 3,000 miles of pipe but produces byproducts linked to increased cancer risk. These byproducts form when the disinfectant, in this case sodium hypochlorite, reacts with organic matter remaining in the water after treatment. Levels rise the longer water sits in the pipes.

The Philadelphia Water Department’s 2025 annual averages were 51 ppb total trihalomethanes and 41 ppb haloacetic acids – both well under federal limits of 80 and 60 ppb, respectively. However, individual samples exceeded those limits. This suggests some homes further out in the distribution system may experience elevated levels.

Finally, sodium levels are a concern for people with sodium-restricted diets, including those with hypertension, heart failure or kidney disease. The American Heart Association recommends that people in these groups limit sodium intake to 1,500 milligrams per day. Depending on which plant serves you, Philly tap water carries 4 to 44 milligrams of sodium per 8-ounce glass. Over eight glasses a day, that’s roughly 30 to 350 milligrams, or up to nearly 25% of the recommended daily limit.

What you can do

Reducing your household exposure to drinking water contaminants isn’t difficult.

A carbon filter certified to NSF/ANSI Standard 53 will measurably reduce disinfection byproducts, PFOA and PFOS, and lead. A certified carbon filter for a pitcher, faucet or refrigerator works well to reduce levels in drinking water; reverse osmosis does more, but it costs more and wastes water.

In addition, if your home has a lead service line or older plumbing, the Philadelphia Water Department recommends running cold water from the tap for 3-5 minutes when it has been unused for more than six hours before drinking or cooking with it. This flushes out water that has been in contact with plumbing.

About the author Christine Kirchhoff is an Associate Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Law, Policy, and Engineering, Penn State. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

The Philadelphia Water Department offers free lead testing of tap water on request. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and EPA recommend that children at risk for lead exposure should have their blood lead levels assessed.

Sodium is a different case: Standard carbon filters don’t remove it, but an ion-exchange pitcher, such as ZeroWater, or a reverse osmosis system will.

News.title: Lily Allen’s West End Girl was the defining album of 2025. Why isn’t it on the Mercury Prize shortlist?
News.content:

When you think of the album that everyone was talking about last year, only one springs to mind: Lily Allen’s eviscerating marriage post-mortem West End Girl. It’s the album that lit up WhatsApp groups around the country, made jaws drop with the sheer bluntness of it all, and may just have inspired more than one woman to ditch their husband. So why, I want to know, is it not on this year’s Mercury Prize shortlist?

The snubbing of the British pop artist’s career-best work – a blistering, jaw-dropping, skin-pinchingly brutal narrative of a marriage in freefall – is one of the industry’s most spectacular fumbles in some time. Especially when it comes to women in music, the UK has a depressing reputation for failing to champion its own artists until they’re a success elsewhere. But Allen being left out is especially surprising, given it was one of the most critically lauded records of 2025, charting at No 2 in the UK and nominated for Album of the Year at the 2026 Brit Awards.

open image in gallery Allen performing ‘West End Girl’ on tour ( Getty )

West End Girl was also the discourse for weeks if not months around its release thanks to its raw studies of non-monogamy, infidelity, betrayal, sexual rejection, loneliness, gaslighting and, erm, more betrayal. With the exception of Rosalía’s Lux and Olivia Rodrigo’s You Seem Pretty Sad For a Girl So in Love, neither of which were eligible for the Mercury Prize, West End Girl is the album that dissects all of our anxieties around the idea of the “modern” relationship and lays them out on the mortuary slab.

Just think of the perky opener “West End Girl”, in which Allen lays out her scene. She’s just won the lead in a play, she’s packing her bags! But she closes with a subdued phone conversation: her partner wants an open relationship. Then comes the suspicion of “Tennis” as she unwittingly sees an incriminating text; her squaring up to “Madeline” (“how long has it been going on?”), the mental health spiral of “Ruminating”. These were songs that became TikTok memes, Instagram profiles, and Halloween costumes. The “bewildered and wounded” Allen delivered, as critic Hannah Ewens said in her five-star review for The Independent, an “emotional post-mortem carried out in public, a death-by-a-million-cuts account of a thoroughly modern marriage breakdown”. It was perfect.

So how does a snub like this happen? Artists and their teams submit themselves for the prize, so there is always the possibility that Allen didn’t put herself forward. Given she was previously shortlisted for her 2018 album, No Shame, though, I find that hard to believe, given her evident pride in making such a masterpiece in just 10 days, and her joy at the rapturous reception it received. The shortlist is chosen by a panel of industry “experts”, among them critics, radio DJs and musicians who have, in recent years, strayed towards more commercial picks.

Shortlisted this year are Olivia Dean’s breakthrough album The Art of Loving (she was also nominated for her 2023 debut, Messy), The Boy Who Played the Harp by former winner Dave, JADE’s debut solo album That’s Showbiz, Baby, and RAYE’s This Music May Contain Hope. Paul McCartney received his first nomination for The Boys of Dungeon Lane, while Britpop stalwarts Suede are up for what many critics felt was a late-career high, Antidepressants. All very safe picks while, perhaps, Allen’s album was too knotty for some of the judges?

One glaring throughline for many of these shortlisted albums is that they are cases of the artist (or band) doing what they’re good at. Dave is deep and introspective, McCartney is sweetly nostalgic, Florence and the Machine are witchy and at gale-force volume. They do all of that very well. But in terms of artistic achievement, a case of an artist putting everything they had on the line, Allen was someone who really went there. She demonstrated how far she’s come from the bratty, day-glo-eyeliner-wearing artist we grew up with (and loved). Failing to acknowledge her for that feels like a real self-own.

A good serum can be one of the hardest-working additions to your skincare routine if you’re looking to target signs of ageing. From fine lines and wrinkles to pigmentation, dryness and dullness, the right formula can help address common skin concerns and minimise their appearance over time.

“The serum is where the real ‘treatment’ step sits,” says aesthetic doctor Dr Nabil Jetha. “They’re so highly regarded because they’re designed to deliver a high concentration of active ingredients directly into the skin.” Unlike moisturisers, serums are made up of smaller, lightweight molecules that can penetrate deeper.

Anti-ageing serums generally fall into three categories: antioxidant formulas, such as vitamin C, which help protect skin from environmental damage; hydrating serums with ingredients like hyaluronic acid that boost moisture; and targeted treatments with ingredients like retinoids and peptides that support skin repair overnight.
