World.title: WestJet flight attendants' union serves 72-hour strike notice
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The union representing 4,400 flight attendants at WestJet says it has issued a 72-hour strike notice, paving the runway for a possible strike during a busy summer travel season.

The Canadian Union of Public Employees says the two sides remain far apart on key issues.

"We have been clear about what needs to change, and we have worked hard to reach a fair deal," Alia Hussain, chair of the union's WestJet contingent, said in a news release early Thursday.

"There's still time to avoid a strike," Hussain added. "We will continue to bargain around the clock until this is resolved."

WestJet, in a statement, said the airline responded to the union's strike notice by issuing a 72-hour lockout notice.

Job action could begin as soon as Sunday at 12:01 a.m. MT if the two sides don't reach a deal. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

The air carrier — the second-largest in Canada — said it is still actively negotiating to reach a deal.

"The decision to issue a lockout notice, in response to the actions taken by the union, was not one that was made lightly. We sincerely regret the inconvenience and uncertainty this continues to cause for our guests," said WestJet CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech in the statement.

Are your travel plans now up in the air with a potential WestJet strike? We want to hear from you. Email us at ask@cbc.ca.

"We greatly value the work and contributions of our cabin crew, and it is our responsibility to ensure the integrity of our network and to minimize the risk of stranding our guests, crew and aircraft."

While serving notice does not commit the union to a strike, job action could begin as soon as Sunday at 12:01 a.m. MT if the two sides don't reach a deal.

WATCH | Canada's second-largest airline could see a summer strike: WestJet preps shutdown ahead of possible flight attendants strike | Duration 2:27 Despite ongoing talks, WestJet and its flight attendants have signed off on a plan to wind down operations ahead of a possible long-weekend strike. Some 4,400 union members could walk off the job this Sunday.

Unless a tentative agreement is reached, some flights could start to be grounded by Friday.

WestJet has been allowing passengers with flights scheduled any time between July 30 and Aug. 4 to make a one-time change or cancel it with no fee.

Travellers booked on its regional WestJet Encore service or code-share flights run by an airline partner such as Delta Air Lines will not be affected by a strike, the carrier said.

Should flight delays or cancellations occur, the airline said impacted guests will be refunded or reaccommodated, "as applicable."

The two sides this week also inked an agreement that lays out how to ground planes and get cabin crew home in the event of a work stoppage.

Unpaid ground duties key issue for union

Cabin crew working a flight when any job action kicks off would complete the trip to its destination. Those who can't immediately return to their home city would receive hotel accommodation for up to a week or a plane ride back to another Canadian city, "subject to seat availability," according to the deal.

The union has said key issues include unpaid work for tasks such as ground duties, while WestJet has said all duties are compensated through a "credit hour" system rather than an hourly rate.

John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University, has said even a brief shutdown would cost the carrier millions of dollars during the height of summer travel — on a long weekend across much of Canada.

The airline says it operates more than 600 flights per day carrying legions of passengers — more than 70,000 on some days.

World.title: Crews called to rescue resident who defied evacuation order, B.C. Wildfire Service says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Wildfire officials in British Columbia are urging people to follow evacuation orders, after they say crews were forced to rescue a resident who had stayed in a fire zone.

The incident happened near Chasm, about 20 kilometres north of Clinton, where fire crews are battling the massive Pear Lake wildfire.

B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) incident commander Bryce Moreira said when crews approached the resident's property Tuesday evening and informed him that staying in the area was dangerous, they were told to leave.

"I won’t repeat exactly what he said, but it was not [in] a nice way, and quite explicit," Moreira said.

WATCH | B.C. wildfires expected to grow: Officials warn wildfires will likely grow this week in B.C. | Duration 1:55



"The crews left, continued the work they were doing, and then later they were called and asked to go back because this person's property was surrounded by fire and they were not able to get out."

Moreira said the firefighters and the resident were able to get out of the area safely.

But he said the incident put everyone in danger, and pulled the firefighters away from duties protecting other properties.

Plumes of smoke from wildfires burning near Clinton, B.C., seen on July 17. (Dustin Bentall)

The incident came the same day the union representing B.C. paramedics issued its own statement about people defying evacuation orders.

Doing so, the Ambulance Paramedics of B.C. said, puts first responders in danger, while also straining the health-care system.

"Every unnecessary rescue diverts valuable emergency resources away from patients and communities who may urgently need them," it said.

No timeline for return

Evacuation orders remain in effect for about 1,600 properties in B.C., with another 3,000 under evacuation alerts.

The lion's share of those are related to the 732-square-kilometre Pear Lake fire which has forced residents of Clinton and nearby communities to flee, and which spurred fresh evacuations on Wednesday.

Wildfire officials said Wednesday the fire had grown to the north, and was within five to six kilometres of 70 Mile House.

LISTEN | Clinton residents wait for word on any damage to properties: Radio West 10:10 Clinton residents to learn in coming days if their homes survived Pear Lake wildfire Roland Stanke, the mayor of Clinton, says the wildfire damaged critical infrastructure, including the hydro transmission system and says the area's watershed and reservior. He adds there is no timeline, yet, for when people can return home.

The Thompson-Nicola Regional District held a virtual information session for residents on Wednesday where Clinton CAO Brian Doddridge said the area's watershed has been "severely damaged."

Clinton Mayor Roland Stanke told CBC's Radio West that the village is still assessing damage, and will inform residents directly if their property has been affected.

Power remains out in the community and crews are still dealing with embers and hotspots from the wildfire which continues to burn nearby, Stanke said, adding there was no firm timeline for residents to return.

“I would probably say it would be at least another week before we could even look at it," he said.

B.C. wildfire crews conduct a planned ignition on the Pear Lake wildfire on July 29. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

The BCWS has warned that persistent heat, drought and wind are likely to cause wildfires across B.C. to grow this week.

As of Thursday morning, there were close to 130 wildfires burning in B.C., about 40 per cent of them out of control.

Those include fires in the Brunswick Creek complex that forced the evacuation of Boston Bar, but which have not grown significantly in days.

On Wednesday evening, the community of Logan Lake issued an evacuation alert for 49 properties due to the new 88-hectare Guichon Creek fire.

World.title: CBC identifies Canadian woman accused of spying at NATO military HQ
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian woman recently arrested by Belgian authorities on suspicion of spying appears to have worked for multiple government agencies before her NATO internship.

A CBC News investigation has identified the woman as Biwei Zhang, a systems engineer with a background in economics whose online resume suggests she previously worked for the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada.

Zhang's public and professional profiles match the information Belgian prosecutors provided, which described the suspect as a "Canadian national of Chinese origin" who was an intern at Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), the military headquarters of NATO in Mons, Belgium.

The suspect's home and workplace at SHAPE were searched last Thursday, according to a media release from the Federal Prosecutor's Office. She was reportedly arrested a day later on charges of "espionage and participation in a criminal organization."

WATCH | CBC identifies Canadian woman accused of spying at NATO military HQ: CBC News identifies Canadian intern accused of spying on NATO | Duration 3:14 A CBC News investigation has identified Biwei Zhang as the Canadian intern at NATO who is facing espionage charges. She previously held positions at the World Trade Organization, the European Space Agency, the Canadian Space Agency and Statistics Canada.

Belgian courts do not publicly identify defendants in criminal investigations until the trial. As such, the Belgian prosecutor's office would not confirm the identity of the alleged spy or her counsel, telling CBC News it "never disclose[s] the identities of individuals suspected in ongoing investigations," an approach aligned with its "respect for the presumption of innocence, which must be guaranteed under all circumstances."

However, using open-source investigative techniques, CBC matched the description of Belgian authorities with identifying information on Zhang's LinkedIn, Facebook and Threads profiles, as well as her graduate thesis and a federal court case.

While Biwei Zhang appears to be her legal name, she uses the name Claire Zhang professionally, and goes by Catina Zhang on her Facebook profile.

In posts to two separate Facebook groups in July 2025, Zhang said she was looking for a room to rent in Mons as she began her internship. She also sought housing in Geneva in 2023 right before an internship at the World Trade Organization — dates that line up with her work experience on her LinkedIn profile.

The details also match information reported by Reuters earlier this week, which identified the woman as Claire Z. A security source told Reuters she was working in SHAPE's IT department, which is consistent with Zhang's background in computer science and systems engineering, for which she completed a master's degree at the University of Ottawa in 2022.

The source also described her as "not a student" and "in her 30s," information that matched Zhang's professional profile. Her Facebook username, "biwei.zhang.93," also suggests she may have been born in 1993, which would make her 32 or 33 years old.

In a July 2025 post to a Mons, Belgium, Facebook group, Zhang identified herself as an incoming intern at SHAPE, NATO's military headquarters, and said she was looking for a room to rent for the next six months. (Catina Zhang/Facebook)

Similar identifying details were reported by independent European investigative news outlet Follow the Money and its media partners on Tuesday.

Zhang did not immediately respond to CBC's requests for comment on her LinkedIn and Facebook profiles.

Belgian officials say the alleged spy will remain in pretrial custody for at least another month as the investigation continues.

National security concerns

The case has also raised concerns around the efficacy of Canada's security screening processes, prompting Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree to commit to investigating whether the person in question worked for any Canadian agencies.

"Ultimately, we need to get to the bottom of this, and we need to ensure that these types of incidents do not occur in the future," Anandasangaree said.

WATCH | Canada investigating alleged spy: Minister commits to 'get to the bottom' of Canadian NATO intern spying allegations | Duration 1:26 As a Canadian woman who was an intern at NATO's military headquarters in Belgium is facing 'quite serious' spying charges, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said that Canada would investigate its security screening processes and 'get to the bottom of what happened.'

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zhang has held a range of positions at federal agencies, including as a data scientist for the National Research Council for six months in 2017, an economist for StatsCan from April 2018 to October 2022, and then as a systems engineer at the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) from May 2022.

She also lists experience as a policy analyst for the European Space Agency, and the economic research and statistics division of the World Trade Organization, as well as positions on "mirror committees" of the Standards Council of Canada, a Crown corporation that acts as "Canada's voice on standards and accreditation on the international stage."

In an emailed statement, the European Space Agency said it applies standard screening procedures for positions that do not require security clearance, and relies on "the relevant national security authority [to] conduct a comprehensive vetting process of the individual concerned" when classified information is involved.

In a LinkedIn profile with the name 'Claire Z.,' Zhang claims over five years of experience working as an economist for Statistics Canada and a data scientist for the National Research Council. (Claire Z./LinkedIn)

The CSA acknowledged CBC's request for comment but did not provide a response by publication time.

A spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada told CBC News that the Canadian government "makes the final decision to grant, deny, or revoke security clearances for Canadians seeking positions with international organizations, including NATO" following Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) security assessments.

Global Affairs refused to comment on the specific case "as it is the subject of an ongoing investigation."

Zhang also requested a judicial review of a Public Service Commission of Canada finding that she committed fraud in an application for a position at the Canada Border Services Agency by applying under two different names and emails and failing to later clarify whether she had submitted multiple applications.

A federal judge dismissed the case in August 2024.

Intern positions an 'Achilles heel': ex-spy

Former CSIS intelligence officer Dan Stanton told CBC News that while he does not have direct knowledge of the case, he can see why NATO would be concerned about possible intelligence breaches.

He says intern positions are an "excellent in-road" that he likened to "an Achilles heel" for an organization like NATO.

"Most of the biggest secrets in espionage aren't as a result of stealing files or accessing data banks. It's conversations, it's hearing things," said Stanton, now the director of the national security program at the University of Ottawa's Professional Development Institute.

Dan Stanton, a former CSIS intelligence officer, told CBC News that intern positions are an 'excellent in-road' for intelligence gathering at an organization like NATO. (Jean-François Benoit/CBC)

Still, the former spy sees the investigation as a "good news story."

"In the world of counter-espionage, these types of things happen," he said.

"It's proof that our processes work."

World.title: The web is being redesigned for AI. What does that mean for human readers?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how humans use the internet. For The National, CBC’s Nora Young breaks down the future of search and what happens to information when bots do most of the reading online.

Say goodbye to the internet as you know it

Deb Perelman has seen a lot of change online.

The food blogger's popular site Smitten Kitchen turns 20 years old this summer.

"I've always had the philosophy that I would just meet people where they were," Perelman said, which is why she established a presence on social media platforms from Twitter to Instagram to TikTok — but always took readers back to the recipes and stories on her website.

Now, she faces a new challenge: AI summaries.

Deb Perelman, creator of the food blog Smitten Kitchen, has seen AI summaries eat into her website's traffic. (Submitted by Deb Perelman)

Perelman said she's seen "a summary or a chunk of my own recipe in the AI blurb that you have in the top of search results."

"It's honestly shocking to me that somebody can publish my work ... without my permission," said Perelman, who is now pursuing AI-limiting protections for her site.

Google recently reimagined the search box for the first time in 25 years, with "AI Mode," a conversational back-and-forth that's similar to using ChatGPT or other AI chatbots. This Google function has surpassed a billion monthly users .

This screen grab shows the landing page for Google's AI Mode. (Nora Young)

Beyond that, Google is also prioritizing extensive AI summaries over links to websites — the result being that people increasingly don't need to leave Google's main page to get an answer.

Similarly, you can rely on Claude, ChatGPT or other LLM chatbots to provide answers, recommend products or take on more complex tasks, like creating an itinerary for a trip.

It's convenient, but it means big challenges for site creators who rely on human traffic. The web is being fundamentally reoriented to accommodate the bots that scrape websites for the information we seek.

Websites for machines as well as humans

Human web traffic is declining. Data from Cloudflare, a U.S. company that provides a range of internet services for websites and apps, found declines in human traffic across retail, software, IT and finance websites. Some hardest hit categories declined by up to 40 per cent between June 2025 and April 2026.

"The biggest impact is … machines going to read your content," said Hamzah Khadim, co-founder of Toronto-based internet marketing service Logik Digital .

Khadim argues that as search has moved "from keywords to conversations," the main goal for any website is not turning up in a list of links but being part of an AI's answer.

Logik Digital has long specialized in SEO (search engine optimization), so that websites turn up in search results, but it's now also focused on GEO (generative engine optimization). That means adding specific information that both indicates a site's credibility and answers the questions a user is likely to ask AI.

Sometimes, that means adding a lot of text to a website — for example, in its "About Us" section.

"People aren't gonna necessarily read all of that, but AI definitely will," Khadim said. "And it'll help establish trust."

The AI chatbot ChatGPT is shown on a smartphone in Mulhouse, eastern France. (Sebastien Bozon/AFP/Getty Images)

Getting paid for content and for the cost of scraping

While many independent content creators monetize their content on social media apps, through moves like brand partnerships, a lot of websites rely on selling ads or subscriptions to fund their content. So what happens if website visitors are AI bots and not humans?

Mark Surman, the president of Mozilla, best known for the Firefox browser, is concerned that "if those incentives to create original, creative, independent content disappear, does content just come from big and powerful companies, or from governments, or from AI itself?"

Even if a publisher is content to let AI have content for free and doesn't rely on advertising, there are real costs associated with AI accessing web content.

Wikipedia is one of the most-visited websites in the world. Lane Becker is president of Wikimedia Enterprise, which makes Wikipedia content accessible to organizations at scale. From an access-to-information perspective, Becker is enthusiastic about AI spreading Wikipedia's content.

Wikipedia articles are free for anyone to access, but the server infrastructure providing that content costs Wikipedia (or any website) a tiny bit of money. The sheer volume of requests from bots means that can really add up.

Lane Becker, president of Wikimedia Enterprise, which operates Wikipedia, says just one bot can click on 50 articles in under a second. (Submitted by Wikimedia Foundation)

Becker says just one bot can click on 50 articles in under a second.

"It's easy for one robot to show up and say, 'Hey, I want to scoop every single page out of every single Wikipedia [edition] and every single language, and I'm going to do it in under half an hour.'"

So Wikimedia Enterprise has deals with a number of AI companies — including Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta — to pay for direct, bulk access to Wikipedia's data.

A new deal for the AI-native web

Other media companies may start pushing back, too, if the decline in web traffic continues. According to reporting by the Wall Street Journal , Reddit and some other prominent publishers are considering cutting off or changing their relationship with Google.

USA Today's CEO recently said the "traditional Google search business model is dead … that traffic is declining … so we are going to be in a position soon where we have to block Google." He seemed to signal a willingness to forego showing up in Google search results at all.

But hope remains for a model that would preserve the open web and its diversity of voices.

For Deb Perelman, AI summaries miss something you can only get from the individual perspectives of creators.

"The context of a recipe is really important," she said, arguing "you're not going to get that from a blurb on top of a search result that has been extracted, perhaps correctly, perhaps incorrectly, from the actual recipe."

World.title: ''Tis but a flesh wound': Montana man hikes 6 hours impaled by trekking pole
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

David Cifaldi, an emergency room nurse, says he chose to hike off Montana's Granite Peak after a trekking pole pierced his torso because he did not believe his injuries were life-threatening — and a helicopter rescue could have cost tens of thousands of dollars.

David Cifaldi and his two hiking companions were crossing Montana's ominous Froze-to-Death Plateau and approaching the top of the state's highest peak when their adventure took a bizarre and dangerous turn: Cifaldi slipped and impaled himself on his trekking pole as he fell.

The 112-centimetre steel-tipped pole passed through the flesh beneath Cifaldi's left arm, missing any vital organs, and protruded from his back. After conferring with his friends — and considering the high cost of a helicopter rescue — Cifaldi knew who would save him: himself.

"I was like, 'We've got to get off this mountain.' And they're both like, 'I don't know about that,'" Cifaldi said of his friends' initial reaction. "I'm pretty confident this is outside my chest wall. 'Tis but a flesh wound."

The 32-year-old nurse, who works in wound care at a hospital in Billings, Mont., did a self-assessment. He was alert. There was little pain or blood. And the pole wasn't moving. The group used a satellite-based communication device, a Garmin inReach, to contact local authorities and inform them of their plan to self-rescue.

Then they started hiking out. They carefully descended from the plateau along an unmarked route, navigating through boulders and snowfields before bushwhacking their way to an established trail.

After more than six hours in which they travelled about 16 kilometres and descended roughly 1,500 metres, the group reached a trailhead where one of them, Cifaldi's friend Jesse Ross, had parked a vehicle.

"The only reason it was possible at all was his confidence," Ross recalled. "Who are we to say anything? He's the medical person. Our job is just to support at that point."

David Cifaldi being treated at St. Vincent Regional Hospital in Billings, Mont. after he impaled himself with a trekking pole while on a hike on July 20. (David Cifaldi/Jessee Ross/The Associated Press)

Cifaldi had long wanted to climb Granite Peak. At 3,900 metres, Montana's tallest mountain is prone to unpredictable weather including dangerous lightning storms and bitter cold. Hundreds of people annually try to reach the rocky summit; many come up short. In 2019, authorities said a 65-year-old Minnesota man who was an experienced climber fell about 45 metres to his death after reaching nearly the top of Granite Peak with his son.

As Cifaldi and his companions started hiking out, the pole awkwardly sticking out of his side, Stillwater County Search and Rescue team commander Ty Williams monitored the group's progress via a dispatcher who took calls from the group.

The first call came in at 9:44 a.m. local time on July 20, right after Cifaldi impaled himself. At 1:30 p.m. the trio said they were getting closer to the trailhead and to let the nearest hospital know they were coming, Williams said.

"There was no danger to anybody else. He didn't want our help and so we're not going to essentially violate his rights or go against his wishes by forcing our help on him," Williams said.

Mystic Lake is seen from the Phantom Creek Trail in the Beartooth Mountains on July 20 near Roscoe, Mont. (David Cifaldi/The Associated Press)

By about 3:30 p.m. the hikers were in Ross's vehicle headed to the nearest clinic, Cifaldi said.

When they arrived, they were told Cifaldi needed more advanced treatment in Billings. So they got back in Ross's truck and kept driving to the hospital where he works, St. Vincent Regional Hospital.

Doctors removed the pole, bandaged him up and Cifaldi was back at work this week.

"I think 99 times out of a hundred I would make the same decision," Cifaldi said as he sat in Ross's front yard in Billings.

"Search and rescue coming to help you is free. The flight's not. That was a factor in me deciding to self-rescue. But the fact that I had two experienced great friends with me and we had the ability to contact search and rescue if something went wrong made that a lot more of an easy decision."

World.title: U.S. FCC approves giant space mirror to deliver 'sunlight on demand.' Here are the implications
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite hundreds of public comments opposing a giant space mirror that would shine a beam of light roughly five kilometres wide back down to Earth, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC), has given it the green light.

The company building the space mirror, Reflect Orbital, is touting its proposal as "sunlight on demand," which could be used for any number of reasons, it says, such as agriculture, solar farms or for search and rescue.

Astronomers and other groups are sounding the alarm about the project, citing numerous reasons, including the threat to species dependent on a pristine night sky, the threat to important astronomical research and more.

"This harm could include damage to sensitive research telescope equipment, potential flash-blinding of pilots and drivers and — as Reflect Orbital stated in its own FCC filings — potential permanent eye damage to anyone looking through a mid-sized telescope," the American Astronomical Society said in a statement .

The FCC said that those concerns are beyond their scope, as they only regulate communications by radio, television, wire and satellite.

So who does regulate where, how and when a giant five-kilometre swath of light can be used? What's stopping someone from paying potentially tens of thousands of dollars for an hour of reflected sunlight at their home? Does that mean neighbours have to endure disruption to their sleep or nightly routines?

Reflect Orbital aims to have more than 50,000 satellites in orbit by 2035. (Screenshot/Reflect Orbital)

While the Reflect Orbital approval is for one satellite, the company proposes launching a whopping 50,000 by 2035.

And this is on top of the millions of satellite proposed by SpaceX and other companies like Blue Origin, which will add to the thousands of satellites already crowding Earth's orbit.

'Far from unregulated'

Internationally, the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) deals with all aspects related to space, including its applications and space law.

More than 115 countries (referred to as "states") have signed the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. There are several articles in the treaty, but overall the message is that countries are responsible for the peaceful use of outer space and that countries must take into account other "corresponding interests of all other States Parties," a UNOOSA representative told CBC News via email, when asked about Reflect Orbital's project.

"So the honest answer to 'how legal is it' is that it is not a yes or no question. Nothing in the treaties prohibits placing a reflective object in orbit (Article I, freedom to use outer space). But such an activity is very far from unregulated," UNOOSA said. "It is subject to due regard and consultation obligations owed to every other State. And any State that considers itself affected is entitled to raise it."

LISTEN | A company wants to sell sunlight after dark. Here's why astronomers are worried: Quirks and Quarks 8:35 A company wants to sell sunlight after dark. Here’s why astronomers are worried A company called Reflect Orbital plans to launch thousands of mirrors into space starting with its first as early as next year, to provide customers with extra sunlight at night. The company says the additional light could help power solar arrays, aid in search and rescue missions, and more. But astronomers are concerned that this practice will interfere with their work, and may also be harmful to human health, animals, and the environment.

International space law expert Cassandra Steer said that it could be up to countries to make some sort of laws around the type of reflected sunlight service that Reflect Orbital is aiming to provide.

"I think that there are environmental protection regulations within Canada where the federal government could say, actually, we are not going to allow anybody in Canada to legally purchase and use these services, because we're going to say it's harmful to their environment," Steer said. "How are we going to enforce it is a different question."

Ram Jakhu, professor emeritus at McGill University's faculty of law, agreed that regulations are needed.

"I think, in five, 10 years, you will see something done about it, not only talk and talk," he said.

"The whole issue of night sky, light pollution, these things, they are being addressed, but nothing has been decided yet. But I think there will be serious concerns and discussion, something we can see in the near future. The night sky is very important. But … astronomers are not a major player in geopolitics."

The UNOOSA also said that of the 193 member states that roughly 50 have their own national space legislation, and that, as Steer said, it could be up to individual countries to set their own regulations.

In response to a question about potential regulations, a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital said, "we recognize that responsible deployment at scale requires clear rules. We welcome oversight and want to play an active role in shaping it. We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them."

'Dark and quiet skies'

UNOOSA's Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) is already working with International Astronomical Union (IAU), and other international observatories on the "protection of dark and quiet skies," and space-based illumination is included in that, UNOOSA said.

Piero Benvenuti, director of the IAU's Centre for the Protection of Dark and Quiet Sky from Satellite Constellation Interference (CPS), said that they have been speaking with Reflect Orbital from the outset.

The company says on its website that they "maintain strict exclusion zones for astronomy and sensitive environments." But Benvenuti said that, once the CPS showed Reflect Orbital a map of all the observatories contributing to astronomical research, they seemed surprised.

"They probably didn't know that the number of telescopes, including the amateur astronomer telescopes, are huge and are dispersed everywhere in the world," he said.

In the email to CBC News, the company spokesperson said, "We’re an industry member of the International Astronomical Union’s Centre for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky, and feedback from the astronomical community has materially informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans."

They also noted that they are "committed to ongoing dialogue with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other interested stakeholders."

CPS doesn't have regulatory oversight, but is working with astronomers and satellite providers on reducing the impact satellite constellations will have on the night sky.

WATCH | Light pollution is getting noticeably worse, study confirms: Light pollution is getting noticeably worse, study confirms | Duration 4:16 A new study that analyzed more than 50,000 crowdsourced observations over 12 years has confirmed that light pollution is getting noticeably worse, brightening the night sky by roughly seven to 10 per cent each year.

"The other thing they didn't consider is that it is not just the direct illumination of the telescope," Benvenuti said. "They are shining through the atmosphere, their reflected sunlight, and that is illuminating the atmosphere, and the light, obviously, is diffused by particle and by scattering."

He also noted that they are working with Reflect Orbital to study the effects of the first satellite, Earendil-1.

"What we are negotiating with them is a campaign of observations. So, we want to quantify the effect of this prototype. And then once we have these measures, these data, we will verify the simulation and, you know, check if the simulations are correct."

And if they are?

"They're saying we want to launch 50,000 mirrors by 2035," Benvenuti said. "That would be catastrophic for astronomy, that is clear."
