Sheinbaum said her government wants former Peruvian Prime Minister Betssy Chávez — who has been at the Mexican Embassy in Lima since being granted asylum — to be given “safe passage” to come to Mexico, adding “we’re going to see how this develops.” 🇲🇽 🇵🇪 No rupture desired: Despite Mexico’s continued objection to the 2022 removal of former President Pedro Castillo, which Sheinbaum has previously called a “coup,” Sheinbaum said “we obviously don’t want a rupture of relations.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

Mexico’s bilateral relationships with the United States and Peru were among the most important topics discussed at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference.

Mexico’s relationships with both countries are currently strained for different reasons.

On the Mexico-United States trade front, U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday added his voice to the ongoing USMCA negotiations, and, unsurprisingly, it wasn’t to offer an endorsement of the three-way trade pact that superseded NAFTA during his first term as president.

Mexican Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard was on hand at today’s mañanera to offer a response to the latest remarks from Trump, who said in January that he didn’t “really care” about the USMCA and that the United States doesn’t need Mexican and Canadian products.

The similar remarks the U.S. president made on Tuesday came four weeks after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. government hadn’t agreed “to renew the USMCA in its current form.”

Beyond Ebrard’s response to Trump’s latest USMCA comments, today’s mañanera was significant as Sheinbaum indicated that a rapprochement between Mexico and Peru might not be far off.

Peru broke diplomatic relations with Mexico last November, but the South American country now has a new president, providing the opportunity for a clean slate in the bilateral relationship, even though the Mexican and Peruvian governments sit on opposite sides of the political spectrum.

Ebrard responds to Trump’s latest USMCA remarks

A reporter asked Ebrard his opinion about Trump’s remarks on Tuesday about the USMCA.

During an interview with Fox News, Trump was asked whether he was looking to update the trilateral trade pact.

“I don’t care. I mean I don’t really want to. I’d rather be independent. Here’s the thing — Mexico and Canada need us. We don’t need them. The deal is important for them. It’s not important for us,” the U.S. president said.

Ebrard pointed out that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer was recently in Mexico and declared that the Mexican government is working “very closely” with his team as they seek to settle differences over trade, including ones related to U.S. tariffs on Mexican products such as vehicles and steel, and to rules of origin for the North American automotive sector.

He noted that in “the overall table of countries, Mexico has the best [trade] deal” with the United States.

That was a reference to the tariffs the U.S. imposes on Mexican goods compared to its duties on products from other countries around the world. Ebrard said that Mexico’s tariff advantage “explains why our exports to the United States have grown.”

The economy minister also highlighted that Mexico is the world’s largest importer of U.S. goods.

“We’re the number 1 customer,” he said.

Ebrard subsequently appeared to downplay Trump’s remarks on Tuesday.

“Obviously there are warnings every week, there are a lot of things. We’re going to see what happens in the coming months but as of today we’re doing well,” he said.

Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum said that the United States has been “setting a new vision” for trade since Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025.

Despite increased protectionism from the U.S., the fact remains that Mexico “is an extremely important trade partner for the United States,” the president said.

“… Our economies are very integrated because of the many years of free trade,” Sheinbaum said.

Foreign Minister speaks to new president of Peru

Sheinbaum told reporters that Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco had spoken to Keiko Fujimori, who was sworn in as president of Peru on Tuesday.

The call between Velasco and Fujimori came almost nine months after the government of Peru announced its decision to sever diplomatic relations with Mexico in light of a former Peruvian prime minister accused of rebellion being granted asylum at the Mexican Embassy in Lima.

On Wednesday morning, Sheinbaum said that her government wants “the person in our embassy” in Lima, former Prime Minister Betssy Chávez, to be given “safe passage” so that she can come to Mexico.

“We’re going to see how this develops,” she said.

Chávez served as prime minister under former Peruvian President Pedro Castillo, who was removed from office by the Peruvian Congress in late 2022, angering then Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who put diplomatic relations with Peru “on hold” and issued a statement with other Latin American leaders expressing “profound concern” at the treatment of Castillo.

Sheinbaum said that Fujimori, whose deceased father was president of Peru from 1990 to 2000, “knows that we have a position related to President Castillo.”

Last September, she described the 2022 ousting of Castillo as a “coup.”

Sheinbaum said that “beyond” the Mexican government’s dissatisfaction with the treatment of Castillo, “we obviously don’t want a rupture of relations” with Peru.

“Within that framework we’re talking [with the Peruvian government] and we hope to be able to provide more news soon,” she said.

World.title: MND Local: Miss Universe Mexico and what else is new in Los Cabos during the second half of 2026
World.content:
The reigning Miss Universe is from Mexico. Fátima Bosch, a native of Tabasco, qualified for the “Super Bowl” of beauty pageants by winning Miss Universe Mexico in September 2025, and was then crowned with the South Sea pearl-adorned “Lumière de l’Infini” tiara as the 74th Miss Universe in Bangkok, Thailand, in November of last year, beating out Thai runner-up Praveenar Singh after a highly publicized bullying episode by a pageant offcial.

Bosch’s reign won’t officially come to an end until Nov. 26, 2026, when she crowns her successor in San Juan, Puerto Rico. But in the meantime, she’s helping to publicize this year’s Miss Universe Mexico, the competition from which the next national contender will emerge. Los Cabos will be the official site of the Aug. 29 event, Bosch recently announced on the Mexican morning television show, “Sale el Sol,” with Corazón Cabo Resort & Spa on Playa El Médano in Cabo San Lucas named as the host.

Miss Universe Mexico and other upcoming events in Cabo San Lucas

Cape cities San José del Cabo and Cabo San Lucas each crown pageant queens at their annual fiestas tradicionales. But Miss Universe Mexico brings a national spotlight to the region, and to Baja California Sur’s contestant this year: Selene Zazueta of La Paz, who also represented the state at the Mexicana Universal pageant in 2023. That, incidentally, was the last Mexicana Universal to act as a qualifier for Miss Universe, as a new organization — Miss Universe Mexico, backed by Raúl Rocha Cantú — was subsequently recognized.

Contestants representing all 32 states are expected to begin arriving in Los Cabos in mid-August for filming and promotional shoots, as well as a preliminary competition featuring interviews and swimwear and evening gown assessments, before the actual event is broadcast live on Aug. 29. For those unable to attend, Mexico’s Imagen Televisión has the broadcast rights.

Miss Universe Mexico will cap a busy month — especially by “low season” standards in Los Cabos — as it follows closely on the heels of two other high-profile events: the 10th anniversary edition of the ATP 250 Los Cabos Tennis Open, which is taking place July 25 to Aug. 1; and the Bisbee’s East Cape Offshore (ECO), the first of three annual Bisbee’s sponsored fishing tournaments in Los Cabos featuring million dollar plus prize pools, with the most lucrative of these, the Black and Blue and Los Cabos Offshore, following in October.

The ECO is a major event in its own right, however. The 2026 edition is scheduled for this week, July 28 to Aug. 1 in Buenavista, with the tournament aiming to top last year’s prize pool of US $1.52 million.

The next resort to open in Los Cabos

By the time the Los Cabos Tennis Open and Bisbee’s East Cape Offshore wrap up, a new resort will also have opened in Los Cabos. That’s Amanvari from Aman, an ultra-luxury brand noted for its intimate and exclusive accommodations in gorgeous natural settings. Amanvari, which officially opens Aug. 1, qualifies on all counts, with only 18 casitas — each with a private heated pool — available at Costa Palmas, the La Ribera-based development that’s also home to the East Cape’s other luxury option: Four Seasons Resort Los Cabos at Costa Palmas.

It’s the first Aman property ever to open in Mexico, and at US $3,000 per night and up, immediately slots in among the very top tier of local ultra-luxury resorts. Restaurants specializing in Mexican, Italian and Japanese cuisine will offer first-class dining experiences, while the on-site spa specializes in Mexico’s traditional sweat lodge-style temezcal therapies.

Other scheduled resort openings in 2026

When the St. Regis Los Cabos at Quivira was first announced in 2017, the estimated open date for the resort and residences project was early 2021. After the many delays that have followed, any forecasts at this point — such as the late 2026 timeline offered by the Los Cabos Tourism Board — must be taken with several grains of salt.

Soho House Los Cabos, the brand’s second private club-style resort in Mexico following the opening of a property in Mexico City in 2023, is still expected to open by November in Cabo del Sol, with 15 available accommodations (in 12 casas and 3 casonas), plus on-site residences, a 50-meter swimming pool, spa, seafood restaurant and beach club. Soho Club also boasts a “200-meter private beach,” although this is a misnomer, since all beaches in Mexico are, by law, public.

The 301-room resort Grand Hyatt Los Cabos, Golf and Spa at Oleada on the Pacific Coast of Cabo San Lucas, meanwhile, is also estimating a late 2026 opening (in December), by which time the development’s new golf course will also be playable.

The next golf course to open in Los Cabos

The Ernie Els-designed Oleada Golf Links has opened for preview play and remains on track to officially premiere in November. It’s the first course in Mexico for “The Big Easy,” a four-time major champion who has now designed over a dozen worldwide, and according to him, easily the best natural site he has had to work with.

Mario Navarro, a Ciudad Juárez native who played collegiately at the University of Texas El Paso and who has worked for several years in Los Cabos at Querencia and Cabo del Sol, including helping to organize the annual Cabo Collegiate tournament, has been announced as the golf pro at Oleada.

Campo Alto and Legacy Club updates

Campo Alto at Querencia, the second design at the upscale residential community from Tom Fazio, is also scheduled to open by the end of the year. Tiger Woods’ Legacy Club at Diamante, however — his third project at the Cabo San Lucas development, following El Cardonal, host of Los Cabos’ only PGA-sponsored tournament, and the 12-hole Oasis Short Course — has seen its opening date pushed back to early 2027.

When these three open, the inventory of local golf courses will increase from 18 to 21. The Campo Alto and Legacy Club courses will be private, while Oleada is expected to “initially allow limited outside play,” per Forbes, before transitioning to a private course for residents and resort guests (both those at Grand Hyatt Los Cabos, Golf and Spa, and the Conrad Los Cabos, anticipated to open at Oleada in 2027).

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Made in Mexico: How the CIA shaped art and culture in Mexico
World.content:
For months now, the same argument has played out in the press on both sides of the border: American voices floating military intervention against the cartels, Mexican officials answering back that nobody sorts out our house but us. This year alone, from The Atlantic to CNN to El País to President Claudia Sheinbaum’s own morning press conferences, the question of where cooperation ends and interference begins has been hard to avoid, sharpened by the Trump administration’s indictment of 10 Mexican officials on cartel-related charges.

It’s not a new argument, even if the vocabulary feels urgent. In security terms, it’s close to a century old. Carlos Pérez Ricart, who studied at El Colegio de México and later worked as a postdoctoral researcher and professor at Oxford, spent years combing archives to write “Cien Años de Espías y Drogas,” a chronicle of the U.S. narcotics agents who have operated inside Mexico for 100 years, and the uncomfortably close relationships some built with the cartels they were sent to dismantle.

The CIA and the ‘shaping’ of Mexican art and culture

There’s a quieter chapter to that history, one that never needed a wiretap because it operated in plain sight, dressed up as good taste. For roughly two decades, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) worked to shape Mexican culture from the inside — funding fellowships for painters, bankrolling literary magazines and cultural supplements and quietly steering the museums that decided whose work counted. It ran through galleries instead of embassies, critics instead of attachés, paintbrushes instead of sidearms.

Call it interference, call it soft power, call it the ordinary behavior of a powerful neighbor with strong opinions about its own image — it is what it is, and it has a long paper trail.

The playbook was built at home first

The method was tested in New York first. Thomas Braden, who later ran the CIA’s cultural operations division, spent the late 1940s as executive secretary of the Museum of Modern Art under Nelson Rockefeller — at various points MoMA’s board president, wartime head of U.S. intelligence for Latin America, and the man who called Abstract Expressionism, apparently without irony, “free enterprise painting.” Braden joined the CIA in 1950 and later admitted, without much regret, that covertly funding cultural organizations abroad had largely been his idea. Writing in the Saturday Evening Post in 1967, after journalists had already exposed the program, he argued that asking Congress to approve it would have gone about as well as asking the John Birch Society to endorse Medicare.

Rockefeller himself helped send the museum’s touring show “The New American Painting” through nearly every major European capital in 1958-59, with no mention that it doubled as a project of the CIA-created Congress for Cultural Freedom. MoMA already had history in Mexico by then: Its Latin American collection dates to 1935, and its 1940 show “Twenty Centuries of Mexican Art” had Mexico’s own institutional backing.

The local front: A magazine in disguise

By the early 1960s, Fidel Castro’s revolution had energized a generation of Mexican writers and intellectuals, and Washington’s anxiety had a specific address: ¡Siempre! and its cultural supplement, La Cultura en México, edited by Fernando Benítez — described in the CIA’s own internal paperwork as sympathetic to Havana. A memo dated June 24, 1963, proposed a rival magazine, code-named Crítica.

It launched in December 1964 as Diálogos, co-edited by philosopher and poet Ramón Xirau alongside a man calling himself “Enrique P. López.” In reality, CIA officer Edward G. Tichborn, operating under a cover so deep his real name barely surfaces in the record. Xirau was chosen, the agency’s own files show, for being too intelligent to be a Marxist and for a Rockefeller Foundation fellowship that already had him in the right rooms. He believed his American benefactor was a sympathetic lawyer with money to spend. He never learned otherwise.

The magazine ran for two decades, eventually finding a home at El Colegio de México, and published Octavio Paz, Carlos Fuentes, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. It was built, in part, by people who never knew what they were part of.

Painting over politics: The night the Salón Esso exploded

If Diálogos shows how the method worked in print, the Salón Esso shows how it played out in a gallery: in public, with fists. By the mid-1950s, Mexican muralism — the state-sponsored, politically committed art of Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros — had become an irritant to U.S. interests for the same reason it had once been celebrated at home. It was explicitly revolutionary. Around the same time, Abstract Expressionism and its European cousin, Informalism, offered something the Escuela Mexicana didn’t: an art without an obvious political message, easy to present as pure, apolitical freedom of expression.

Art historian Shifra Goldman argued, in “Contemporary Mexican Painting in a Time of Change,” that the shift was no accident of taste. She pointed to the CIA and USIS’s documented involvement in cultural programming, and to the OAS’s Visual Arts Unit, run by Cuban-born critic José Gómez Sicre, as a vehicle for promoting abstraction over social realism. Standard Oil’s Mexican subsidiary, Goldman noted, sponsored the very competition that bore its name: the Salón Esso.

The Esso salon, held at the Museo de Arte Moderno on Feb. 2, 1965, was an open competition for young painters and sculptors, with winners advancing to a showcase at the OAS in Washington. Only about 30% of the works submitted were figurative; the top prizes went to two abstract paintings, by Fernando García Ponce and Lilia Carrillo, and García Ponce’s own brother sat on the jury.

A fistfight over art

The opening turned into a brawl. Muralist loyalists confronted Tamayo, the García Ponce brothers and José Luis Cuevas — mocked for years as having sold out to the OAS ever since Gómez Sicre sponsored his first solo show in Washington in 1954. Writer Raquel Tibol recalled one socialite fleeing the scrum in her mink coat, taunting that the communists had nothing left but hammers and sickles. Cuevas and critic Francisco Icaza came to blows. Tamayo used the moment to declare that Mexican art no longer needed nationalism as a shield.

Whether the Salón Esso was a CIA operation with a paintbrush or an art-world grudge match that happened to have American money in the room is exactly what Goldman’s critics still argue about, and that ambiguity may be the most honest way to leave it. What isn’t in dispute is that the money, the institutions and the timing all pointed the same direction.

Fernando Gamboa, a senior National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBA) official, spent the 1950s and 1960s denouncing American cultural influence and dismissing abstraction as decorative and second-rate. In 1972, he was named director of the Museo de Arte Moderno — the same institution at the center of the Salón Esso affair — and defended the art he had spent two decades attacking.

What this is and isn’t

None of this means every Mexican abstract painter was a witting or unwitting asset. Artists like Gunther Gerzso and Lilia Carrillo pursued serious, original work with little to do with Washington’s Cold War anxieties. Goldman’s thesis remains contested among art historians, not a settled verdict. What the documented record does show is that, for roughly two decades, U.S. agencies and U.S.-linked institutions treated Mexican museums, magazines and art prizes as worth a memo, a grant or a quiet word to the right curator.

Three vignettes, three decades: Braden built the model in a New York museum, Xirau ran it out of a Mexico City magazine office without knowing it, and Gamboa ended up defending it from the director’s chair of the very institution where it once nearly came to blows. None of it required a single mastermind, just money, prestige and institutions patient enough to let the shift happen slowly.

Pérez Ricart’s century of spies worked the border and the cartels; this article worked the galleries and the newsstands. Neither settles the argument still playing out in this year’s headlines, over where cooperation ends and interference begins. That’s a question with room for real disagreement. What both suggest is that the motive shifts by the decade: sometimes ideology, sometimes economics and sometimes simply a tighter grip on the region. In the years this piece covers, it came down to something as specific as whose paintings got hung on the wall.

Three of Four Quarters Down

Canada’s real GDP contracted in three of the last four quarters through Q1 2026, meeting the textbook definition of a technical recession.

BMO Economics reports the economy shrank 0.1 per cent annualised in the first quarter, deepening the sense of fragility.

Inflation Holds, Central Bank Waits

USA – Geopolitics (Iran Negotiations)

Diplomacy and Deterrence

President Trump announced that negotiations with Iran are ‘back on,’ signalling a diplomatic channel alongside military tensions.

The U.S. claimed it intercepted what it called an Iranian ‘surprise attack’ on American forces, keeping regional risk elevated.

Canada feels fragile and economically besieged, grappling with a technical recession and new U.S. tariff blows, while the U.S. projects resilient growth and structural confidence.

The Bigger Picture North America enters the final days of July with two very different economic moods. Canada is absorbing the psychological blow of a technical recession — three contracting quarters out of four — while staring down fresh 35 per cent U.S. tariffs that make the path to recovery steeper. The United States, by contrast, carries structural confidence from resilient growth, yet its trade escalation with its northern neighbour and stubborn inflation keep the outlook complicated rather than fully optimistic. Across the Atlantic, the Middle East remains a wild card. Trump’s mixed signals on Iran — diplomatic talks ‘back on’ even as the U.S. reports intercepting an attack — inject uncertainty into energy prices that both central banks must watch.

Ukraine – Russian Missile and Drone Barrage Kills Civilians Across Multiple Cities

Saturation attack overwhelms defences

Russian forces launched overnight missile and drone attacks on at least five Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, killing several civilians and injuring dozens. People were reported trapped under rubble after residential buildings were struck in the coordinated barrage.

Ukrainian air defences were activated nationwide but could not fully repel the saturation attack. The mood across the country is one of grief and defiance, as the nation steels itself for more strikes while pressing allies for additional air defence systems.

Netherlands – Government Apologises for Forced Infant Adoptions Between 1956 and 1984

Acknowledging historical injustice

The Dutch government issued a formal apology for forced infant adoptions that occurred between 1956 and 1984, acknowledging the profound suffering caused. The apology promises the establishment of redress mechanisms for victims.

Thousands of children were taken from their mothers, often unmarried women, and placed for adoption without proper consent. The mood is one of solemn reflection and a sense of belated justice settling over the country.

Europe is on edge today, torn between the grim toll of Russia’s missile barrage on Ukrainian cities and the relentless pressure of a climate crisis made visceral by heatwaves, wildfires, and drownings.

Grief and defiance characterise the mood in Ukraine as the nation presses its allies for more protection. In a moment of grim historical reckoning, the Dutch government formally apologised for decades of forced infant adoptions, acknowledging the thousands of mothers and children affected between 1956 and 1984. The promised redress mechanisms offer a path toward healing for victims. —Maritime Flare-up The Philippines formally rejected Chinese academic claims over an island province near Taiwan, escalating diplomatic friction. —Flood Tragedy The Southeast Asian monsoon death toll has surpassed 1,200 people, with catastrophic flooding overwhelming regional relief systems. —Press Freedom Award-winning Cambodian investigative journalist Mech Dara remains detained following his reporting on online scam compounds. —Taiwan Warning A senior Taiwanese official cautioned that China’s escalating patrol activity risks creating a dangerous new status quo. —Border Talks Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim and Thailand’s Anutin Charnvirakul met to discuss a fishing dispute and a special border economic zone.

Asia Intelligence Brief July 30 — Asia faces a morning of raw nerves and deep grief, as diplomatic fires over the Taiwan Strait burn alongside a historic political rupture in Seoul. The region feels governed by crisis management, its public mood swinging from wary defiance on the water to exhaustion and anger at home.

Taiwan, Philippines, China – Maritime Tensions Surge

Philippines Pushes Back on Sovereignty Claims

The Philippine government formally dismissed assertions by Chinese academics claiming historical sovereignty over an island province near Taiwan. The rejection adds a fresh diplomatic spark to already simmering regional waters.

The exchanges occur amid a broader pattern of increased presence by the People’s Liberation Army Navy in the region. This stand-off over historical claims is deepening anxiety among neighbours.

Taiwan Cautions Against a ‘New Status Quo’

Taiwan’s coast guard reported heightened Chinese patrol activity and organised visits by foreign legislators aboard its own vessels as a diplomatic counter-move. A senior Taiwanese official then issued a stark public warning that Beijing’s actions risk imposing a dangerous new reality.

The mood in Taipei is resolute but deeply wary, with officials actively working to show that the self-governed island will not passively accept a shift in the long-standing balance. The psychological pressure is being met with a show of international solidarity.

Malaysia and Thailand – Neighbours Hold Border Talks

Looking for Calm and Cooperation

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim of Malaysia and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul met for bilateral discussions focused on cooling a fisheries dispute. Their agenda also included a proposal for a special border economic zone, aiming to create shared prosperity.

The diplomatic engagement seeks a sliver of stability against a backdrop of domestic crises for both leaders, particularly the immense strain on Thai public services. It was a practical demonstration of regional neighbours attempting to manage tensions through dialogue.

A senior Taiwanese official warned that China’s escalating maritime actions risk creating a new and dangerous status quo in the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters.

The Bigger Picture Asia enters Thursday with its institutions being tested to their absolute limits, from the historic impeachment verdict in Seoul to overstretched rescue boats in flooded Thai towns. The public mood swings wildly between anger at authorities, deep grief for monumental human losses, and a wary vigilance over disputed seas. The most immediate diplomatic flashpoint is in the Taiwan Strait, where a Chinese academic claim has been met with a swift Philippine rejection and a pointed Taiwanese warning that Beijing is unilaterally forging a new and dangerous status quo. It is a calculated war of words on the water, watched nervously across the region. Behind the geopolitics, a staggering human toll from more than 1,200 flood deaths demands attention, with suffering in cut-off areas of Myanmar bordering on despair. This conflict of crises leaves the entire region feeling that it is surviving events, rather than shaping them.

Asia Intelligence Brief July 30: What We Are Watching

Today – South Korea begins its 60-day countdown to a snap election while Taiwan closely monitors Chinese patrol patterns.

This week – Any new Philippine response to Chinese claims and further international reaction to the journalist’s detention in Cambodia.

Economic strain and constitutional showdowns add to the restless mood, with households in Egypt and South Africa feeling the pinch of weak governance.

Sudan – ICC Investigation Breakthrough

Prosecutors Link Atrocities to National Command

International Criminal Court prosecutors have made a significant breakthrough in connecting atrocities in Darfur directly to Sudan’s national-level leadership, a senior ICC official told Reuters on Thursday.

The development allows investigators to trace field-level violence up the chain of command, bringing the prospect of high-level accountability closer for a population described as horrified and exhausted by a brutal war.

DR Congo – Ebola Outbreak Worsens

Death Toll Reaches 1,405 as France Confirms Imported Case

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo continues to spiral, with total deaths reaching 1,405 out of roughly 3,200 reported cases, further deepening a mood of desperation and fear.

France recorded its first Ebola case in a healthcare worker returning from the country, raising international biosecurity alarms even as the DRC-Rwanda border reopened with strict health screening measures in place.

A continent stalked by violence and disease is simultaneously grappling with fragile institutions and the high cost of simply getting by.

Egypt – Urban Inflation Eases Slightly

June Rate Slips to 14.3 Per Cent

Egypt’s annual urban consumer inflation slowed to 14.3 per cent in June, down from 14.6 per cent in May, according to figures released by the statistics agency CAPMAS.

The modest cooling offers a small measure of relief in a country where economic pressures are a constant, low-grade fever, though the data arrives amid heated debates over monetary policy and subsidy reform.

Kenya – Government Appeals Cabinet Ruling

Court Declared Cabinet Unconstitutional on Gender Grounds

Kenya’s Parliament will appeal a court ruling that declared President William Ruto’s cabinet unconstitutional, arguing it fails to meet legal requirements for gender balance.

The defiant government stance sets up a direct institutional clash, asserting executive discretion and the separation of powers against a backdrop of a restless youth-led political awakening.

South Africa – Municipal Financial Crisis Deepens

Record Consultant Spend While Funding Frozen

South African municipalities spent a record 1.6 billion rand on consultants even as clean audit outcomes fell, intensifying a picture of deep local-government dysfunction.

Funding has been frozen for Johannesburg and dozens of other municipalities, stoking a fearful and angry mood on the streets as communities brace for worsening service delivery breakdowns.

The Bigger Picture Prosecutors have made a landmark breakthrough at the ICC, linking Darfur’s bloodshed to Sudan’s national leadership in a step towards command-responsibility charges. The DR Congo’s Ebola crisis crossed another grim threshold with 1,405 dead and a first imported case in France, widening a health emergency with global implications. Economic and institutional strains are deepening local anxieties, from Egypt’s inflation battle and Kenya’s cabinet standoff to a South African municipal spending scandal.

Africa Intelligence Brief July 30: What We Are Watching

Today – Africa Special Economic Zones Forum convenes in hybrid format, focusing on infrastructure, industrial parks, and regional trade.

This week – An Africa Health Financing Forum fellowship event runs alongside Nairobi financial inclusion innovation week on 5 August.

World.title: Latin America Nomad Visa Income: 2026 Cost Breakdown in US$
World.content:
Latin America · Immigration

Key Facts The spread is huge. The income floor ranges from about US$1,400 a month in Colombia to about US$4,400 in Mexico.

The income floor ranges from about US$1,400 a month in Colombia to about US$4,400 in Mexico. Cheapest entry. Colombia, Brazil and Chile sit near US$1,400–1,500 a month of foreign income.

Colombia, Brazil and Chile sit near US$1,400–1,500 a month of foreign income. Panama is annual. Its remote-worker visa asks US$36,000 a year and does not tax foreign income.

Its remote-worker visa asks US$36,000 a year and does not tax foreign income. Mexico costs more but leads somewhere. A higher bar, but a four-year path to permanent residency.

A higher bar, but a four-year path to permanent residency. Tax is the hidden cost. The number to earn is only half the story; where you become tax-resident is the other.

“Digital-nomad visa” is a loose label in Latin America, and the money each country actually asks for varies more than most guides admit — from around US$1,400 a month to US$36,000 a year. Here is a plain, side-by-side look at what you need to earn or show across seven hubs in 2026, and the tax catch behind each one.

The income you must prove for a Latin American nomad or residency visa ranges widely by country in 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What each visa asks in 2026

Country (visa) Income floor Max stay Tax note Colombia (Migrant Type V) ~US$1,400/mo up to 2 years tax-resident after 183 days Brazil (VITEM XIV) US$1,500/mo or US$18,000 saved 2 years tax-resident after 183 days Chile (temporary residence) ~US$1,500/mo (service contract) apply from abroad 183-day tax trap Argentina (Nómada Digital) ~US$2,000–2,500/mo (practical) up to 12 months DNI possible after 90 days Panama (Short-Stay Remote Worker) US$36,000/year up to 18 months territorial: foreign income untaxed Uruguay (remote-worker residency) case-by-case renewable tax holiday, now tightened Mexico (Residente Temporal) ~US$4,300–4,500/mo or ~US$73–75k saved up to 4 years, PR path US tax treaty since 1994

The cheaper tier: Colombia, Brazil, Chile

If the income floor is what matters most, the three most accessible hubs cluster around US$1,400 to US$1,500 a month of foreign income. Colombia’s Migrant Type V visa runs on roughly three times the local minimum wage, Brazil’s VITEM XIV asks US$1,500 a month or US$18,000 in savings, and Chile expects around US$1,500 a month, usually via a foreign service contract.

The catch is tax residence: spend more than 183 days in any of them and you generally become a tax resident, which is where planning matters more than the visa fee.

The middle: Argentina and Panama

Argentina publishes no statutory figure, but in practice applicants show about US$2,000 to US$2,500 a month; a 2026 protocol lets nomads obtain a DNI identity document after 90 days, which unlocks local banking. Panama frames its bar annually — US$36,000 a year — and, crucially, taxes only Panama-source income, so foreign earnings are left alone.

Panama’s territorial tax is the standout feature here: for many remote workers, the higher headline number buys a cleaner tax outcome.

Mexico: the highest bar, but a path to stay

Mexico has no dedicated nomad visa; remote workers use the Residente Temporal, whose solvency test is now pegged to the UMA (117.31 pesos, about US$6.70, a day). That works out to roughly US$4,300–4,500 a month in income or about US$73,000–75,000 in savings — the steepest floor on this list.

What you get for it is a four-year route that can convert to permanent residency, plus a US–Mexico tax treaty in force since 1994. It costs more up front but leads somewhere.

Uruguay: watch the tax holiday, not the income

Uruguay assesses remote-worker income case by case, so the headline is not the monthly figure but the tax holiday. Under the 2026 reform (Law 20.446), the long exemption on foreign income now requires either 183 days of presence, roughly US$2 million in property, or about US$100,000 into an approved innovation fund; those who do not qualify face a 12% tax on foreign income.

For higher-net-worth movers, Uruguay can still be very attractive; for a modest remote salary, the tax terms have tightened.

What the numbers don’t show

The income floor is only the entry ticket. The bigger variable is tax residence — most of these countries treat you as resident after 183 days — and whether foreign income is taxed, exempt or covered by a treaty.

US citizens carry their own rules everywhere: you still file, report foreign accounts under FBAR and FATCA, and can use the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (about US$132,900 in 2026). Figures here vary by consulate and exchange rate and change annually, so confirm each with the consulate and a local tax adviser. This is general information, not legal or tax advice.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Rio Scenarium If you only have one night in Rio, spend it inside this breathtaking three-floor antique warehouse in Lapa. It is the city’s most iconic samba and MPB house, mixing infectious live music with a crowd of locals, expats, and wide-eyed visitors. The energy, the decor, and the sheer scale make it unmissable, and Thursday is its gateway to the weekend.

Tonight at a Glance —Rio Scenarium (Lapa) The essential Rio night. Multi-floor antique palace with live samba and MPB. Best for a big, classic night out; tourist-friendly but authentic. Arrive by 21:30. —Lapa Arches Street Party (Centro) The pulsing street soul of Rio. Open-front bars, caipirinha kiosks, and spontaneous dancing on Av. Mem de Sá. Best for an affordable, messy, local Thursday warm-up. Arrive 22:00. —Rua Dias Ferreira (Leblon) Rio’s most polished bar strip. Upscale cocktails, wine bars, and a glamorous after-work crowd. Best for date night or a sophisticated start. Arrive 20:30. —Botafogo Bar Hub (Nelson Mandela/Voluntários) The hipster heartland. Craft beer, indie patios, and a young, creative crowd. Best for meeting locals in a laid-back scene. Arrive 21:00. —Ipanema Jazz & Bossa Lounges (General Osório) Sophisticated sips and smooth sounds. Bossa nova and jazz bars where you can actually hear the music. Best for a chilled, stylish evening. Arrive 21:00.

Tonight, Thursday, July 30, 2026, Rio de Janeiro breathes a sigh of relief as the weekend warm-up begins. The action spans the historic samba houses of Lapa, the polished cocktail dens of Leblon, and the hipster patios of Botafogo—start with street-side caipirinhas under the Lapa Arches and end in a live-music club that doesn’t close until 4 am.

What’s On Tonight

Live Samba & MPB Night (programming confirmed day-of on Instagram Stories) — at Rio Scenarium, 21:00 – 03:00. Thursday kicks off the weekend with the city’s most celebrated live music house. Multiple acts across three floors set the standard for a classic Carioca night.

Street Bar & Boteco Crawl — at Avenida Mem de Sá / Arcos da Lapa, 21:00 – 02:00. The Thursday warm-up sees crowds spilling out of bars onto the pedestrian strip. The vibe is noisy, cheap, and unpretentious—perfect for a newcomer to feel the city’s pulse.

After-Work Cocktails & Dinner Scene — at Rua Dias Ferreira, Leblon, 20:00 – 01:00. Leblon’s glitziest strip comes alive, packed with professionals and expats. A strong Thursday date-night energy with some of the best mixology in Zona Sul.

Hipster Bar & Patio Night — at Rua Nelson Mandela / Cobal do Humaitá, Botafogo, 20:00 – 01:00. A younger, artsy crowd gathers on the lively streets of Botafogo for craft drafts and casual conversation, a perfect low-pressure entry into the city’s social scene.

Bossa Nova & Jazz Evenings — at Lounge Bars around Praça General Osório, Ipanema, 21:00 – 00:00. Subtle, sophisticated sounds fill the intimate bars of Ipanema. Go for a quieter, romantic alternative to the samba chaos of Lapa.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm-up (20:00-22:00): Start in Leblon or Ipanema for an upscale dinner and cocktails. Rua Dias Ferreira is where the well-heeled Carioca begins the night.

Pre-peak (22:00-00:00): Head to Botafogo’s Rua Nelson Mandela for a more casual, indie bar crawl with a younger crowd, or dive straight into the Lapa street bars under the arches.

Late-night peak (00:00-04:00): The serious samba and MPB fans pile into Rio Scenarium or the Lapa street party peaks until 3 am. This is where the night hits its sweaty, musical stride.

Sunrise (04:00+): The hardcore migrate to all-night botecos or post-club street food in Lapa. Grab a pastel and a final beer before Ubering home.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba & Pagode — The percussive heartbeat of Rio. Live drums, cavaquinho, and call-and-response singing in historic heritage buildings or boisterous backstreet bars. Where: Rio Scenarium, Bar do Omar, Beco do Rato (Lapa)

MPB & Bossa Nova — Smooth, poetic, and melodic Brazilian popular music. Intimate settings where the songwriting takes center stage. Where: Toca do Vinícius, Vinícius Show Bar (Ipanema)

Electronic & House — Deep house and techno in dark, industrial spaces or open-air parties, often with a sophisticated, international crowd. Where: D-Edge (occasional pop-ups in Rio), Fosfobox (Copacabana)

Forró — Accordion-driven northeastern dance music. Sweaty, close-hold partner dancing, extremely accessible for beginners. Where: Feira de São Cristóvão (weekends), some Lapa clubs

Funk Carioca — Rio’s raw, bass-heavy baile sound. 150 bpm beats, often in favela parties or specific Zona Norte clubs; approach with a trusted local. Where: Baile da Gaiola (complex access), specific Zona Norte venues

Sertanejo — Brazilian country-pop. Huge in mainstream clubs, with singalong anthems about love and heartbreak. Where: Various large halls in Barra da Tijuca

Pick Your Night

Date night: Rua Dias Ferreira in Leblon. The street is essentially one long, glamorous restaurant row. Book a table for two, people-watch, and enjoy top-tier cocktails.

Solo and safe: Rio Scenarium in Lapa. It’s structured, secure, has a cloakroom, and uses a comanda system. You can enjoy the music alone without feeling out of place, and the security guards are visible.

Dance till sunrise: The Lapa Arches street circuit. Start at the kiosks on Av. Mem de Sá, follow the live music spilling from bars, and end up in an all-night samba joint like Beco do Rato.

Meet locals: Botafogo’s Rua Nelson Mandela and Cobal do Humaitá. Patio tables are communal by necessity, the beer is craft, and the crowd is a friendly mix of students and artists.

Chill and conversation: A live bossa nova bar near Praça General Osório in Ipanema. Tables are small, the music is low enough to talk, and the ambiance is pure Zona Sul sophistication.

Where to Go

Rio Scenarium — Lapa Rio’s most famous nightlife institution. A three-story antique shop by day, transforming into a spectacular live samba and MPB venue by night. The dance floor is a mix of foreign visitors and middle-class Cariocas. Tonight: Thursday is traditionally the start of the busy weekend with live bands playing from 9:30 pm. Exact lineup is typically posted on Instagram Stories the day of. Best time: Thursday-Saturday; live music starts 9:30 pm, peak energy at midnight. Arrive by 9:15 pm to secure a table without a painful queue. Cost: Entry coupon typically R$50-80, usually including a first drink. Caipirinhas R$30-40. Card and cash accepted; comanda system used. Address: Rua do Lavradio, 20, Lapa, Centro Getting there: Metro to Carioca/Cinelândia then a short Uber, or direct rideshare from Zona Sul. Do not walk on dark side streets. Good to know: Highly recommended for groups; smart-casual dress is essential. No beach flip-flops or singlets.

Lapa Arches & Av. Mem de Sá Street Bars — Lapa The open-air engine room of Rio’s nightlife. A dense strip of botecos and live-music bars spilling onto the pedestrianized street under the iconic white arches. Tonight: Thursday is a lively warm-up for the weekend, with crowds, street vendors, and cheap drinks from 9 pm. It feels like one large, informal street party. Best time: Wednesday through Saturday. The street fills up by 11:30 pm and goes until 3 am. Arrive at 10 pm if you want a seat. Cost: Street caipirinhas R$15-25, bottled beer R$10-15. Some indoor bars have a small couvert artistico if a band is playing. Cash is faster at kiosks; bars take cards. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá and surrounding streets near Praça Cardeal Câmara, Lapa Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia, then a 10-minute walk up the main lit avenue, or take an Uber directly to the Arcos. Good to know: No booking needed; casual streetwear. Keep phone and wallet in front pockets.

Rua Dias Ferreira Strip — Leblon The Beverly Hills of Rio’s nightlife. A single street housing dozens of high-end wine bars, gastropubs, and innovative cocktail lounges. Tonight: A buzzing Thursday night scene for the local ‘after-work’ crowd. The street is packed with well-dressed patrons from 8 pm spilling out of venues. Best time: Tuesday to Saturday, 8 pm-1 am. The prime time for a table is 8:30 pm. Cost: Cocktails and imported wines R$35-55. Card widely preferred; 10% service added to bills. Address: Rua Dias Ferreira, Leblon Getting there: Metro to Antero de Quental (Line 4) and a short, very safe walk, or direct Uber. Good to know: Book a table for dinner to avoid disappointment; dress smart-casual, no beachwear.

Bar Urca & Mureta da Urca — Urca A classic, no-frills boteco famous for its caipirinhas and empadas. Locals sit on the seawall (‘mureta’) across the street, watching the boats and the Christ the Redeemer statue. Tonight: A sunset ritual rather than a late-night bash. Go before 8 pm to grab a spot on the wall. Best time: Any sunny day; sunset hours. Arrive by 5:30 pm-6:30 pm for the best wall seats. Cost: Caipirinhas R$25-30, empadas R$8-12. Cash and cards both fine. Address: Rua Cândido Gaffrée, 205, Urca Phone: +55 21 2295-8747 Instagram: @barurcaoficial Getting there: Not on the metro line; an easy Uber ride from Botafogo or Copacabana. Good to know: No bookings; a casual pre-drink stop. Arrive early, order at the counter, and cross the street to the wall.

Cobal do Humaitá — Botafogo/Humaitá A large, vibrant gourmet market square ringed by bars and restaurants with open-air communal seating. It feels like a food-truck park with fixed infrastructure. Tonight: Always busy on Thursdays with a young, post-work crowd; it’s the social hub of Botafogo’s creative class. Best time: Tuesday to Saturday, 7 pm-1 am. The sweet spot is 8:30 pm. Cost: Craft beer R$20-30, dishes R$40-70. Most vendors accept cards. Comanda system common. Address: Rua Voluntários da Pátria, 446 – Humaitá Instagram: @cobaldohumaita Getting there: A 10-minute walk from Botafogo metro station, or a quick Uber. Good to know: No booking needed for the common areas; find a free spot and order at the bar counters.

Fosfobox — Copacabana A subterranean ‘club-in-a-box’ with a grungy, indie feel. The soundtrack varies from rock and pop to deep house, attracting a cool, alternative crowd that rejects the mainstream beach vibe. Tonight: Check Instagram @fosfobox for tonight’s specific DJ or party theme. It usually runs Thursday-Saturday. Best time: Friday and Saturday are peak, but Thursday offers a more relaxed door policy. Doors open 11 pm, peak at 1:30 am. Arrive after midnight. Cost: Entry R$30-60 depending on the event. Drinks R$20-30. Card accepted. Address: Rua Siqueira Campos, 143, Copacabana Instagram: @fosfobox Getting there: Metro to Siqueira Campos station, then a 3-minute walk. Safe area on main streets. Good to know: No booking needed; casual alternative dress. Bouncers are strict about IDs.

Pavão Azul — Copacabana An unfussy, legendary cheap-chop bar (‘pé sujo’) famous for its icy draft beer, stuffed crab, and chaotic sidewalk seating. A true Carioca cultural experience. Tonight: Packed every Thursday with a noisy mix of locals, expats, and beachgoers who never left. Best time: Any night; get there by 8 pm to grab a plastic chair on the pavement. Cost: Chopp (draft beer) R$10-12, portions R$40-60. Cash preferred, though cards are likely accepted. Address: Rua Hilário de Gouveia, 71, Copacabana Phone: +55 21 2236-2381 Getting there: A 5-minute walk from Cardeal Arcoverde metro. Streets are busy, but avoid the beach side at night. Good to know: Impossible to book; squeeze in where you can. Don’t be precious about personal space.

Leviano Bar — Lapa A cornerstone of Lapa’s club-bar hybrid scene, serving food and drinks upstairs, with a sweaty, raucous dance floor downstairs featuring samba, samba-rock, and MPB. Tonight: Thursday has a solid local turnout for the live band and DJ sets that mix classic samba with soul and funk. Best time: Thursday through Saturday, 10 pm-3 am. The band usually starts around 11:30 pm. Cost: Entry R$20-40; caipirinhas R$20-30. Address: Mem de Sá, 47, Lapa Instagram: @levianobar Getting there: Directly on Av. Mem de Sá under the arches. Easy access from the street party. Good to know: No booking needed; come as you are, but avoid beach flip-flops.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: The bohemian, chaotic cradle of samba. A loud, dense, and intoxicating clash of tourists, students, and street-party veterans.

Leblon: Affluent, polished, and airy. Where wealthy Cariocas and expats go for long dinners that turn into cocktail crawls on a single, chic street.

Ipanema: Sophisticated and balanced, mixing beach-life ease with serious bars, jazz clubs, and a strong LGBTQ+ presence.

Botafogo: Young, indie, and creative. The epicentre of Rio’s craft-beer and casual-patio movement, buzzing with students and young professionals.

Copacabana: A nostalgic, demographically mixed blend of old-school botecos, tourist traps, and hidden indie clubs, all set against a dramatic crescent beach.

Urca: Sleepy, safe, and scenic. A timeless village neighbourhood where the nightlife is literally sitting on a wall with a cold drink.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Teatro Odisséia (Lapa) — A three-floor club in a historic building with diverse music and a very inclusive, mixed crowd. The Thursday night scene draws a queer and alternative audience that bridges music genres.

Rua Farme de Amoedo (Ipanema) — Known colloquially as Rio’s gay street. The bars and beach kiosks near this strip are heavily frequented by the LGBTQ+ community and are safe, welcoming, and lively, especially on a Thursday evening.

Money & How Paying Works The Comanda Card: At almost every club and large bar, you swap your ID for a paper card upon entry. Every single drink or food item is marked on it. You pay the total at the exit cashier. Losing this card incurs a heavy penalty, often a flat fee of R$200-300, so guard it like your passport. Live Music Cover (Couvert Artístico): If there is a band playing, expect an automatic charge of R$30-80 per person added to your bill, regardless of whether you asked for it. It is standard and unavoidable. Card vs. Cash: Zona Sul’s major venues all take credit and debit cards, including contactless. For the Lapa street bars and kiosks, carry R$100-150 in cash for speed. Tipping: The standard ‘serviço’ is 10%, almost always included in your final bill total. You do not need to add extra tip unless the service was truly outstanding.

Getting Home Safe

Metro closes at midnight exactly (Monday-Saturday). If you plan to use the metro home, you must leave the venue by 11:30 pm to walk to the station safely.

99 and Uber are your lifelines after midnight. Wait for your ride inside the venue or the building lobby; never wait on a dark, empty street staring at your phone screen.

At 3 am in Lapa, surge pricing can be brutal. Walk up to one of the official yellow taxis parked near the main Police Post on the square under the Lapa Arches to negotiate a fixed fare or insist on the meter on night tariff ‘bandeira 2’.

Stay on the main lit strips. In Lapa, this means Av. Mem de Sá and the immediate Arches area. Avoid the cobblestone backstreets and empty squares. In Copacabana, use the Avenida Atlântica or Nossa Senhora de Copacabana, never the beach sand.

Adopt the ‘burner’ or secondary phone strategy. Keep your main smartphone hidden in your front trouser pocket or a cross-body bag. Use a cheap older phone for checking maps and Uber if you need to do so on the street.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I really arrive? If a venue says ‘starts 10 pm’, isn’t 10:15 pm fine?

For Lapa samba clubs, arriving at 10 pm gets you the last available table. For Botafogo bars, 8 pm is empty, 9 pm is buzzing. For a street party, showing up before midnight is an early warm-up; the real mess starts around 1 am.

Can I wear shorts and flip-flops to the club?

No. Even in Rio’s heat, nightlife dress codes, especially at samba houses like Rio Scenarium or Leblon bars, explicitly or socially reject beach flip-flops and singlets. Jeans, a t-shirt, and trainers or casual shoes are the universal safe uniform.

Is my English going to be a problem?

At the tourist-famous spots and high-end cocktail bars, staff often speak some English. At the gritty street botecos in Lapa or Pavão Azul, almost nobody will. Having a few key Portuguese phrases (‘Dois chopps, por favor’ – ‘Two draft beers, please’) will transform your night.

Sources: metrolinehub.com, rio.com, planrio.com

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — July 30, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Bar Brahma The most classic corner in São Paulo for live MPB and cold draft beer on a Thursday; you get the downtown glamour without the Saturday chaos.

Tonight at a Glance —Vila Madalena boteco crawl Grab a plastic table at Posto 6, Filial, or São Cristóvão; mixed crowd of locals, students, and expats; best on a Thursday from 7 pm. —D‑Edge World‑class electronic music in a spaceship‑style club with a mixed, open‑minded crowd; Thursdays are solid but the line moves fast if you arrive before 11:30 pm. —Selva A roving tropical‑house party that pops up in warehouses or gardens; check Instagram for tonight’s location; draws a stylish, international crowd. —Casa Fluida Affordable LGBTQ+ bar in the centre with a friendly mix of queer locals and visitors; it fills up from 9 pm on Thursdays. —Bar do Luiz Fernandes No‑fuss samba and feijoada crowd in Casa Verde; the sort of place where you make friends just by squeezing into a table.

Thursday in São Paulo is the city’s stealth weekend launchpad: Vila Madalena fills by 8 pm, Centro’s live‑music temples hum with MPB, and after midnight the electronic and LGBTQ+ crowds move to Barra Funda and Santa Cecília. Plan to start with a chopp and a pastel, trust the comanda card system, and let Uber carry you home when the metro shuts around midnight.

Tonight across Sao Paulo. (Photo internet reproduction)
