What’s On Tonight

Live MPB and samba‑rock with a rotating house band — at Bar Brahma, 8 pm. The stage that launched a thousand careers; the Thursday crowd is lively but not overwhelmed, perfect for a newcomer to breathe in downtown Paulistano glamour.

DJ sets ‑ check Instagram for tonight’s headliner — at D‑Edge, midnight. A reliable Thursday for house and techno with an international‑friendly dance floor, excellent sound, and a bar that keeps going until the sun comes up.

Open‑mic samba circle and cold‑beer conviviality — at Bar do Luiz Fernandes, 7:30 pm. Old‑school Zona Norte warmth; arrive early to grab a seat inside the pavilion, order a coxinha, and watch the roda de samba form as families and friends pour in.

Rooftop sunset DJ and after‑work crowd — at Terraço Jardins, 6 pm. A polished skyline view that transitions from post‑work drinks into a low‑key dance night; smart‑casual, easy place to meet fellow expats and English‑speaking Brazilians.

Queer‑friendly pop and funk DJ party — at Casa Fluida, 9 pm. Affordable entry, a warm door policy, and a courtyard where everyone chats; a brilliant introduction to São Paulo’s LGBTQ scene without a velvet rope.

Roving Selva party ‑ see Instagram for tonight’s location — at Selva, 11 pm. Tropical house and visuals under the stars or inside a repurposed factory; strong expat and digital‑nomad turnout on Thursdays.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm‑up (6–9 pm): Rooftops and botecos in Jardins and Pinheiros ‑ try Terraço Jardins for sunset or a plastic table at Bar Veloso in Vila Madalena, where the caipirinhas are legendary.

Prime time (8–11 pm): Live MPB and samba ‑ head to Bar Brahma in Centro or the samba‑rock of Ó do Borogodó in Pinheiros; arrive by 8 pm for a good spot and to beat the couvert surcharge that often rises later.

After midnight: clubs and queer parties ‑ cross the river to D‑Edge in Barra Funda for electronic, or stay central for Casa Fluida; Fridays are technically tomorrow so Thursdays feel like a holiday preview.

Late late (3–6 am): after‑hours ‑ D‑Edge runs until 6 am; smaller underground spots near Santa Cecília keep going with a more intimate vibe (look for Stories on Instagram the night of).

Scenes & Sounds

MPB — Brazilian Popular Music: a warm, lyrical, 20th‑century‑rooted sound that is the soul of the city’s neighbourhood bars. Expect well‑dressed locals singing along to every word. Where: Bar Brahma (Centro), Porto Gentil (Pinheiros).

Samba — From rowdy roda de samba circles to polished pagode bands; the beat is infectious and the crowd spans three generations. Where: Ó do Borogodó (Pinheiros), Bar do Luiz Fernandes (Casa Verde), Bambolina (Vila Madalena).

Funk — Carioca‑born favela funk with São Paulo’s own mandelão edge; heavy bass, raw energy, and a young, diverse crowd. Where: Clubs and street parties around Baixo Augusta and República; check local Instagram flyers.

Electronic — Deep house, techno, and Brazilian‑flavoured electronica in world‑class clubs and roving parties. Where: D‑Edge (Barra Funda), Gop Tun parties, Carlos Capslock, Selva (roving locations).

Sertanejo — Brazilian country music that dominates the mainstream; big‑production bars where couples dance the university‑style sertanejo universitário. Where: Villa Country (Barra Funda) and large houses in Tatuapé.

Forró — Northeastern accordion‑driven dance music; close, sweaty, and incredibly friendly for beginners. Where: CTN (Casa de Tradições Nordestinas) in Limão; Canto da Ema in Pinheiros.

Pick Your Night

Date night: Terraço Jardins for sunset cocktails and a skyline view, then a short Uber to Bar Brahma for live MPB – romantic lighting, strong drinks, and music loud enough to fill the pauses but not kill conversation.

Solo and safe: Bar do Luiz Fernandes or Casa Fluida. Both are easy to enter alone: the samba crowd at Luiz Fernandes will pull you into the circle, and Casa Fluida’s courtyard is built for mingling, with a zero‑judgement door.

Dance till sunrise: D‑Edge – arrive by 12:30 am, stay until the sun comes over Barra Funda; the marathon nights are legendary, and the crowd is a mix of serious dancers and first‑timers.

Meet locals: A boteco crawl in Vila Madalena – start smart at Posto 6 for pastéis and a cold chopp, then wander downhill into Filial or São Cristóvão; Brazilians are at their most open with a beer in hand at a plastic table.

Meet other expats: Selva (if the Thursday party is running) or the terrace at Selina Aurora hostel in Pinheiros – digital‑nomad central, with shared‑table setups and language‑exchange vibes spilling into the bar.

Where to Go

Bar Brahma — Centro A cathedral of MPB since 1948, with a polished wooden interior, a house band that knows every classic, and a crowd mixing downtown old‑timers, curious tourists, and local music lovers. Tonight: Live MPB with the house band, typically from 8 pm. Best time: Thursday–Saturday; arrive by 8 pm to get a table near the stage. Cost: Couvert artístico around R$40–80; draft beer about R$15; credit/debit cards accepted. Address: Av. São João, 677, Centro Phone: +55 11 3331-0855 Instagram: @barbrahmacentro Website: barbrahma.com.br Getting there: Metro República (red/blue line); rideshare after midnight. Good to know: Reservation recommended for a good table via website or phone; smart‑casual, no shorts at night.

D‑Edge — Barra Funda A three‑floor electronic music institution with a stellar Funktion‑One sound system, LED‑lit walls, and a cosmopolitan crowd that takes dancing seriously. Tonight: DJ set – check @dedgeclub Instagram for the Thursday resident. Doors open 11 pm. Best time: Fridays and Saturdays are biggest, but Thursdays are a local secret with a loyal crowd; arrive before 11:30 pm to skip the line. Cost: Entry R$50–120 depending on the night; drinks from R$25; comanda card system. Address: Al. Olga, 170, Barra Funda Phone: +55 11 3666-0066 Instagram: @dedgeclub Website: dedge.com.br Getting there: Metro Marechal Deodoro or Barra Funda plus a short Uber; plenty of rideshare pickup right outside. Good to know: Buy advance tickets via Sympla; no strict dress code but dark, clubby wear fits the vibe.

Bar do Luiz Fernandes — Casa Verde A beloved North‑zone samba temple where families, couples, and solo strangers share long tables under a covered courtyard; the beer is ice‑cold and the snacks are pure Brazilian comfort food. Tonight: Weekly samba circle from around 7:30 pm. Best time: Thursday and Saturday; arrive by 7 pm to get a seat before the roda starts. Cost: No couvert; generous portions and draft beer around R$12–15; cash and cards accepted. Address: R. Augusto Tolle, 610, Casa Verde Phone: +55 11 3966-6693 Instagram: @bardoluizfernandesoficial Getting there: Rideshare recommended; the nearest metro is Santana (blue line) then a short Uber. Good to know: No reservations for the public area; come early. Relaxed, no dress code.

Casa Fluida — República An accessible queer space in the centre with a welcoming bar, outdoor courtyard, and a calendar that mixes drag, funk, and pop parties. Tonight: Pop/funk DJ night, typically from 9 pm. Best time: Thursday nights are a steady draw; the mix of LGBTQ locals and curious visitors peaks around 11 pm. Cost: Entry R$10–30; drinks from R$15; comanda system. Address: Lgo do Arouche, 473, República Instagram: @casafluida Getting there: Metro República then a short walk; rideshare for late exits. Good to know: Pay at the door; no dress code, come as you are – zero tolerance for discrimination.

Selva — Roving (usually Centro or Barra Funda) A nomadic party that turns warehouses, gardens, and rooftops into lush tropical‑electronic wonderlands; the crowd leans international, artsy, and very friendly. Tonight: Check Instagram @selva.sp for tonight’s venue and lineup; Thursdays often host a smaller edition. Best time: For Thursday events, doors usually open 11 pm; arrive before midnight to settle in. Cost: Advance tickets R$50–100; comanda system for drinks. Address: Location announced on Instagram Instagram: @selva.sp Getting there: Rideshare strongly recommended; pickup points are busy and well‑lit. Good to know: Buy online; no strict dress code but tropical‑chic is the unofficial uniform.

Terraço Jardins — Jardins A sleek rooftop bar on top of a shopping centre with a panoramic skyline view, a pool, and a well‑heeled after‑work crowd that transitions into a DJ‑driven night. Tonight: Sunset DJ, typically 6 pm–midnight. Best time: Thursday and Friday; go at 6 pm for the golden hour, stay until 10 pm then head elsewhere. Cost: No cover; cocktails around R$40–50; credit cards preferred. Address: Av. Brigadeiro Faria Lima, 3491, 7º andar, Jardim Paulistano Phone: +55 11 94349-3882 Instagram: @terracojardins Website: terracojardins.com Getting there: Metro Faria Lima (yellow line) and a short walk; rideshare after dark. Good to know: Reservation recommended for a poolside table; smart‑casual.

Ó do Borogodó — Pinheiros A sweaty, joyful samba‑rock club where the band plays classic Jorge Ben and Tim Maia, and the dance floor fills with couples who actually know how to move. Tonight: Samba‑rock night; doors open 9 pm, music from 10 pm. Best time: Thursday is samba‑rock night and it is packed by 10:30 pm. Cost: Entry R$30–50; drinks from R$18; comanda card system. Address: R. Horácio Lane, 21, Pinheiros Phone: +55 11 99777-0544 Instagram: @odoborogodo Website: odoborogodo.com.br Getting there: Metro Fradique Coutinho (yellow line) then a 15‑minute walk; rideshare for late exit. Good to know: Can sell out; buy advance tickets on Sympla. Comfortable shoes – you will dance.

Bar Veloso — Vila Madalena The caipirinha capital of the neighbourhood; a tiny corner bar that spills onto the street with a chilled, unpretentious crowd of locals and savvy travelers. Tonight: Standing‑room boteco, busy from 6 pm. Best time: Any weekday from 6 pm for the after‑work crowd; Thursdays prime for starting a crawl. Cost: No cover; caipirinhas around R$25–35; cash and cards. Address: R. Wisard, 112, Vila Madalena Phone: +55 11 3031-7710 Instagram: @barveloso Getting there: Metro Fradique Coutinho or Vila Madalena; short walk. Good to know: Walk‑in only; no dress code, just come as you are.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Vila Madalena: Bohemian and buzzing: tree‑lined streets crammed with botecos, young crowds in flip‑flops, and the sound of clinking glasses from early evening.

Pinheiros: Artsy and transitional: live‑music venues and craft‑beer bars sit beside old‑school bakeries, drawing a creative, slightly older after‑dark set.

Centro: Gritty and grand: classic MPB halls and new queer bars share blocks with 20th‑century towers; the energy is raw and completely Paulistano.

Barra Funda: Warehouse and club district: D‑Edge and mega‑houses dominate, with spillover crowds that come straight from the nearby metro terminals.

Jardins: Polished and pricey: rooftop bars, upscale restaurants, and a crowd that dresses to impress – the São Paulo you see in fashion magazines.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Casa Fluida — A casual, mixed queer bar in República with affordable drinks, outdoor seating, and a warm unpretentious crowd; great for newcomers on any Thursday.

Bco. 112 — A bi‑monthly queer warehouse party with house and disco; check Instagram for the next edition – it draws a hip, diverse crowd across the spectrum.

Money & How Paying Works Comanda card system: at most clubs and larger bars you get a tab card at the door; every drink and snack is scanned to it, and you pay the total on exit. Losing the card often triggers a heavy fine (sometimes R$300+) – treat it like cash. Couvert artístico: in live‑music venues a per‑person artist cover (around R$30–80) is added to your bill automatically when music is playing; you cannot opt out if you are seated. Payment: credit and debit cards are widely accepted (contactless is standard); carry some cash for small botecos but you can survive 95 percent cashless. Tipping: most bills include a 10 percent serviço (service charge); if it is missing, leaving 10 percent is the norm. You do not need to tip bartenders per drink – just settle the bill at the end.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: lines close around midnight (Monday–Saturday) and 11 pm on Sundays; plan your exit from bars before then if you want to use the metro, or commit to rideshare.

Uber and 99: the universal way home after midnight. Use the app, verify the plate, and share your trip with a friend. Both apps have a strong presence everywhere, even in far‑flung neighbourhoods.

Surge and safe pickup: on busy Thursday club exits a short ride may surge; wait inside the venue or a well‑lit shopfront until the car arrives, and avoid standing on dark, empty corners waving your phone.

São Paulo is a city of neighbourhood islands: stay within the busy ‘bolhas’ (Pinheiros, Vila Madalena, Jardins, Centro’s main strips) and avoid walking into unknown side streets alone at night.

Keep your phone in your pocket when you are on the street, and minimise flashy jewellery; Paulistanos are pros at this – follow their lead and you will blend in.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time do people really go out?

A drink at 7 pm, dinner at 9 pm, a bar by 10 pm, and the club from midnight – the night flows late and Thursdays in São Paulo often stretch to 2–3 am even on a ‘school night’.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

In Vila Madalena and major clubs someone will speak English, but learning a few phrases (‘uma caipirinha, por favor’) goes a long way and opens doors at the traditional samba houses.

Is it okay to go out alone?

Absolutely – many of the best spots (Bar Brahma, Casa Fluida, a boteco crawl) are very solo-friendly if you arrive early and aren’t afraid to smile. Use the same rideshare safety steps you would in any global city.

Sources: metrolinehub.com, rio.com, planrio.com

World.title: Costa Rica Wins Its First Surfing Gold Medal in Regional Games History
World.content:
Costa Rican surfer Rachel Agüero Cabezas won the women’s shortboard title at the Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic tpday, delivering Costa Rica its first gold medal in surfing in the history of the regional competition.

The 20-year-old beat Barbados’ Chelsea Tuach 10.50 points to 7.33 in the final at Playa Encuentro in Cabarete, on the northern coast of Puerto Plata province. Agüero’s score came from two waves graded 5.83 and 4.67, while Tuach posted a 5.00 and a 2.33. According to the National Olympic Committee, Agüero took control of the heat from the opening minutes and never surrendered the lead. Tuach needed a wave scored at 5.51 or better to overturn the result and never found one.

Agüero reached the final by eliminating the surfer most observers had installed as the favorite. In the fourth round she defeated Nicaragua’s Candelaria Resano, an Olympian and world championship medalist, by 12.57 points to 11.33. She had opened the competition on the first day of the event with 11.16 points, built on waves of 7.33 and 3.83, to win her heat ahead of Puerto Rico’s Havanna Cabrero and Colombia’s Margarita Conde. That 7.33 stood as the highest-scoring women’s wave of the opening day.

The result caps a season that has established Agüero as the leading woman in Costa Rican competitive surfing. She arrived in the Dominican Republic as the two-time national Open champion, having sealed her second consecutive title only weeks earlier at the closing round of the Banco LAFISE national circuit at Playa Hermosa de Jacó, the beach where she lives and trains.

In March she won the Denga Santa Teresa Pro at Playa Carmen. She has also been competing on World Surf League regional events, the tier where surfers accumulate the results and ranking points that open the door to the sport’s professional circuits. Costa Rica had never won a surfing gold medal at these Games before Wednesday. The country’s only previous podium finishes in the sport came at San Salvador 2023, when Lía Díaz and Anthony Flores each took bronze in longboard.

Sam Reidy added another on Tuesday, beating the Dominican Republic’s Gian Marco Oliva 14.50 to 11.60 in the men’s shortboard bronze heat, a result the Costa Rican Surf Federation described as the first shortboard medal at the Games. Flores finished fourth in the men’s longboard event this year after losing his bronze heat to Mexico’s Heriberto Torres.

The surfing competition ran from July 25 until today at Playa Encuentro, a break that has become one of the Caribbean’s most reliable competitive venues, and drew 71 surfers from 12 countries across shortboard, longboard and stand-up paddle surf. Agüero’s medal was Costa Rica’s third gold of Santo Domingo 2026. The first two came in taekwondo, through Jaycee Bassett and Neshy Lindo.

This edition of the Games is the 25th and marks a century since the first was held in Mexico City in 1926. Organizers programmed 40 sports, more than the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic schedule, and more than 6,200 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing over 16 days.

Costa Rican surfing has been producing this kind of result with increasing regularity. Díaz became the first surfer from Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America to qualify for the World Surf League’s Longboard Tour, a circuit that opened its season at Huntington Beach in California this month.

Leilani McGonagle won a place on the 2026-27 Challenger Series, the qualifying tier immediately below the elite Championship Tour. Bodyboarder Dulce Agüero reached a podium at Pipeline in Hawaii in March. The national federation has said its planning is now oriented around the qualifying events for the 2028 Olympics, where surfing will again be on the program.

For Agüero, the initial reward is a regional title at 20 and a clear line of sight to the next stage. The Pan American Games in Lima in 2027 come first, and the Olympic qualifying calendar follows behind it.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Treat Illegal Mining as Organized Crime
World.content:
Costa Rican lawmakers have given initial approval to legislation that would allow authorities to pursue illegal mining and other serious environmental offenses using organized-crime laws. The Legislative Assembly approved the proposal in first debate with 53 votes.

All five political groups represented in Congress supported the measure, reflecting growing concern about criminal networks involved in illegal gold extraction, logging and wildlife trafficking. The bill would apply when environmental crimes are carried out by a structured group of at least two people working together.

That change could give prosecutors access to investigative tools normally reserved for organized-crime cases, including intercepted communications, longer investigative periods and extended pretrial detention. Supporters argue that the current system is better suited to prosecuting individuals caught carrying out an illegal activity than identifying the financiers, organizers and logistics networks behind it.

The problem has become particularly visible in Crucitas, a rural area near the Nicaraguan border where illegal gold mining has continued for years. Authorities have repeatedly found organized operations involving machinery, transportation, fuel, processing equipment and the illegal sale of gold.

The proposal would increase penalties when mining offenses are linked to a coordinated criminal group. Mining exploration or extraction inside national parks, biological reserves, wildlife refuges and other protected state land would carry sentences ranging from three months to five years. When the crime is committed by an organized group, the penalty could rise to between three and six years in prison.

The changes would also cover illegal logging, wildlife trafficking, fishing offenses and crimes involving sea turtles. For some offenses under Costa Rica’s wildlife, forestry, fisheries and marine turtle laws, organized-crime involvement could add between two and four years to the existing prison sentence.

The reform would also eliminate situations in which defendants accused of serious environmental crimes can avoid prison by paying only a fine. Lawmakers backing the measure said many existing penalties are so low that prosecutors cannot use the investigative powers needed to dismantle larger networks.

The legislation is intended to distinguish between someone acting alone and a structured group that recruits workers, supplies equipment, transports illegally obtained material and collects the profits. The proposal does not authorize gold mining in Crucitas.

A separate bill would allow regulated gold exploration and mining in the Cutris district of San Carlos. That proposal remains under discussion in the Legislative Assembly’s Environment Committee. The distinction is important because debate over the future of Crucitas has divided Costa Rican political parties and environmental groups.

Some lawmakers and government officials argue that regulated mining would allow the state to regain control of the area and collect revenue from its gold deposits. Opponents say reopening large-scale mining could cause further environmental damage and reward the failure to stop illegal extraction.

The organized-crime proposal has attracted broader political support because it addresses illegal activity without changing Costa Rica’s general prohibition on open-pit metal mining. The bill still faces additional legislative steps before becoming law.

A second debate was scheduled for tomorrow. However, lawmakers are expected to return the proposal to an earlier point so they can make changes agreed upon by the political parties before holding another final vote. If eventually approved and signed, the reform would strengthen penalties in future cases where prosecutors can prove that environmental crimes were committed through an organized structure.

World.title: Costa Rica Warns of Poor Air Quality as Saharan Dust Arrives
World.content:
A new push of Saharan dust is expected to spread across Costa Rica this week, bringing hazy skies, reduced visibility and poorer air quality, with Thursday and Friday forecast to be the most difficult days. The dust will affect nearly all of Costa Rica, although higher concentrations are expected in Alajuela, western parts of the Central Valley and some areas of Cartago.

Residents may notice a pale or milky appearance in the sky known as calima, caused by fine particles suspended in the atmosphere. Visibility over mountains and other distant landmarks could also become noticeably worse. The conditions are expected to become more apparent beginning Wednesday before reaching their strongest point on Thursday, July 30, and Friday, July 31. Air quality should begin improving Saturday as the dust moves north toward other parts of Central America and Mexico.

People with asthma, allergies and other respiratory conditions face the greatest risk. Children and older adults should also reduce the amount of time they spend outdoors during the highest concentrations. The warning extends beyond people with existing health problems. Residents in generally good health are being advised to avoid long periods of strenuous outdoor activity on Thursday and Friday, including extended runs, cycling or outdoor exercise lasting several hours.

Fine particles carried within the dust can enter the respiratory system and cause irritation. Possible symptoms include coughing, itchy eyes or throat, headaches, chest discomfort, breathing difficulty and worsening asthma or allergy attacks. People who must remain outdoors should limit their exposure and consider wearing a well-fitting mask, particularly if they have respiratory problems. Anyone who develops discomfort while exercising should stop the activity and move indoors.

The Saharan dust originated over North Africa and traveled thousands of kilometers across the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea before reaching Central America. These events are common during the middle of the year, when strong trade winds carry dry air and mineral particles westward.

The approaching dust will combine with stronger winds, locally raised soil particles, pollen and smoke still present from regional burning. Together, those elements can increase the amount of material suspended in the air even when the Saharan particles are not clearly visible. Lower rainfall will make the situation more noticeable. Rain normally helps remove dust and other particles from the atmosphere, but Costa Rica is expecting a significant reduction in precipitation over the next several days.

The dry air associated with Saharan dust can also limit the development of rain clouds, allowing particles to remain suspended longer. The episode is not expected to produce dangerously polluted conditions across the country. However, prolonged exposure could cause problems for sensitive people and make outdoor activity uncomfortable even for otherwise healthy residents.

You may also encounter hazier views from mountain overlooks, volcanoes and higher-elevation destinations. Flights are not currently expected to face major disruptions, although distant visibility could be reduced. Conditions are forecast to improve considerably over the weekend as the main concentration of dust moves away from Costa Rica.

World.title: Costa Rica Expels Second-Division Club for 10 Years Over Match-Fixing
World.content:
The Costa Rican Football Federation has thrown a second-division club out of the sport for ten years after its investigators concluded the team took part in manipulating four matches during the 2025 season, in what is now the fifth match-fixing case in Costa Rican football to end in sanctions.

The Disciplinary Commission of the Federación Costarricense de Fútbol found that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, which competed in the Liga de Ascenso under the name San Carlos FC, breached Article 66 of the federation’s Disciplinary Code. The resolution bars the club from any football-related activity for a decade. The federation’s legal department has since notified every affiliated league — the first division, the Liga de Ascenso, the amateur Linafa structure, futsal, beach football and women’s football — that the prohibition applies to the legal entity regardless of category or format.

The case rests on a report by the federation’s Integrity Office, led by Carlos Ricardo Benavides, which examined four Liga de Ascenso fixtures from the 2024-2025 season. All four ended in lopsided defeats. San Carlos FC lost 8-2 to Quepos Cambute on January 19, 2025, fell 5-1 to Cofutpa on February 9, lost 6-2 away to Municipal Grecia on March 1, and lost 5-2 to Jicaral on March 9. According to the resolution, the investigation found a sustained pattern of irregularities in sports betting linked to matches the club played, together with atypical movement in betting markets.

Much of that evidence came from outside Costa Rica. Sportradar, the sports data firm that assists FIFA with integrity investigations, issued alerts on several of the club’s fixtures after analysing both the state of betting markets before kickoff and the swings recorded while games were in progress. In the Quepos Cambute match, San Carlos FC was leading 1-0 at the 27th minute when heavy money began moving on a San Carlos defeat; the game finished 8-2 to Quepos Cambute.

Sportradar filed a report flagging irregular movement five days later, on January 24. Investigators also drew on reports from the bookmakers Betway, VBet and 9 Olybet and from the International Betting Integrity Association. The Integrity Office concluded that the relationship between the market swings and what happened on the pitch pointed to a high probability of deliberate intervention by the club.

The commission’s finding, as set out in the resolution, is that Municipal Garabito Fútbol Club SAD, known as San Carlos FC, played an active part in the conduct. The franchise had been based in the Pacific canton of Garabito before its owners moved the operation north; the club then competed as San Carlos FC in the Northern Zone. It was relegated from the Liga de Ascenso at the end of the 2024-2025 season and did not subsequently compete in Linafa. The club has no connection to AD San Carlos of the first division, nor to Inter San Carlos, which recently won the Liga de Ascenso title.

Three players who turned out for the club were sanctioned in a separate resolution that became final on June 25 of this year. That file concerned an approach made in April 2025 to players at Deportivo Upala, who were offered money to lose a Liga de Ascenso fixture against San Carlos FC.

The attempt failed because the Upala players reported it. Hansell Arauz Ovares, a retired forward who won four national titles with Deportivo Saprissa between 2014 and 2016, and Henry Cooper Bennett, a former Limón FC striker, were each banned for 15 years. Goalkeeper Fabián Rodríguez Esquivel received 15 years in the same file and a further 20 years in a separate case in which the Integrity Office concluded he had approached a Guadalupe FC player about fixing a first-division match, bringing his total ban to 35 years. All three bans cover any football-related role, whether as a player, coaching staff or club official.

The club expulsion is the second of its kind in Costa Rica. Puerto Golfito FC was excluded for ten years in 2024 on similar grounds. In 2025, three Municipal Turrialba officials — Enrique Valencia, Ernesto de la Torre and Rolando Pereira — were suspended for five years over an alleged manipulation attempt. Each of the cases sanctioned so far has originated in the lower tiers of the Costa Rican game, where budgets are thin, wages are low and matches still attract enough betting volume abroad to make manipulation worth someone’s while.

In notifying every affiliated league of the expulsion, the federation asked each to apply its integrity protocols and strengthen preventive measures. The Integrity Office has indicated that further resolutions are pending.

World.title: Belizean Pride: Inspector Ester Cal named Valedictorian of regional Junior Officers’ course in Guyana
World.content:
Belizean Pride: Inspector Ester Cal named Valedictorian of regional Junior Officers’ course in Guyana

By Zoila Palma: Belize Police Department Inspector Ester Cal has been named valedictorian of the Junior Officers’ Course No. 1/2026, following the successful completion of the two-month internationally accredited leadership programme at the Guyana Police Force Academy.

The course was held from June 1 to July 31, 2026, and brought together officers from across the Caribbean to strengthen leadership, professional competence and regional collaboration.

Inspector Cal trained alongside officers from 10 Caribbean countries and various security and public service institutions.

Her dedication and academic performance earned her two of the programme’s top distinctions: Valedictorian of Junior Officers’ Course No. 1/2026 and the Best Academic Paper Award, which she shared with Assistant Superintendent of Police D. Chaitram of the Guyana Police Force.

The Belize Police Department congratulated Inspector Cal on her achievements, highlighting her belief that leadership is not defined by rank or authority, but by character, service and the positive influence one leaves behind. Her guiding principle, “Serve to Lead,” reflects her commitment to using every opportunity to learn and grow to better serve her colleagues, the police department and the communities it serves.

Following the graduation of 31 officers, Inspector Cal returned to Belize with new knowledge, strengthened regional partnerships and renewed commitment to public service.

World.title: Stann Creek students explore Agriculture at Summer Camp
World.content:
Stann Creek students explore Agriculture at Summer Camp

By Zoila Palma: Schoolchildren from across the Stann Creek District, ages 7 to 17, are getting hands-on experience in agriculture this week through a summer camp hosted by the Ministry of Agriculture at George Technical High School.

The camp is being guided by extension officers from the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries.

Participants are being introduced to various areas of agriculture, including horticulture and livestock care.

During the camp, students are participating in activities focused on honey production, with agroprocessing and aquaculture scheduled for Friday.

Through the interactive sessions, the Ministry aims to expose young people to the wide range of opportunities within the agricultural sector and inspire them to develop a lifelong interest in agriculture and food production.

World.title: Sunshine returns as the tropical wave moves on
World.content:
Sunshine returns as the tropical wave moves on

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The midweek tropical wave has crossed and cleared, and Belize returns to sunshine as July enters its final stretch, with only isolated showers on the map and the tropics staying quiet.

According to the National Meteorological Service, a moderate and relatively moist easterly airflow prevails. Skies will be sunny today with a few cloudy spells, turning partly cloudy tonight, with showers or thunderstorms staying isolated.

The heat climbs back with the clearing. Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 82 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will return to 94 degrees Fahrenheit (34 Celsius) before dropping to 74 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a low of 68 (20 Celsius).

At sea, the water carries some bounce, with easterly winds of 10 to 20 knots, choppy seas, and waves of 3 to 5 feet, so smaller vessels should take the usual care.

On the tropical front, the calm holds. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the region over the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead to Friday and Friday night, skies turn partly cloudy, becoming cloudy at times, with a few morning showers or isolated thunderstorms developing mainly along the coast and over the south, gradually decreasing by afternoon.

Today’s high tides are at 10:09 AM and 11:18 PM, with a low tide at 5:23 PM and another low at 4:40 AM tomorrow. The sun rose at 5:31 AM and will set at 6:26 PM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Catherine Cumberbatch.

World.title: 23 New Peace Corps volunteers sworn in to support Youth and Education in Belize
World.content:
23 New Peace Corps volunteers sworn in to support Youth and Education in Belize

By Zoila Palma: Twenty-three new Peace Corps Volunteers were sworn in on Wednesday marking the completion of their training and the start of their service in communities across Belize.

The U.S. Embassy in Belize noted that the new cohort includes 15 Youth Development Volunteers, representing the fourth group serving under the Youth Empowered by Sports (YES) Project, and eight Education Volunteers serving as Peace Corps Response Volunteers.

The Volunteers will work in partnership with government ministries, community leaders and local organizations to support national priorities in youth development and education across all six districts.

The YES Project, implemented in collaboration with the Ministry of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations, uses sports, mentorship and resiliency-building activities to help young people lead healthy and empowered lives.

Meanwhile, education initiatives, carried out in partnership with the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology and PathLight International, focus on STEAM, early childhood education and literacy support.

Senator Janelle Chanona delivered the keynote address, while U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Rhonda Slusher administered the oath of service.

Peace Corps Belize Country Director Dr. Nadine Rogers commended the new Volunteers for their commitment, saying, “These 23 Americans came to Belize ready to serve; literally bringing our new mission to life.”

The swearing-in ceremony comes as the Peace Corps celebrates its 65th anniversary and highlights its mission of putting “purpose, passion, and skills to work for America and the world.”

Peace Corps has partnered with Belize for 64 years to advance community-led development, with Volunteers continuing to support efforts that expand opportunities for young people and strengthen education nationwide.

World.title: The Cameras Leave. The Soldiers Stay.
World.content:
The Cameras Leave. The Soldiers Stay.

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

Belize’s defence procurement debate should force us to ask a bigger question about transparency, responsibility and national security.

By Lennox Lamb: Every day in Belize, another story breaks. Breaking Belize News breaks it. News 5 investigates another angle. 7 News asks another difficult question. Love FM keeps the country talking. KREM gives the people another perspective. By six o’clock, the country is listening. By seven o’clock, social media has already decided who is guilty, who is innocent, who should resign and who should go to jail.

Then the cameras are switched off. The microphones are packed away. The headlines begin to fade. But Belize does not stop. The soldiers still report for duty. The patrol boats still leave the dock. The border patrols still head into the field. Joint operations against narcotics trafficking continue. Support for the Belize Police Department continues whenever gang violence overwhelms available manpower.

The cameras leave. The soldiers stay. That simple reality has stayed with me throughout the Ministry of Defence procurement controversy. Before anyone misunderstands me, let me be clear. This article is not written to defend any government, minister, supplier or political party. Nor is it written to criticize the media.

A free press is one of the greatest strengths of any free nation. Journalists must investigate. Governments must answer. Public money must be accounted for. If corruption exists, it must be exposed, and those responsible must answer before the law. That is how a free society protects itself. But accountability is not our only responsibility. We also have a responsibility to protect Belize. And that is where this discussion becomes much bigger than politics.

Defence Is Different. The Belize Defence Force is not just another government department. It exists to defend the sovereignty, security and people of Belize.

Belize continues to pursue a peaceful legal resolution of its territorial, maritime and insular dispute with Guatemala before the International Court of Justice. Yet while the lawyers argue in courtrooms, our soldiers continue to patrol the border. There are still periodic tensions involving Guatemalan civilians and security personnel near the adjacency zone. Those realities have not disappeared. Neither have the threats inside our own borders.

The Belize Defence Force supports anti-narcotics operations, assists in combating organized crime, and reinforces the Belize Police Department during serious outbreaks of gang violence. For a country our size, that is an enormous responsibility. When Information Becomes Intelligence. Military professionals around the world understand what is often called the mosaic effect.

One supplier’s name.

One invoice.

One payment.

One procurement document.

Viewed alone, each may reveal very little. Viewed together over time, they can sometimes reveal patterns that no single document was ever intended to disclose. That does not mean every defence story creates a national security risk. It does not mean journalists should stop asking difficult questions. It does not mean governments should hide behind the words “national security.” It means Belize should begin discussing where the line exists between legitimate public accountability and legitimate operational security.

That is not an anti-media argument. It is a pro-Belize argument. Procurement Reform Must Strengthen Both Accountability and Readiness. Several years ago, concerns about financial management resulted in procurement responsibilities being progressively transferred away from the Belize Defence Force and into the Ministry.

Those concerns required action. But every reform should be judged by one question:

Did it make the institution stronger?

The military understands logistics, operational readiness and the realities of supporting soldiers in the field. Civilian oversight protects taxpayers and strengthens accountability. Neither responsibility should eliminate the other. The answer to procurement concerns is not weaker oversight. Nor is it weakening the military’s ability to determine and support its operational needs.

The answer is stronger institutions, independent auditing, clear financial controls, meaningful military participation in procurement planning, and transparent reporting.

That is how responsible nations build confidence. The Uniform Belongs to Belizeans. Sometimes we speak about “the military” as though it were an institution separate from society. It is not.

The young man standing on the border is somebody’s son. The woman wearing the uniform is somebody’s daughter. The soldier boarding a patrol boat is somebody’s husband, wife, brother, sister, uncle, aunt or neighbour. Before they are soldiers, they are Belizeans. A threat to the effectiveness of the Belize Defence Force is not simply a military concern.

It is a national concern. Protecting the institution that protects Belize is ultimately about protecting Belizean families.

Responsibility Belongs to All of Us

Government has responsibilities.

The Opposition has responsibilities.

Public officers have responsibilities.

The military has responsibilities.

The media has responsibilities.

Citizens have responsibilities.

The media should continue investigating matters of public interest.

Government should never misuse “national security” as a shield against accountability.

The Opposition should exercise judgment when handling sensitive information.

Public officers should recognize the consequences of unauthorized disclosures.

Citizens should remember that forwarding every leaked document without reflection is not always an act of patriotism.

Freedom and responsibility have always walked together. One should never exist without the other.

A Better Way Forward

Rather than allowing this controversy to become another political battlefield, Belize should use it to strengthen the system. We should reinforce independent oversight of defence procurement. We should ensure military professionals remain meaningfully involved in determining operational requirements. We should improve auditing and financial controls. We should continue demanding transparency over public spending.

And we should begin a serious national conversation about how a small country balances the public’s right to know with the responsibility to protect those entrusted with defending it.

This conversation should never be about protecting politicians. It should always be about protecting Belize.

One Final Thought:

Afta aal di naiz don…

Afta evribadi don aagyu…

Afta di politishan dehn don mek dehn point…

Afta di media dehn don tel di stori…

Di soalja dehn stil ga da wok.

They still patrol the rivers.

They still walk the border.

They still support the police.

They still answer the call whenever Belize needs them.

Tomorrow there will be another headline.

There will be another political debate.

There will be another breaking story.

The cameras will leave.

The soldiers will stay.

Perhaps that is the lesson this controversy should leave with all of us. Not that transparency matters more than national security. Not that national security matters more than transparency. But that a mature nation understands it has a duty to protect both. Because when the news cycle ends, when the politics quiets down, and when the cameras have all gone home, someone is still standing watch over Belize.

They deserve our accountability. They deserve our support. And they deserve a national conversation that is thoughtful enough to protect both the people’s right to know and the country’s duty to defend itself.

World.title: Support for students
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith (right) confabs with Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange at the post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, where Johnson Smith updated the nation on the situation with Jamaican medical students in Cuba.Garfield Robinson

THE Government of Jamaica has pledged continued support for the roughly 270 Jamaican students still studying in crisis-hit Cuba, with Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith reaffirming the Government’s commitment to the students’

welfare.

Johnson Smith told a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday that her ministry has been closely monitoring the students who remain in Cuba, 40 of whom are sponsored by Cuban scholarships, which are supported by the Government of Jamaica, further noting that one private student has formally advised of his return home.

Meanwhile, she noted that more than 65 students, including five on government scholarships, have completed their medical studies for the 2025-2026 academic year.

“Three others have indicated that they are in the process of continuing their studies elsewhere through academic transfer, and we have to caveat these numbers because we understand anecdotally that others have returned, but they have not formally notified us,” Johnson Smith said.

“And this is understandable, they are there privately, and on their own steam, but just to say that we have the information…and we also have a line of communication that allows for them to not only indicate their return, but to request assistance if they so need,” said the minister.

Johnson Smith noted that those students who remain are offered pathways to repatriation should they express a desire to return.

“This is because our concern remains for their safety, well-being, and academic continuity. We know that prolonged power cuts and reduced public transportation causes challenges for their way of life, and the Government has communicated our preparedness to assist with one-way return tickets should they wish to return but have a difficulty with affordability,” she said.

“We continue to engage the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Health, as well as medical tertiary institutions on what, if anything, can be done for those who may wish to return and continue their studies here,” she added.

Many of the Cuban medical students have seen classes suspended or moved online with limited connectivity, as Cuba faces an ongoing energy crisis, worsened by a United States blockade on fuel shipments.

The island’s fuel shortages have been triggering frequent, lengthy, and unpredictable electricity interruptions, affecting not only education but also access to food, medical supplies, and transportation.

Back in February, Johnson Smith said some students had been reaching out and advised that their institutions either closed for a period, in one case for four weeks; and others said that classes had been suspended in favour of virtual studies, which saw challenges with Internet and electricity.

To maintain direct contact, Johnson Smith noted the ministry created a WhatsApp group, at that time linking roughly 320 students with officials in Kingston and the Jamaican Embassy in Havana, a move that allowed the Government to register many privately funded students who were previously outside formal channels.

In the meantime, Johnson Smith said Wednesday that the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to Cuba by contributing US$100,000 through the Caribbean Community (Caricom) as a humanitarian relief effort.

She said Jamaica joined Caricom heads of Government in continuing to express deep concern over the worsening humanitarian situation in Cuba and reaffirmed its commitment to a coordinated regional response to provide humanitarian assistance to the Cuban people.

“While speaking as long-standing friends of both the United States and Cuba, Caricom underscored in our joint single statement that civilian needs must remain the highest priority. We welcomed recent rounds of discussions between the governments and continue to advocate for constructive dialogue as the most effective path to relieve hardship on the people of Cuba,” said Johnson Smith.

The minister added that many Cuban medical professionals who had left the island following an abrupt end to the long-standing health technical cooperation arrangement in March 2026 have since returned to Jamaica and are continuing work under new arrangements with the health and wellness ministry. Johnson Smith added that those who chose to remain are still being accommodated as they continue to work under individual contracts.

“We all continue to value the significant contribution that Cuban medical professionals have made to our health sector over many years, and following the conclusion of the technical cooperation programme, you’d recall that a number of Cuban medical professionals chose to remain in Jamaica and continue to work under personal contracts,” she said.
