World.title: Human trafficking in Mexico: the dark side of tourism
World.content:
By May, a record-breaking 20 million tourists had visited Mexico so far in 2026. But with increased tourism comes a heightened risk of human trafficking and sexual exploitation. Women and children are most vulnerable.

Warning: This article discusses sexual violence, which some readers might find distressing.

Mixi Cruz was just 13 years old when her mother died. At first, she lived on the streets, then she turned to her elder stepsister for help. Once there, she was forced to manage household chores and pressured into sexual exploitation.

"The hardest part was accepting that none of that happened simply because I was naive or stupid," the young woman, now 33, tells DW. "It happened to me because there are bad people who sell other people. And there are bad people who buy other people."

In Mexico human trafficking has become one of the most lucrative economies in organized crime. According to the 2025 Global Organized Crime Index by the Swiss-based Global Initiative organization combating transnational organized crime, criminal synidicates are becoming more and more involved. These include the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion, CJNG) and the Sinaloa Cartel.

Within just one year, the number of incidents reported to authorities spiked by 45%.

India's lost children at risk in rail stations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, July 30, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) is calling for tighter, cross-border cooperation between judiciaries and law enforcement. Experts say that so far, only a fraction of the actual cases are being reported, let alone solved.

Perpetrators exploit vulnerabilities

Mixi Cruz was exploited by her own family. She was made to look after five children, and iron laundry until late at night. She still has scars on her hands, from when she'd fall asleep and burn herself with the iron, she says.

Not longer after, she was pressured into sex work for money. She was 14.

Many survivors don't know at the time that they are experiencing sexual violence, she says.

"Many think they're in love, or their own family sells them," Cruz explains. "From the time they're little, they're made to believe violence is normal, and just part of what love is."

Online sexual abuse of children in Philippines To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Mexico, the civil-society organization Consejo Ciudadano para la Seguridad y Justicia (Citizens' Council for Security and Justice) estimates that seven out of 10 human trafficking survivors are female. More than half of them are minors.

Hidden human trafficking figure much higher, experts say

"Human trafficking is a game of deceit, it involves a high level of emotional manipulation to isolate victims and prevent them from reaching out and building support networks," Gabriela Gonzalez Garcia explains. She is the director general of citizen services for the Citizens' Council.

Her organization runs Mexico's only specialized 24-hour hotline , as well as a live chat, for people affected by human trafficking. Since it was founded in 2007, the organization has counted some 26,000 cases. But the real number, Gonzalez says, is far higher, likely around 98%.

Ana Torres and three volunteers are in a red-light district near the edge of Mexico City. She's asked not to be mentioned by her real name. Now in her late 20s, she's been leading a street project for the past five years for El Pozo de Vida ("The Well of Life" in Spanish) that combats human trafficking and sexual exploitation. Each week, Torres and her colleagues visit a different part of Mexico's capital, speaking with the women there and offering help.

Gabriela Gonzalez Garcia heads the non-profit organization Consejo Ciudadano, which operates Mexico's only 24-hour hotline for human trafficking victims Image: Consejo Ciudadano/Oliver Villalobos Méndez

Before this year's soccer World Cup in Mexico, Canada and the United States, many sex workers had hoped for higher earnings, but Torres says the demand remained virtually unchanged. But what did increase noticeably was the number of foreign tourists, and with it, another source of danger for the women on the streets: the language barrier.

"Maybe they reach an agreement (with clients) on the street," Torres explained. "But what really happens when they get a room?"

Raising awareness for human trafficking

The UNODC and its Mexican partners the like Citizens' Council used campaigns like Mundial sin Trata ("A World Cup Without Human Trafficking" in Spanish) to make the tourism industry more aware of the increased risk of human trafficking during the World Cup. A popular driving service joined the campaign, and an online homestay operator teamed up with the UNODC to offer workshops for hosts.

But Cruz says she's skeptical that was enough to curb trafficking and exploitation.

"Men don't pay for sex because they traveled here just for that. They do it because an opportunity presents itself," Cruz said. "In any tourist district, people can tell you where to find prostitution, where you can find women, or children."

Mixi Cruz was forced into sexual exploitation by her own family. Today, she raises awareness for the issue to protect others Image: Bastian Kaiser

'They're locked away and guarded'

In the red-light district, it's starting to rain. Many sex workers have disappeared into nearby houses. A young woman is standing at the corner, wearing black high-heels, a short green dress, grey denim jacket, dark hair to her shoulders. Rain drops bounce off her umbrella. Ana Torres approaches her.

The young woman says she's worried about one of her colleagues, from Colombia, who's currently hiding somewhere in the city. She talks about a family of pimps that targets Colombians, luring them to Mexico with fake promises.

The pimp's wife, she says, has an iron grip on operations: "She makes them work 12 to 15 hours a day, they're not even allowed to eat alone," the woman told DW. "They're locked away and guarded in houses."

Ana Torres asks the woman to pass her organization's number on to her colleague who has fled. The young woman has tears streaming down her face as Ana Torres commends her for her courage to speak up for others.

On the way back, Ana says she's under the impression the pimps and their overseers were watching the women more closely that evening than they usually would. She says she's not quite sure why, but it worries her.

Trapped in the human trafficking network To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mixi Cruz was 16 when she finally managed to run away. Today, she's part of a survivors' network that visits schools and universities to raise awareness for human trafficking. Her stepsister was eventually sentenced to four years in prison, her stepsister's husband got five years. In the end, they weren't convicted for human trafficking, but for other serious offenses. But even that is unusual.

This article was translated from German.

If you or someone you know have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world.

World.title: Are Iran and Ukraine wars getting tangled in Caspian Sea?
World.content:
Tehran has threatened a response after a Ukrainian strike on a Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv says was carrying weapons to Russia. Still, Ukraine says it wants to avoid escalation with Tehran.

A recent Ukrainian strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea has drawn concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine and the war in Iran are becoming entangled.

Ukraine has said the ship was carrying military equipment from Iran to Russia. Iranian state media, citing Iran's ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, reported that the cargo vessel "Anna" was anchored approximately 5 kilometers (3 miles) from the entrance of the Volga River when it was attacked by drones causing an explosion. One sailor was reported killed.

Iran summoned Ukraine's charge d'affaires and described the incident as an act of aggression.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said Ukrainian forces had carried out successful long-range strikes against a Russian warship and vessels that Kyiv says were transporting military cargo.

Ukraine has long accused Iran of helping Russia wage war through the supply and development of Iranian-designed drones.

Tehran has acknowledged earlier drone sales to Moscow but has rejected accusations that it supplied weapons specifically for use in the Ukraine war.

However, the Ukrainian military has extensive documented physical evidence that Iranian-designed Shahed drones have been deployed throughout the war that has dragged on for more than four years.

How Ukraine shoots down Russia's drones on a budget To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In March 2026, Russia launched nearly 950 Shahed, Gerber and other types of attack drones at Ukraine in a 24-hour period, according to Ukraine's Air Force.

Iran's Foreign Ministry has accused Ukraine of attempting to expand the geographical scope of its war with Russia. Kyiv, by contrast, presents its attacks in the Caspian Sea as part of an effort to disrupt military logistics supporting Moscow.

Will Iran strike Ukraine?

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a statement the attack "cannot go unanswered."

However, Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, told DW that Tehran is unlikely to respond immediately with a direct military strike against Ukraine.

"I believe the Islamic Republic will avoid an emotional reaction and choose a diplomatic response instead of a military one," he said, pointing to Tehran's summoning of the Ukrainian diplomat and the possibility of raising the matter at the UN Security Council.

On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on X that Iran's accusations were "unjustified and groundless."

"The regime in Tehran is a direct accomplice to Russian aggression against Ukraine, fueling Moscow's criminal war with weapons that have killed Ukrainians since 2022," he wrote.

A day later, in a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Sybiha softened his tone and said that Ukraine wants to avoid unnecessary escalation with Iran.

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos considers the likelihood of an Iranian retaliatory attack on Ukraine to be very low.

"Attacks on ships or ports in the Caspian Sea are one thing, since this is related to Russia," which attacked Ukraine.

"However, an Iranian missile attack on Ukrainian territory is an entirely different matter. That would be a direct act of war," said Semyvolos, adding that such an attack "would only complicate the situation for Iran."

Austrian military expert Markus Reisner told DW that an Iranian missile attack on Ukraine is unlikely, even though Tehran possesses medium-range missiles.

Reisner said it would make little sense for Iran to actually launch a missile at a target on Ukrainian territory when there could be more important or higher-value targets elsewhere.

No 'new front' in Iran war

Reisner, currently head of research at Austria's Theresian Military Academy, added that the attack in the Caspian Sea does not indicate that Ukraine is now a participant in the Iran war.

Reisner points out that the Ukrainian military has been increasing attacks on maritime facilities, particularly in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea since May. Around 200 Russian ships, tankers, and tugboats have already been hit.

Ukraine's goal is not "to open a new front against Iran, but rather to disrupt supply routes between Iran and Russia in the Caspian Sea as well," said Reisner.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh said, however, that the attack "can be seen as a signal and an indication that the geography of the Ukrainian war is expanding from the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea."

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos agrees. He finds it logical that Ukraine would expand its strategy to control sea lanes for arms deliveries and attempt to impose a general economic naval blockade against Russia in the south.

Ukrainian coordination with the US?

There is no direct evidence that the operation in the Caspian Sea was coordinated with the US, and the issue has not been publicly discussed, Semyvolos said.

"But it's obvious that Ukraine uses American intelligence data. Therefore, the Americans were most likely aware of it," Semyvolos believes.

Austrian military analyst Reisner emphasizes that the timing of Ukraine's attack plays a crucial role.

"Zelenskyy wants to clearly demonstrate here that Kyiv and Washington share a common enemy in Iran," Reisner said.

The Ukrainian attack could also be seen as a demonstration from Kyiv that it is actually a better ally in fighting Iran than some NATO countries, he added.

Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, as ties between Kyiv and the Trump administration have turned positive along with Ukraine's advances on the battlefield.

Zelenskyy and Trump had perhaps their most cordial meeting this week in Washington Image: Zelenskyy Social Media Account/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Will Ukraine's Caspian Sea attacks continue?

As Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha's statement on X indicates, Kyiv increasingly sees Iran and Russia as part of the same military ecosystem.

And Ukraine has also demonstrated tactical momentum in carrying out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russian territory.

Ukrainian analyst Semyvolos expects Ukraine to continue its operations in the Caspian Sea. He explains the timing of the operation by noting that the Ukrainian military now has the technical ability to carry out long-range strikes.

However, if Ukraine again targets Iranian vessels, Tehran faces an uncomfortable strategic choice.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh argues that a direct Iranian military response against Ukrainian territory risks creating a new front at a time when Tehran is already confronting attacks now concentrated in southern Iran.

Vakhshiteh also suggested that Iran could instead look for indirect ways to impose costs on Ukraine, including measures against shipping connected to Ukrainian interests.

However, such options would carry their own considerable escalation risks and there is no indication that Tehran has decided to pursue them.

World.title: How crypto miners are stealing power in Southeast Asia
World.content:
Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids and exposing links to organized crime.

A raid in Malaysia last week exposed how cryptocurrency mining is becoming entangled with electricity theft and organized crime across Southeast Asia.

In Malaysia's southern state of Johor, 71 cryptocurrency-mining machines had been running around the clock across four rented premises for about a month before police moved in.

During the raids on July 22 and 23, officers arrested three suspects and seized computers, routers and vehicles alongside equipment used to illegally mine Bitcoin.

Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said the syndicate bypassed electricity meters, leading to an estimated €14,500 ($16,600) in losses in about a month, according to local media reports. The machines were thought to be generating between €17,200 and €21,500 in monthly revenue.

The case was relatively small by Malaysian standards. Between 2020 and 2025, national utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) identified almost 14,000 premises linked to electricity theft for cryptocurrency mining. Its cumulative losses reached around €1.1 billion.

Detected cases increased from 610 in 2018 to 2,397 in 2024, according to Malaysia's Energy Ministry, which has described illegal mining as a serious threat to public safety, economic stability and the national electricity system.

"In Malaysia, thousands of incidents have triggered investigations into illegal mining for cryptocurrency purposes," said Sonny Zulhuda, an associate professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

"This poses a huge problem for the security of electricity resources, economic sustainability, competition and revenue loss," Zulhuda told DW.

"Enforcement has been lagging behind due to a lack of legislative preparedness and limited agency capability in enforcement and investigation. This is unfortunate because Malaysia is fast developing its digital infrastructure."

Where crypto mining meets organized crime

Cryptocurrency mining is not inherently criminal. However, authorities are increasingly finding links between illegal crypto mining, online gambling, money laundering and Southeast Asia's industrial-scale cyber scam networks.

Last October, the United States and the UK sanctioned Cambodia-based Prince Group and associated companies, alleging that the network operated forced-labor scam compounds and laundered proceeds through cryptocurrencies and other assets.

US authorities also seized Bitcoin worth around $15 billion at the time from wallets whose private keys were held by Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi, describing the cryptocurrency as proceeds and instruments of fraud and money laundering.

Inside Cambodia's scam industry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thailand's Department of Special Investigation has made the clearest connection between stolen electricity and transnational crime.

In 2025, investigators dismantled three major illegal crypto mining networks, seized more than 6,390 machines and estimated losses to the Provincial Electricity Authority at more than €24.9 million.

In one operation, authorities found around 1,900 mining machines at warehouse sites. The electricity authority estimated that the network was consuming power worth around €575,000 each month while paying only a fraction of the amount due.

Indonesia has seen similar cases. In December 2023, police in the province of North Sumatra raided ten sites and seized more than 1,100 Bitcoin-mining machines. State utility PLN estimated losses over six months at around €700,000.

Governments have responded with raids, tougher penalties and cooperation between police, utilities, regulators and anti-corruption agencies. Malaysia has created a multi-agency committee and deployed smart meters at substations to identify abnormal consumption.

But enforcement remains difficult. Equipment can be moved quickly, premises can be rented through intermediaries and meter tampering may involve organized networks or insider assistance.

Saaidal Razalli Azzuhri, a telecommunications expert at the University of Malaya, told DW that raids should be supported by transformer-level monitoring, mandatory licensing, disclosure of companies' beneficial owners and investigations tracing bank transfers and cryptocurrency wallets.

"The objective should not be to prohibit blockchain technology, but to ensure that miners pay the full economic cost of their electricity and do not transfer their costs and infrastructure risks to the public," he said.

Zulhuda said that Southeast Asian governments need to deal with this issue properly so they don't send the wrong message to companies that want to invest in the region's growing digital sectors.

Malaysia has several laws to curb illegal cyber activities, including the Cyber Security Act 2024 to protect its National Critical Information Infrastructure and the recently enacted Cybercrimes Act 2026 to address digital system misuse and abuse, he added.

Laos pulls the plug

Laos shows that even legal, state-backed cryptocurrency mining can struggle to deliver the promised benefits.

Scam factory: Behind Asia's cyber slavery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In mid-2021, the government authorized six companies to mine and trade cryptocurrencies. The plan appeared suited to a country that had invested heavily in hydropower and sometimes produced more electricity than its economy could absorb. Mining offered a way to monetize surplus energy.

At its peak in 2021 and 2022, the industry consumed around 500 megawatts. But the surplus proved unreliable.

Some miners accumulated unpaid bills. More importantly, officials concluded that the industry created few jobs and little demand for domestic suppliers compared with manufacturing or other commercial activities.

Deputy Energy Minister Chanthaboun Soukaloun said last October that the government intended to end electricity supplies to miners.

Laos wants to redirect the power towards metals processing, electric-vehicle manufacturing and artificial-intelligence data centers, while increasing electricity exports to neighboring countries.

The experiment offered a broader warning. Cheap electricity can attract crypto miners, but it does not guarantee lasting investment or wider development. When operators steal power, or consume subsidized electricity without creating much value, the public is left carrying the cost.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: BMW to Volkswagen: How deep is Germany's auto industry cull?
World.content:
BMW joins VW, Porsche and Mercedes-Benz in cutting thousands of jobs, as Chinese rivals erode their market share. DW recaps the major reforms German automakers are pursuing to safeguard their future.

BMW makes five

BMW on Wednesday became the fifth German carmaker to announce major job cuts, as the country's auto sector seeks to tackle rising competition from China.

The Munich-based firm said it would cut up to 8,000 jobs globally, representing about 5% of its 154,000-strong workforce.

BMW, which also owns the Mini and Rolls-Royce brands, said the job losses would primarily affect operations in Germany and be achieved through natural staff turnover and a voluntary redundancy program.

Although BMW was seen as more resilient to Chinese competition, the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.

Chinese rivals have intensified competition for electric vehicles (EV), which has crushed BMW's sales volumes and pricing power.

Last year, BMW's vehicle deliveries in China dropped to their lowest level since 2017 and in the three months to June, they fell 30% year-on-year.

US PresidentDonald Trump's tariffs have also contributed to BMW's woes, along with higher energy prices from the Iran war and the growth of Chinese EV-makers in other major markets, including Europe, Asia Pacific and Latin America.

BMW joins other German automakers in announcing large job cuts Image: Jade Gao/AFP

On Thursday, the company disclosed that second-quarter net profit dropped 35% to €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion), while revenue fell to €31 billion from €34 billion.

BMW has adjusted its guidance for the rest of the year, warning of a "significant decline" in profit.

Are AI-powered robots German carmaker BMW's future? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even Porsche isn't immune

Two days earlier, Porsche announced plans to cut an additional 5,000 jobs in Germany by the end of 2035. The figure represents about 1 in 5 workers

The sports performance brand said the new measures would hit Porsche's main production plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen and its research and development (R&D) center in nearby Weissach.

Last year, Porsche announced a restructuring program to cut 1,900 jobs in the Stuttgart region by 2029 and allow 2,000 fixed-term contracts to expire.

The company will also defer wage increases, while performance bonuses will be more closely linked to profits.

Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen Group but run with a high degree of independence, has also reduced jobs at its Leipzig plant and is closing three subsidiaries that employ about 500 people.

At the end of last year, Porsche employed nearly 41,800 people, with about 85% of them in Germany.

Volkswagen plans the deepest cuts

Volkswagen, Europe’s largest carmaker, last month doubled its job-cull program, announcing plans to slash up to 100,000 jobs.

The company also wants to close four German factories.

Unions and the German state of Lower Saxony, which holds a 20% voting stake and can veto major decisions, have rejected the latest plans. VW had originally stated it would cut 50,000 positions.

VW is well-known for its oversized headcount of 630,000 globally — 680,000 including Chinese joint ventures.

The Wolfsburg-based giant employs around 60% more workers than Toyota, despite producing a similar number of vehicles.

Once a sign of German industrial strength, the huge workforce has become a costly burden amid intensifying competition from Chinese EV-makers.

VW controls more stages of production in-house than rivals, driving up labor demand, while German factory costs are often twice those of rivals.

Slow progress on electric vehicles further eroded sales in China, which once accounted for a third of VW’s total, as well as Europe.

VW is bringing out the axe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mercedes trims without mass firings

In March last year, Mercedes-Benz agreed with its works council plans to deliver €5 billion in savings by 2027.

However, the company ruled out compulsory redundancies at German plants, insisting that voluntary departures could achieve the reforms.

Until March this year, around 5,500 administration, R&D and IT workers accepted severance packages and left. Production workers remained protected.

Additional headcount reductions have been reported in the firm's China operations.

Last month, Mercedes postponed a bonus payment for nearly three-quarters of its German workforce until 2027 and proposed extending the work week from 35 to 40 hours without extra pay.

Mercedes bosses also indicated that some jobs could be moved abroad.

On Tuesday (July 28), Mercedes said it had written off more than €700 million due to fierce competition in China.

Although second-quarter net profit grew 13.5% to €1.09 billion, core earnings at its key cars division fell by a quarter to €909 million.

Audi's premium brand under pressure

VW-owned Audi last year announced plans to cut up to 7,500 jobs in Germany by the end of 2029.

The company has ruled out compulsory redundancies and said the job losses in administration and R&D would be achieved through voluntary schemes and early retirement.

Last month, however, Audi's Neckarsulm plant was listed for possible closure in 2030 by parent company VW. This could impact about 15,000 workers.

The site, which makes the A5, A6 and A8, has already cut production from 300,000 to 225,000 vehicles a year.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: Ceuta asks Spain to declare emergency over Morocco migrants
World.content:
Authorities in the Spanish city of Ceuta have asked Madrid to declare a national emergency and offer military assistance. Footage showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters to gain entry to the territory.

Officials in the Spanish territory of Ceuta on the northwestern tip of Africa on Thursday asked the government in Madrid to declare a national emergency and send the army to help secure its border with Morocco.

The call came as video footage showed crowds of people trying to walk around the breakwaters separating Moroccan and Spanish territory or otherwise scale the border fence. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged an "immediate response."

The AP news agency showed video footage shot by a freelance photographer of crowds reaching a beach and roads in the city, while Spanish news agency EFE reported that hundreds had climbed over protective barriers at places and a time when a police presence was not on hand.

A spokesman for Spain's Guardia Civil police told Reuters that migrants had overwhelmed police at the city's breakwater, after swimming over from the Moroccan side, and were entering en masse. They did not estimate how many people crossed the border.

In recent days, rescue parties had noted increased numbers of people trying to swim around the border checks.

The scenes were reminiscent of a similar flashpoint at the border crossing in May of 2021 when more than 8,000 people entered the territory in just two days.

The head of the regional government said its migrant reception center known as CETI had nearly a thousand people waiting outside. Here you see a much smaller crowd outside the facility on Sunday. [FILE: July 26, 2026.] Image: Antonio Sempere/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

What did the regional government say?

Juan Jesus Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, called for the Spanish government in Madrid to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border. This followed a meeting of the city's board of spokespeople, who reached a unanimous agreement.

"Yesterday, I spoke out to warn of the extreme gravity of the migration crisis we are enduring," Vivas wrote online. "Today, mere hours later, the situation is even more critical: another night of mass arrivals, nearly a thousand people waiting outside the CETI [Temporary Migrant Reception Center], our reseources completely overwhelmed, and another life lost at sea."

He said that the small city was facing "a humanitarian and social emergency" of national proportions.

"We cannot face this pressure alone — pressure that has resulted in the arrival of between 1,500 and 2,000 people in just 10 days, equivalent to 2% of our population."

He wrote that "with every passing hour, the situation becomes more difficult."

How did Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez respond?

Soon after the call for help from Ceuta, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government in Madrid was "fully committed to providing an immediate response" to the situation.

"We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necesssary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sanchez wrote, adding that he had just said as much directly to Vivas.

"This is the moment to build solutions, with responsibility and cooperation," he said, not going into specifics in the post.

Why is the rush happening now?

It's not yet clear why large groups are suddenly seeking entry to Ceuta in the past few days, even though a couple of relatively recent developments at least bear a tangential relationship to the issue.

Earlier in July, the Spanish Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not immediately be pushed back across a border in the same way as they could at a land border crossing.

The Ceuta and Melilla enclaves in North Africa bordering Morocco do present exceptional cases where this ruling is concerned, in that it is technically possible to enter them "by sea" despite the fact that you are essentially circumventing a border crossing on land, not crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mediterranean.

One less recent development that attracted international attention, meanwhile, is the Spanish government's offer of amnesty and residency permits to migrants who can demonstrate that they had already entered the country without legal authorization. However, that rule only applies to people who can prove they were already in Spain when it came into force, so it does nothing to improve the prospects of staying for people entering by irregular means now.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Eurozone sees GDP growth of 0.4%, most since early 2025
World.content:
Eurozone economies expanded by 0.4% in the second quarter of 2026, exceeding expectations and marking the strongest quarterly growth since early 2025.

The gross domestic product of the eurozone — which comprises the 21 countries that use the euro currency — grew by 0.4% in the second quarter of 2026, according to a preliminary estimate from Eurostat .

That rate exceeded economists' forecast of 0.2% for the bloc and was the largest growth since the first quarter of 2025.

Compared with the same quarter of the previous year, seasonally adjusted GDP increased by 1.0% in the euro area and by 1.2% in the European Union as a whole.

How did individual economies perform?

Economic growth varied sharply among member states. Ireland recorded the highest quarterly growth rate at 3.9%, followed by Lithuania at 1.7%.

Economists have long cautioned that Ireland's economic growth numbers can be highly volatile because of the outsized influence of large multinational companies that have chosen the country as a European base.

At the other end of the scale, Austria and Belgium recorded no growth during the quarter.

What's fueling economic growth in Spain? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Major economies post modest gains

The eurozone's largest economies delivered steady, if modest, growth, despite the adverse economic impacts of the US-Iran war.

The bloc's economic heavyweights — Germany, France and Italy — expanded by 0.2%, during the quarter, while Spain, one of the bloc's strongest performers in recent years, posted growth of 0.7%.

World.title: Wildberries, el ‘Amazon ruso’, en el punto de mira de Ucrania
World.content:
Kiev ha intensificado desde hace una semana sus ataques contra el mayor minorista en línea de Rusia, en medio de una escalada general de la guerra lanzada por Putin

La guerra entre Rusia y Ucrania no tiene vistas de acabarse pronto, con instalaciones nuevas sumándose al listado de objetivos cada día. Wildberries, conocido como el equivalente ruso de Amazon y el mayor minorista en línea del país, es el blanco más reciente de Kiev. Los últimos ataques han ocurrido este jueves contra dos almacenes de la compañía, en las regiones de Penza (centro de la parte europea de Rusia), Udmurtia (al oeste de los Urales) y Perm (Urales). Por ahora, se han registrado al menos ocho ataques contra almacenes de la compañía desde el inicio de la nueva campaña de Kiev, el pasado día 18.

Los drones han causado daños en casi una docena de almacenes de Wildberries, destruyendo alrededor del 10% de su capacidad de almacenamiento y provocando pérdidas a decenas de miles de pequeñas empresas que utilizan la plataforma, según informa Reuters, citando a la propia empresa y autoridades locales, aunque la agencia sostiene que no ha podido verificar de manera independiente la totalidad de los informes. Una persona resultó herida y unas 200 personas fueron evacuadas de las instalaciones en Penza.

¿Qué es Wildberries?

Wildberries es el mercado digital más conocido de Rusia. Fundado en 2004 por Tatyana Kim, una antigua profesora de inglés y madre de siete hijos, que se convirtió en emprendedora, ahora multimillonaria, y la mujer más rica de Rusia, según Forbes. Actualmente, su patrimonio neto se calcula en 8.100 millones de dólares (7.060 millones de euros). La revista la situó en el puesto número 18 de las mujeres más ricas del mundo que han hecho fortuna por sí mismas.

Conocida a nivel mundial como el ‘Amazon ruso’, la empresa presume de procesar más de siete millones de pedidos diarios y cuenta con más de 110 millones de usuarios activos, según el ICEX, el organismo público español dedicado a la internacionalización de las empresas. Al igual que la multinacional estadounidense, Wildberries ofrece una amplia variedad de productos, desde moda y electrónica hasta herramientas y artículos de belleza, lo que resulta en un tráfico de consultas que supera los 1.000 millones de consultas de compra cada día.

Cuenta asimismo con un servicio de reserva para billetes de aviones, hoteles, tours y experiencias para turistas, además de una plataforma de compra y venta de segunda mano y un servicio de seguimiento para los pedidos.

La empresa gestiona el mayor negocio de comercio electrónico del país con un volumen de 6,1 billones de rublos (unos 66.800 millones de euros) en base a datos del año pasado, informa Efe.

¿Por qué Ucrania ataca sus instalaciones?

Ucrania ha acusado a Wildberries de suministrar al ejército ruso piezas para drones y otro tipo de equipamiento, aunque la empresa ha desmentido estas acusaciones, informa The Moscow Times. En la misma línea, el think tank británico Chatham House añade que Kiev ha justificado los ataques asegurando que las instalaciones de la compañía se estaban utilizando para almacenar material militar, incluidos componentes de drones.

Por otro lado, los ataques contra Wildberries también buscan aumentar la presión económica sobre Rusia. Según los medios británicos The Guardian y The Independent, que citan a un ejecutivo de Fire Point, empresa ucrania líder en tecnología y defensa, el ‘Amazon ruso’ está en el punto de mira de Kiev debido a su asociación con el banco VTB, controlado por el Estado ruso.

Una imagen de satélite muestra el humo que se eleva desde las instalaciones de Wildberries en San Petersburgo, el 24 de julio. 2026 PLANET LABS PBC (via REUTERS)

El miércoles, Reuters informó de que el Gobierno ruso estaba estudiando formas de apoyar a Wildberries y a otras empresas relacionadas tras los ataques con drones ucranios, y se espera que VTB desempeñe un papel fundamental en ello. La agencia británica añadió que el Kremlin había reconocido que se habían mantenido conversaciones en el seno del Gobierno sobre un posible apoyo, pero señaló que aún no se había tomado ninguna decisión.

Los ataques contra almacenes de la compañía empezaron en la noche del 17 al 18 de julio, y tuvieron como objetivo las instalaciones situadas en Kotovsk (región de Tambov) y Elektrostal, cerca de Moscú. Wildberries informó de que ocho personas fallecieron. El segundo gran ataque se llevó a cabo unos días después, en la noche del 21 al 22 de julio, contra los centros logísticos de Krasnodar y Nevinnomyssk.

“Ha sido una noche terrible, con sucesos terribles para nuestra empresa y nuestro país. Es un dolor que no se puede describir con palabras”, escribió Kim en Telegram tras los ataques en Krasnodar y Nevinnomyssk. “Simplemente no hay palabras para expresar los sentimientos y las emociones que provocan los ataques contra la gente corriente, contra nuestros empleados, contra todos nosotros, que simplemente estamos haciendo nuestro trabajo”, añadió la propietaria de Wildberries.

El periódico digital ucranio Ukrainska Pravda subraya que, en línea con un discurso del presidente Volodímir Zelenski tras los primeros ataques, la ofensiva lanzada contra las instalaciones de Wildberries representaría una respuesta a los ataques rusos contra la infraestructura civil de Ucrania, y destaca principalmente los llevados a cabo contra la empresa de correos Nova Poshta. Cita asimismo a un alto cargo ucranio que, en declaraciones a The Financial Times, confirmó el motivo de la represalia.

¿Cómo impacta a la sociedad rusa?

Desde el inicio de la ofensiva de Rusia contra Ucrania, la sociedad rusa depende cada vez más de las compras en línea, o e-commerce, debido a las sanciones impuestas por Occidente y las dificultades económicas que atraviesa el país por los elevados costes y daños ocasionados por la guerra, ya que las plataformas digitales permiten a los consumidores comparar fácil y rápidamente los precios.

Varias personas esperan cerca de una pantalla en la que se anuncia la tienda 'online' Wildberries en Moscú, este martes. Anastasia Barashkova (REUTERS)

Chatham House afirma que la red de Wildberries representa más del 50% de todos los pedidos minoristas en línea de Rusia, por lo que la nueva estrategia de Kiev acerca aún más el conflicto a los ciudadanos rusos.

World.title: Rosa Vañó (Castillo de Canena): “Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego con las que he trabajado”
World.content:
Economista de formación, dejó su exitosa carrera de directiva en Coca-Cola para desarrollar, junto a su hermano Francisco, la explotación olivarera que había creado su padre en Jaén. Además, conoce muy bien el mundo de las discográficas ya que trabajó para Warner Music y Universal

Es la gran dama del aceite español. Rosa Vañó (Madrid, 63 años), economista de formación, abandonó una exitosa carrera como directiva de Coca-Cola, donde se dedicaba al desarrollo de nuevas líneas de negocio, lanzamientos y reposicionamiento de productos, para dedicarse, junto a su hermano Francisco, al sueño que inició su padre, Luis Vañó: impulsar Castillo de Canena, una explotación olivarera con almazara situada en Canena (Jaén), propiedad de su familia y reconocida con numerosos premios nacionales e internacionales. Anteriormente trabajó en las discográficas Warner Music y Universal, “donde aprendí a gestionar egos y a entender que hay que contar con los medios de comunicación como embajadores y transmisores de la creatividad y el valor añadido de los músicos”. Ejerce también como tesorera de la Real Academia de Gastronomía.

Pregunta. Con este bagaje, decide desarrollar su propio negocio.

Respuesta. Sí, porque teníamos la enorme suerte de tener campo, almazara y también el castillo. Se puede empezar de cero, pero de distintas formas. Es un recorrido profesional que te va formando y quitando miedos. La ignorancia es muy valiente y te hace creer que puedes hacer las cosas mejor, de forma diferente y de manera especial. Todo esto cuesta mucho trabajo. Primero, porque no es fácil hacerlo y porque hay mucha gente que lo hace igual o mejor que tú. Al final, la fórmula no es otra que trabajo, pero bien entendido.

P. ¿Qué significa esto?

R. El trabajo no son horas, es calidad y flexibilidad. Los peores resultados los he tenido cuando he trabajado 14 horas al día. He sido menos resolutiva y creativa. Me parece importante la conectividad para mi conciliación como madre, como hija y como profesional. Son las tres prioridades de mi vida. El teléfono me permite tener mi sitio de trabajo en cualquier lugar.

P. Comentaba que sabe manejar los egos. ¿Se ha encontrado con muchos?

R. Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego que he conocido y con la que he trabajado en mi vida. Me tocó trabajar con ella en promoción y en gira. Por el contrario, con Phil Collins o los hermanos Young [Malcolm y Angus], de AC/DC, me he divertido mucho. Son personas que han dejado el ego a un lado. Y no tiene nada que ver con que sean hombres o mujeres. Por ejemplo, Prince era un hombre que tenía inseguridades, pero con una gestión muy peculiar de su ego. Porque el ego no es solo el de tipo Madonna, en el que tienes que interpretar su gestión, sino también cómo se siente, cómo es su timidez y cómo tienes que relacionarte con él. Seal tampoco era una persona fácil. Fue mi primer artista y era complicado de manejar.

P. ¿Qué se hace en esos casos?

R. Callar, entender y destensar la situación, aunque no tengas la culpa. Hay que intentar destensar y tratar de ser empático y resolutivo. El ego es más complejo que creerse superior, por eso hay que entender cómo es la personalidad de cada uno. Ha sido una gran escuela de vida.

P. Salir a vender aceite por el mundo habrá sido mucho más fácil, ¿no?

R. La primera vez que salí a vender aceite fue en España. Entré en un restaurante, que no voy a decir cuál, por la puerta principal. Me preguntaron a qué iba y les dije que a vender aceite. Me dijeron que eso era por la puerta de proveedores, que estaba por detrás, donde estaban los cubos de basura y los cascos de botellas. Entré por ahí. Hoy, si no me dicen lo contrario, siempre entro por la puerta de proveedores. Entiendo que, si el cocinero me tiene que recibir en su cocina para probar el aceite, esa es la puerta. Hay que entender cada situación.

P. ¿Ha hecho mucha calle?

R. Al principio hay que hacer mucha calle. Ahora también, pero tenemos más gente que te ayuda. Estoy en un momento de mi vida en el que tengo que mirarlo todo con mucha positividad. Lo mejor es hoy y tengo que estar preparada para el día de mañana. Debe haber un relevo. Hay decisiones que ya no me toca tomar a mí, sino al equipo, a mi sobrino y a mi hijo [ambos se llaman Luis y llevan el apellido Vañó]. Me pueden pedir opinión, pero no puedo empecinarme en que la decisión es mía porque hay gente alrededor que tiene que liderar. Odiaría ser la típica persona que es la primera que llega a la oficina y la última que se va. O la que va todos los días, con 80 años, a ver qué pasa.

P. ¿A qué dedica el resto del tiempo cuando no trabaja?

R. Voy a ir por orden de frivolidad. Me gusta jugar al golf; hago pilates tres días a la semana, que me divierte mucho, y camino. Soy una gran aficionada a viajar, pero con causa. Mi afición siempre ha sido la antropología, la arqueología y el arte antiguo. Me ha interesado saber cuándo el hombre deja de ser animal y adquiere un toque divino o humano. Me gusta viajar con contenido, por ejemplo, para ver el románico del norte de España, el misterio de las catedrales, conocer culturas antiguas... Es algo que no he hecho en los últimos años todo lo que me habría gustado y me gustaría retomarlo. Coger un barco y recorrer las esclusas francesas, pararte en los vignerons y vas viendo el paisaje, me gusta. Me voy a dedicar a viajar más. También he descuidado mucho mi afición a las exposiciones. Antes iba prácticamente todos los meses a ver dos exposiciones en Madrid y, si tenía que irme fuera, también lo hacía. Pero ahora, por mi situación personal, he descuidado un poco esa faceta. Me encantaba ir con toda la familia a ver una exposición y luego irnos a comer. Me parece gratificante. Adoro leer.

P. ¿Cuál es su género preferido?

R. Leo mucha historia, pero como formo parte de varias tertulias literarias me hacen leer todo tipo de libros. Uno de los más recientes ha sido Historia de una escalera. También acabo de leer varias obras de Hermann Hesse para una tertulia. Me esfuerzo por leer cosas diferentes de las que suelo leer durante el insomnio.

P. ¿Qué lee en esas noches en vela?

R. Leo a Agatha Christie y a sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Quiero lecturas ligeras para quedarme dormida. La ópera me ha encantado toda la vida. He estado en distintos teatros, como el Bolshói o La Scala de Milán. Verdi y Puccini me encantan porque mi madre me los ponía de pequeña. Voy a cuatro o cinco óperas al año. También me encanta la música barroca. No me pierdo los ciclos de Händel en el Auditorio Nacional de Música de Madrid.

P. ¿Qué restaurantes frecuenta?

R. Tanto de producto y muy clásicos como sorprendentes y de vanguardia. Me gustan los dos extremos. Estuve hace poco en Desde 1911 y trabaja con un gran producto. También me gustan las verduras de Saddle o el ganso de Navidad, que tomo con mis hijos. Los atunes guisados de El Campero me encantan. No me gustan los crudos. Estuve hace poco en Tetsu y me pareció espectacular y divertido. De Jaén me gustan Juan Carlos García, de Vandelvira, y Pedro Sánchez, de Bagá; también Dani Carnero, del restaurante Kaleja en Málaga. Son maravillosos. Y José Álvarez, en la costa de Almería, con su proyecto de tomates.

P. ¿Su desayuno preferido?

R. Una tostada de pan bien caliente, restregada con ajo, aceite de oliva virgen extra y sal. El ajo es maravilloso de todas las maneras. No soy muy cafetera, tomo uno al día. Me gusta su olor, pero no tanto el sabor.

P. ¿Le gusta darse caprichos?

R. No, salvo gastronómicos. Comprarme ropa siempre tiene que ser algo organizado. Hace años, una compañera de trabajo me dijo que salía con la misma ropa en todas las fotografías. Nunca se lo agradeceré lo suficiente porque no había caído en ello. Soy muy estructurada con lo que me pongo, pero ir de compras me aburre. También me aburren las obras en casa y comprar cosas para decorarla.

P. ¿Tiene algún viaje pendiente?

R. Cuando era pequeña leí los libros de Jack London y sus viajes a los mares del Sur. Por eso me atrae la Polinesia, aunque luego quizá sea un coñazo y tenga que llevarme 200 libros, preguntándome qué hago yo en un palafito. Me gustaría conocerla. También me gustaría ver una aurora boreal. La Antártida me resulta muy atractiva. Y me apetecería hacer un viaje en barco entre Moscú y San Petersburgo.

P. ¿Algún remedio para el insomnio?

R. La edad no perdona. He probado todo lo que no es químico y, a veces, funciona y otras no. Ya convivo con él, incluso cuando estoy de vacaciones en Granada, frente al mar Mediterráneo, al que tanto quiero. Lo que no me gusta es pensar por la noche porque es muy mala compañera. También escucho pódcasts ligeros y de true crime; eso me evade y evita que me invadan los malos pensamientos, porque soy una persona muy positiva y estable.

World.title: One person dies, six injured in crash between lorry and minibus
World.content:
One person has died and six others have been seriously injured in a head-on collision between a minibus and a lorry in Overijssel.

The crash happened on the N48 near Balkbrug, around 20km east of Zwolle, at around 11.30am on Thursday. All the victims were sitting in the minibus, which had Belgian numberplates.

Fire appliances, ambulances and an air ambulance were called to the crash site. Six passengers were taken to different hospitals in the area, while the seventh was pronounced dead at the scene. The lorry driver was unharmed.

The road is likely to be closed for several hours while police carry out investigations and the road is cleared of debris.

World.title: University launches ethics probe into Red Bull professor’s work
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Utrecht University has begun an investigation into its pharmacology department after a professor was accused of not declaring payments for research from companies, including energy drinks manufacturer Red Bull.

Joris Verster published several papers on energy drinks and alcohol in his capacity as associate professor, without disclosing that he was also paid as a consultant for Red Bull and US-based Sen-Jam Pharmaceuticals.

The university does not prohibit consultancy work, but academics are required to disclose any relevant secondary activities when they publish papers under conflict of interest rules.

The investigation follows reports in several Dutch and international media outlets, including Trouw, De Groene Amsterdammer and Investico, that Verster’s research was published without any reference to his paid work for Red Bull and Sen-Jam.

Verster set up a private company, NeuroClinics, for his consultancy work, which frequently overlapped with his academic research.

Hangover pill

He carried out a study into a hangover pill produced by Sen-Jam which concluded, based on a questionnaire circulated around his students, that the medicine did not encourage people to consume more alcohol.

Mariëtte van den Hoven, professor of medical ethics at Amsterdam’s UMC medical centre, said Verster’s methods amounted to a conflict of interest “by using the university to promote your personal goals.”

Another study, published in 2010, concluded that drinking a can of Red Bull improved driving performance, based on observing drivers for four hours in a simulator. It was publicised under the heading “Can Red Bull fuel better driving?”

Verster also published research that disputed claims that mixing energy drinks with alcohol were damaging to people’s health and could lead to aggressive behaviour or unsafe sexual practices.

His conclusion was that combining the drinks meant users consumed less alcohol and were less prone to reckless behaviour.

Sick leave

Verster himself, who has been on sick leave since the start of May, told Trouw he had always been transparent about his private work.

“I have been a consultant for many companies and stated it in all my papers, even when it concerned a minor role,” he said. “I informed Utrecht University about my work as a consultant and the university approved it.”

World.title: Eighth species of American crayfish found in Dutch rivers
World.content:
A new species of crayfish has been found in Dutch rivers, the eighth type to establish itself in the Netherlands after being introduced in the upper Rhine.

The calico crayfish (Faxonius immunis), originally from North America, was spotted in Gelderland by ecologist Pim Lemmers, who first encountered the creatures in a nature reserve near Karlsruhe decades ago.

“I’d been expecting them and looking out for them for a while,” he told NOS. “Last year I found a crayfish pincer and I knew straight away that it might be a significant one.“

The discovery of the pincer, together with the results of DNA samples, are enough to confirm that the crayfish have made it to the Dutch river system.

The water authority in Rivierland has reported the presence of the crayfish to the food standards regulator NVWA, which will in turn notify the European Union, and triggered the protocol for dealing with invasive exotic species.

The Dutch agriculture ministry has set up a working group to investigate how the crayfish can be prevented from spreading. Crayfish damage the local environment by eating indigenous plants and animals and digging in river banks.

“We’re at a very uncertain stage, because are they just in the Klompenwaard area of the Rhine or are they already in our regional waters? Can we keep them out of the waters?” said José Vos, senior policy adviser for the water board.

World.title: Post-Covid fatigue not just caused by inactivity, study finds
World.content:
Patients with post-Covid syndrome suffer muscle damage that cannot be fully be explained by inactivity, research led by scientists at Amsterdam’s Vrije Universiteit (VU) has found.

The team compared the blood and muscle tissue of patients with long Covid and chronic fatigue (ME) with a group of healthy people who spent 60 days in bed as part of a study simulating the effects of space travel.

The post-Covid and ME patients had suffered from energy dips that caused them to avoid exercising or spend long periods in bed, which has a degrading impact on the skeletal muscles.

But the researchers, led by Rob Wüst, a movement scientist at the VU, found differences in the colour of the muscle fibres between the two groups, indicating that the post-Covid patients had a much lower oxygen capacity.

“As skeletal muscle characteristics differ between patients and healthy individuals after bed rest, physical inactivity cannot solely explain the lower exercise capacity and skeletal muscle adaptations in long Covid and ME/CFS patients,” they wrote in a paper published in Nature Communications.

The healthy individuals from the space programme still had bright red fibres, which are still oxygen-rich, while the patients had white fibres, which become exhausted much faster.

Rapid tiredness

The researchers said the difference could explain why post-Covid and ME sufferers become tired so quickly even after modest levels of exercise or exertion. “The redder the fibres, the more stamina a person has,” Wüst explained.

Lung specialist Merel Hellemons, of the Erasmus MC teaching hospital in Rotterdam, told the Volkskrant that the findings were a crucial development in understanding how to treat patients with conditions such as post-Covid syndrome.

“Many patients hear that they need to move more or that being less active is bad for them,” she said.

Wüst said patients should still be encouraged to be more mobile to avoid damage to their muscles, skeletons and cardiovascular system caused by inactivity. “The question is: what is possible? We need more tailored solutions,” he said.

Dutch airline KLM booked a higher-than-expected profit in the first half of the year, despite the rise in fuel prices caused by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

The company reported revenue of €6.9 bn in the six months to June, an 8% increase compared to the same period last year.

The airline benefited from a decrease in flights from competitors like Qatar Airways and Emirates because of the unrest in the region.

“The measures we are implementing are having a positive impact on our results,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement.

Those measures included passing on higher fuel prices to customers, particularly on long-haul flights.

Yesterday, the Air France-KLM airline group announced they had put in an offer for a stake in Portugal’s TAP airline. Lisbon said last year that it was seeking a major international airline to buy most of the 49.9 percent stake that it planned to sell.

German airline Lufthansa also submitted a bid.

World.title: Man who strangled partner jailed after new forensic method used
World.content:
A man has been convicted of attempting to kill his partner in the first case to use new techniques to detect signs of strangulation in domestic violence.

The 33-year-old man from Rozenburg grabbed the woman by the neck as an argument turned violent last November. Police were alerted by neighbours and pulled the man away from his victim, who later said she was “turning blue”.

She was examined by a medical specialist using a new procedure developed in Rotterdam to gather forensic evidence faster in suspected cases of strangulation.

The doctor said the attack could have been fatal if it was prolonged, a detail that allowed prosecutors to argue that the attack should be classed as attempted manslaughter.

The procedure was introduced last December to try to detect strangulation, which is seen as an early warning sign of femicide, in domestic abuse investigations before the victim’s injuries heal and the evidence disappears.

200 referrals

The medical agency FARR, based in Rotterdam, anticipated receiving 200 inquiries a year, but was called on 150 times in the first three months. In 92% of cases doctors concluded the injuries could have been caused by strangulation. Nine in 10 victims were female and 78% of inquiries were related to domestic violence.

“It’s a huge number,” the agency’s managing director Geranda Zeelenberg told NOS. “Previously we hardly ever saw these people. They were probably always there, but the research we’ve begun has increased awareness of these cases.”

The man from Rozenburg was sentenced to 360 days in prison for attempted manslaughter, including 169 days suspended, and a community service order of 150 hours, in line with the prosecution’s demands.

His lawyer told the court he had no recollection of the events on the night of the attack because he had been taking alcohol and amphetamines, but argued that he had attacked her to try to force her to have sex rather than attempting to kill her.

World.title: Middle East conflict adds to pressure to fill Dutch gas reserves
World.content:
The Netherlands is lagging behind its European partners in filling its gas reserves for the winter, just as a key supplier in the Middle East has announced further restrictions on supplies caused by the conflict between the US and Iran.

QatarEnergy extended “force majeure” restrictions on its LNG cargoes until the end of September, affecting a total of 24 cargoes to European customers.

The company signed a contract to supply up to 3.5 million tonnes of liquified gas to the Netherlands per annum, which came into force this year, but the invocation of force majeure has put this commitment in jeopardy.

The Netherlands’ gas reserves are currently at 36.6% capacity, well below the EU average of 56%.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which triggered a spike in prices, the EU set a target of reaching 90% capacity by November 1. Since then European nations have had to find alternatives to Russian gas.

The Netherlands achieved this level for the first three years, but in 2025 it peaked at just 74% and at the start of April this year the four Dutch storage facilities were at less than 5% capacity.

Energy minister Stientje van Veldhoven said last month she was “confident” that the gas reserves would be filled for the winter, but admitted that the government needed to be “vigilant”.

Demand for gas has also increased during the summer as more consumer and businesses install air conditioning, putting more pressure on energy.

The Dutch government also has agreements to buy gas from Norway and the United States, or could resort to the open market.

The wholesale price of gas on the TTF market, operated by Gasunie, has risen by 50% since mid-June as a result of ongoing attacks by Iran and the US on facilities in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Sitting targets: thieves make off with 88 museum cafe chairs
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Thieves walked off with all of the chairs from the Bonnefanten Museum café in Maastricht in the early hours of Monday.

Café manager Freek Joosten told local news network L1 that camera footage showed the perpetrators making several trips carrying stacks of chairs at around 4am.

The designer seats are valued at more than €21,000.

The chairs were tied down with iron cables and the grounds are monitored by multiple cameras. The museum has reported the theft to the police.

The museum, which sits on Avenue Céramique in the Limburg capital, specialises in visual arts.

The terrace was recently renovated and the chairs were from designer Fermob Luxembourg. The thieves also took a waste container.

Visitors are still welcome in the café. Joosten has temporarily reallocated the chairs from his catering business to use on the terrace.

Police have asked anyone who saw anything unusual in the vicinity on the night of July 26 to 27, or who may have camera footage, to contact them.

Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped Poland improve its international recognition. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. An unidentified object was detected in Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m. travelling westward, DORSZ said. An F-16 fighter jet was dispatched to identify and intercept it. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. “This initial information clearly indicates that the relevant services, the military, our pilots, and our aircraft acted very quickly and efficiently. There was no immediate threat due to the missile falling in an undeveloped area,” Tusk said. He added that he had discussed the incident with opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. An early warning system was activated in Lublin and several other areas of the province because of Russian air attacks on Ukraine. The alarm lasted about 13 minutes, according to the interior minister. The opposition criticised the authorities for not providing residents with further information about the reason for the alarm. “A few minutes of alarm, no information in the mainstream media about what was happening, some residents didn’t even hear the sirens, and no text messages with an alert from the Government Centre for Security (RCB),” wrote Michał Dworczyk, a Law and Justice (PiS) MP, on social media. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski defended the decision to sound the alarm. “If it hadn’t been for that alarm, if those sirens hadn’t gone off, and if the object hadn’t landed in a field but instead in a block of flats, a house or any other place where it could have caused injury or, God forbid, death,” he told Polsat News. Polish airspace has been violated several times in recent years by objects entering from the direction of Ukraine amid the war there. In September last year, an estimated 20 Russian military drones were recorded repeatedly violating Polish airspace. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.title: Newly sworn-in judge of Poland’s constitutional court stages boycott over blocked colleagues
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A newly sworn-in judge of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has said he will refuse to sit on the court until four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year, but blocked by the president, are allowed to take their seats. It is the latest development in a months-long dispute between the opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki and the government, which considers the TK to be improperly staffed and therefore illegitimate. Although Nawrocki swore in Sławomir Patyra, who was appointed by the ruling majority in parliament in June, as a TK judge on Tuesday, he continues to refuse to swear in four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year. Po złożeniu przysięgi Patyra ogłosił, że zamierza odmówić orzekania. To gest solidarności z czwórką sędziów, od których prezydent nie chce przyjąć przysięgi https://t.co/jdbKusQ3H9 — OKO.press (@oko_press) July 28, 2026 Shortly after his swearing-in ceremony at the presidential palace on Tuesday, Patyra arrived at the TK headquarters in Warsaw, where he was accompanied by four other judges appointed by parliament this year, including two whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. There, he announced that his decision not to sit on the court was a matter of loyalty to the constitution and his belief in judicial ethos. “I cannot imagine taking an oath today to uphold the constitution, only to start breaking that constitution tomorrow,” he said. Patyra told journalists that he would “submit a declaration of refusal to adjudicate” due to his solidarity with judges who are “unlawfully deprived of the chance to participate in the work of the tribunal”. He added that, along with the other judges chosen this year, he is “fully mobilised to restore the Constitutional Tribunal to its proper, constitutional, systemic form”. Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK, the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, TK’s chief justice Bogdan Święczkowski has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again later in the month, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. After repeated requests, Nawrocki finally decided last week to invite Patyra to the presidential palace. The president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, noted that “there were some doubts” but “the president dispelled them” and added that Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”. Nowo wybrany przez Sejm Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej uchwałą z dnia 11 czerwca 2026 r. sędzia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Sławomir Patyra złożył wobec Prezydenta RP ślubowanie. pic.twitter.com/VLMRAIg1Yj — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
