World.title: Parents of Australian facing possible death penalty in Syria question confession
World.content:
The family of a Gold Coast man facing a possible death penalty for allegedly murdering another Australian in Syria has gone public to express frustration at the lack of progress made by the federal government in the case.

Patrick Stevenson, 20, has been detained for nearly seven months in north-western Syria accused of the shooting murder of Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess, 40, from northern New South Wales.

Mr Stevenson's mother, Angela Bell, said Australian officials had told her diplomatic efforts had gone nowhere.

She told the ABC she was disappointed by her dealings with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT).

Patrick Stevenson travelled to Syria late last year. (Supplied)

"They say … that their policy is that he shouldn't have been travelling to Syria … and that's where the conversation gets stuck," she told the ABC's 7.30 program.

"They use the word 'limited' a lot. They don't use the word failure, but basically the sense is they … have limited capacity to help in this situation."

The ABC has established that Mr Burgess was a tree lopper from the village of Eltham, near Lismore, who spent months in Afghanistan before settling in Syria last year with his Australian wife and their daughters.

Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess was shot dead in the town of Darkush on December 31, 2025. (Supplied)

According to Syrian authorities, Mr Burgess was shot dead in his home in the town of Darkush in Idlib province on December 31, while his wife and daughters were in another room.

Mr Stevenson was arrested nearby soon afterwards and later charged with premeditated murder, an offence punishable by death in Syria.

Syrian authorities allege he confessed to firing at least eight shots from an AK-47 at Mr Burgess.

But his family and Australian legal team say they do not know how the alleged confession was obtained and have raised serious concerns about whether he will receive a fair trial.

"Not a single document has come from Syria explaining the charges," Ms Bell said.

"There's no paperwork, there's no access to Patrick."

No Australian government representative has visited Mr Stevenson in prison, attended his court hearings or independently assessed his welfare.

Clay Stevenson says his son's health has deteriorated severely. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

Last week, Mr Stevenson's father, Clay, travelled to Syria carrying his son's Australian medical records and a psychiatric report for the court.

He visited Mr Stevenson in Sarmada prison and attended a court hearing on Sunday — the first time a member of the family had seen him since he secretly left Australia last October.

His parents say his mental health has deteriorated severely in detention.

Mr Stevenson has learning disorders, ADHD and probable autism spectrum disorder, according to a 2025 psychiatric report.

He travelled to Syria late last year and came to the attention of counterterrorism police after becoming radicalised, an ABC investigation has established.

Do you know more? Contact Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop on Signal: @seanrdunlop.01 and on Protonmail: seanrdunlop@protonmail.com

on Signal: and on Protonmail: Please use this form to get in contact with the ABC Investigations team, or if you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

The family's Australian lawyer, Bernadette Zaydan, said the alleged confession raised "alarm bells" because it was unclear how it had been obtained.

"Was it given under duress? Was it given in writing? Was it given orally?" she said.

"We have grave concerns for his welfare."

Ms Zaydan urged the federal government to press for Mr Stevenson to receive a transparent trial before an independent court, rather than one associated with Syria's administration or armed forces.

Canberra struggling to gain access

The ABC understands Australia has made representations about Mr Stevenson's case, but DFAT told his family last month that the Syrian government had shown little engagement.

Correspondence seen by the ABC shows the department repeatedly told the family it could not obtain information from Syrian authorities and had no access to the country's detention facilities.

Australia has no embassy or consulate in Syria, severely limiting the consular assistance it can provide.

Canberra has also been unable to independently monitor the investigation into Mr Burgess's death.

After the ABC revealed the case, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that Australia was providing support to both families.

"Legal processes will take their course overseas, of course, and that is appropriate," he said.

"I feel for the family of the person who's lost their life, and we're connected to them and providing support for them.

"We're also providing support for the family of the man who's been charged."

But Canberra has struggled to establish relations with Syria's new government, unlike allies including the United States and France.

Australia continues to impose sanctions on Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the militant group from which Syria's new leadership emerged, and lists it as a terrorist organisation.

The group, which formally dissolved last year, was previously affiliated with Al Qaeda.

Parents discovered police were investigating son

Mr Stevenson left Australia on a flight to Bali on October 10 before travelling to Syria.

His parents said they had no idea he had left the country.

"I was shocked to find out that he was there," Clay Stevenson said.

"It's just like, 'Wow, what's going through his head to be in Syria and who helped him get there?'"

Patrick Stevenson's parents said he told them he intended to study at a Syrian university and hoped to find a wife.

They tried desperately to convince him to return home.

Patrick Stevenson is facing a possible death penalty in Syria. (Supplied)

The family said they discovered he was overseas only after officers from the Queensland Police Security and Counter-Terrorism Command contacted them.

His parents said officers searched his bedroom at his father's home and questioned them about extremist material he had allegedly posted in a group chat.

"He was talking to someone in a group chat that the Australian government were investigating and Patrick had come up as peripheral to another investigation," Ms Bell said.

She said ASIO later questioned her about her son's associations on the Gold Coast.

Mr Stevenson converted to Islam during his final year of high school in 2023, according to his family.

Patrick Stevenson converted to Islam in his final year of high school in 2023. (Supplied)

By last year, he was showing signs of radicalisation, including sharing speeches by Anwar al-Awlaki, the US-born Al Qaeda cleric and propagandist killed in a US drone strike in Yemen in 2011.

He also volunteered with Muslim Youth GC (MYGC), a youth group connected to the Worongary Mosque on the Gold Coast.

The group's leader, Abdul Rahman Nasiri, said neither it nor any other local organisation had supported Mr Stevenson's journey and he was free to make his own choices.

"We created MYGC to help young people [both Muslim and non-Muslim] steer away and overcome the negative challenges they face daily and give them the correct understanding of Islam, free from the stereotypes and misinformation that can appear online or in the media," he said in a written statement.

Case referred to civilian court

DFAT advised Mr Stevenson's family that Syrian authorities initially treated the shooting as an accident.

They later investigated whether he was affiliated with the Islamic State terrorist group.

According to information provided to the family, that investigation ended in February when authorities referred the case to the civilian criminal courts as a murder prosecution, rather than as a terrorism case.

The prosecution is likely to test Syria's fractured legal system as the country attempts to rebuild its institutions after 14 years of civil war.

Syrian legal sources told the ABC that it could take up to a year for the court to reach a verdict.

Any death sentence imposed by an ordinary criminal court would have to be reviewed by the Court of Cassation, considered by a clemency committee and approved by Syria's president before it could be carried out.

Patrick Stevenson travelled to Syria late last year. (Supplied)

Quiet man who avoided the camera

Those who knew Mr Burgess described him as quiet, devout and reluctant to be photographed.

"He was a very soft-spoken, gentle sort of guy," said Shahz Rana, a former president of the North Coast Muslim Association.

"Not too talkative, just used to keep to himself, but was still nice and polite to others."

Mr Rana said the news of his death had shocked the community.

"It was a little bit surprising that he was in Syria, but it was shocking news and I feel sad for him," he said.

Mr Rana said Mr Burgess told community members in about 2024 that his family was moving to Malaysia to live in a Muslim community and learn more about the faith.

He was unaware the family had spent at least six months travelling through Taliban-ruled Afghanistan before moving to Darkush, near Syria's border with Türkiye.

It is not known what brought the family to Syria. The ABC does not suggest they had links to extremist groups.

People who knew the two men said Mr Burgess took Mr Stevenson under his wing and that they became close before the shooting.

Widow could spare Stevenson's life

Mr Stevenson's fate may ultimately rest with a third Australian: Mr Burgess's widow, Amatullah Laurie Duniam.

Under the Syrian legal system, she could spare him execution by granting forgiveness, potentially in exchange for a payment of blood money, known as diya.

Ms Duniam and other members of Mr Burgess's family declined to speak to the ABC.

World.title: 'Take them seriously': CFMEU administrator on Setka threats
World.content:
CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby has opened up on threats from John Setka, cast doubt on a statement made by former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan and questioned the value of royal commissions during an extensive 7.30 interview.

Mr Crosby was appointed to the role in May following the resignation of its previous administrator, Mark Irving.

At the time, Mr Crosby said he was committed to changing the culture of the union, which in 2024 was placed into administration by the Albanese government following revelations it had been infiltrated by organised crime.

Mr Irving had said he had received death threats during his tenure.

Mr Crosby says he too has received threats, a first for him, from former CFMEU boss John Setka.

"I take them seriously," Mr Crosby told 7.30.

"There's not much I can do about it. The police have taken out the Victorian equivalent of an AVO.

"I'm basically ignoring it and moving on.

"I think about the work that we're doing in this union, [and] I'm incredibly proud of the people who have come into this union to reform it."

John Setka is accused of threatenig CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby. (AAP: Stefan Postles)

Asked if he would take a meeting with Mick Gatto, who had wanted one with his predecessor, Mr Crosby said he would not.

"Why would I associate with anybody like that and give him credibility?" Mr Crosby said.

Mr Crosby said in his view the union had done well to weed out corruption since it went into administration, telling 7.30 that he believed criminal elements no longer held sway.

"They have very little grip on the union," Mr Crosby said.

"We've moved off 27 leaders, 150 staff members of various kinds have gone away. We've got a whole new team in there rebuilding that union from the ground up."

Scepticism on royal commission

With corruption and criminality having been major problems for the CFMEU, Mr Crosby was adamant that corruption had also been responsible for a blowout in costs on major Victorian projects.

The CFMEU is being rebuilt "from the ground up", Michael Crosby says. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

That was something former premier Jacinta Allan had refused to admit, when she blamed inflation rather than CFMEU corruption for the skyrocketing costs on Victoria's Big Build.

"That's difficult to accept," Mr Crosby told 7.30.

Mr Crosby said criminality had generally caused the cost of construction in Australia to be more expensive.

"Inevitably … somebody is clipping the ticket on the way through," he said.

Former Victorian premier Jacinta Allan blamed cost blow outs on Victoria's Big Build on inflation. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"Some of the corruption is about who gets to do the work, and these are rich contracts because they're big projects.

"If you can get that job, then you get paid by the government to do that."

Mr Crosby said that process was a major problem for the construction industry to reckon with.

"Criminality comes out of the way in which the industry is organised," he said.

"Governments hand over control of a particular infrastructure project to a head contractor, the head contractor then hands over control to subcontractors, and then they get labour hire agencies in.

"Right through that, that's where supervision breaks down, and you get these criminals coming in, subverting the union, corrupting the union and its leadership, but lining their pockets all the way through."

New Victorian premier Ben Carroll has called a royal commission into the construction sector in the state. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A major question for any royal commission into construction, as called for by new Victorian Premier Ben Carroll, is if it can fix the major issues around corruption in the sector.

It is something that Mr Crosby is unsure of.

"Will [we] cooperate with the royal commission? Absolutely," he said.

"I am sceptical about royal commissions. There's been four into the CFMEU [and] they've all failed."

World.title: Toy library makes statement grieving loss of Helena Wright and children
World.content:
A South Australian toy library has expressed sadness following the deaths of a mother and her two children, which police are treating as a murder-suicide.

The bodies of Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were retrieved from waters off Cape Northumberland in SA's south-east on Monday.

The search for her three-month-old son was formally called off by South Australian Police on Wednesday afternoon, after receiving advice the child could not have survived.

Ms Wright was a volunteer committee member at the Mount Gambier Toy Library, which issued a statement on Thursday.

"Mt Gambier Toy Library is deeply saddened by the tragic loss of a member of our committee and her children. Our thoughts are with their family, friends and everyone affected by this devastating event," it said. "Our volunteer committee and toy library community are grieving and supporting one another."

Police on Wednesday confirmed Ms Wright had attended a local police station on Sunday and officers had attended her home to conduct a welfare check on Monday morning following a call from a friend. Her car was found later that morning at Cape Northumberland.

The three deaths have shaken the Port MacDonnell community, which has rallied around locals who volunteered to help the police search.

The matter is now the subject of a coronial investigation.

World.title: Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years
World.content:
Sydney Roosters sent a warning to the rest of the NRL about their premiership credentials with a 82-12 whipping of North Queensland in Townsville, the most points by a winning team in 91 years.

Halfback Sam Walker, in the midst of a multi-million dollar contract negotiation, showed why Roosters supremo Nick Politis wants to keep him at the club for life in a masterclass display.

This was a muscle flex of epic proportions as the visitors scored the equal most first half points in premiership history to lead 48-6 after 40 minutes.

The Roosters scored eight first half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker's 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at halftime with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

North Queensland were helpless before the Tricolour onslaught. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock )

The Roosters temporarily joined Penrith on 34 competition points at the top of the table in their most complete performance of the season.

It was their sixth win in a row and a sign that come September they will be in prime position to challenge their bogey team Penrith.

The Cowboys are hanging on in eighth position but will drop back to ninth if Canterbury beat Melbourne away on Friday night.

The nature of the thrashing will test Cowboys coach Todd Payten's ability to get an appropriate response

Captain Tedesco, fresh from a hat-trick of tries last week, started and finished the opening try and it was carnage from that moment.

Roosters forwards Naufahu Whyte and Salesi Foketi monstered the hosts early and the spine of Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Walker and Reece Robson ran riot.

Tedesco, also the NSW custodian, is making a compelling case to oust Reece Walsh from the fullback position for Australia at the World Cup later in the year.

The Cowboys levelled at six-all when halves Jake Clifford and Jaxon Purdue combined to put Braidon Burns over but that was the only moment the match was in the balance.

A brilliant interchange of passing between halfback Walker and Tedesco led to the No.7 slicing over.

Tedesco then laid on a try for centre Hugo Savala with a left-foot grubber and it was clear which way the match was heading. . Walker's left foot step on the last tackle to score his second was elite.

The dazzling half set up runaway Foketi for a 40m rampage to the line.

The last try of the match, scored by replacement fullback Cody Ramsey, featured Walker grubbering and then kicking the ball over the head of the last dismal line of Cowboys defence.

World.title: 'Sadness' falls across coastal community after double murder-suicide
World.content:
Residents of a South Australian coastal town rocked by a double murder-suicide say a "sadness" has fallen across the tight-knit community.

Helena Wright, 36, and her 23-month-old daughter were pulled from the ocean near Port MacDonnell on Monday, with Ms Wright's two-month-old son still missing.

Helicopters and planes flew over the scene on Monday while boats scoured the ocean nearby searching for the boy.

Weather hampered search efforts on Tuesday and Wednesday, limiting searchers to foot patrols along the coastline.

Police made the call to end the formal search for the baby boy as of Wednesday afternoon, saying he could not have survived almost three days in the conditions.

Police are treating the death of Helena Wright and her two children as a murder-suicide. (Supplied)

Also on Wednesday, police said Ms Wright had attended a local police station the day before the deaths.

Police conducted a welfare check at her home at Compton, near Mount Gambier, just hours before the public found Ms Wright's vehicle running near the cliffs at Cape Northumberland.

Country Fire Service Kingsley Group officer Grant Fensom's team is based in Port MacDonnell, and he helped with rescue efforts.

He said volunteers told police the best chance of finding Ms Wright and her children was on Monday during the more favourable weather conditions.

"The locals, let alone the SES and the police, did their absolute best to locate them on the first day, which obviously you know resulted in two people being found and not the third," Mr Fensom said.

"The last two days it has been hard, been wet, it's been windy, and the sea has definitely been rough.

Police say they are continuing to search for the missing baby boy. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

" So it's been a trying time knowing that you can't get out there and actually probably continue a search to give some closure to some people. "

Mr Fensom said the incident was hard on a town that prided itself on being welcoming.

"So to have something happen in our town is hard because people want to think that they can always help someone out that's in need," he said.

Strength in speaking up

Salt cafe owner Mel Lewis donated more than 30 meals to those on the ground as police and SES volunteers from around the state descended on Port MacDonnell to aid the search.

Mel Lewis says the deaths have taken a toll on the tight-knit town. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

She said the entire town felt a "sadness".

"People are coming together, maybe connecting a little bit more, reaching out to family, friends, hugging their children a little bit tighter," she said.

Ms Lewis said it was important the town took the time to support one another.

"It shows more strength to reach out and ask for help than to not," she said.

"I know personally to do that, and it is very, very tough, but we have a lot of services around for us to be able to reach out.

"But even just your friends and your family, but like I said, it just shows so much more strength asking for help than not."

Emergency services volunteer Roger Bobolka said the impact spread beyond those on the ground aiding the search effort.

Roger Bobulka said the incident would "stick" with locals. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

"You can talk to anyone in town now and you can tell they've been impacted in some way because it's not the sort of thing you can just shut off and push aside and move on," he said.

"It's the sort of thing that hangs around for quite some time and it will for the community.

"I mean it's happened in a fairly prominent location within Port MacDonnell, so you can't get away from it."

Shoreline monitoring continues

Police Commissioner Grant Stevens told 891 ABC Adelaide officers would continue to monitor the shoreline for the missing baby boy despite ceasing the formal search.

"We will continue searching the shoreline in the coming days in the hope of being able to recover the little infant, but we're not holding a lot of hope in that regard," he said.

He said the deaths of children were "distressing" not only for police but for the community.

Commissioner Grant Stevens says the incident is distressing. (ABC News)

"It's heartbreaking to think we can't find the little infant, that sits heavily on the shoulders of the people involved, and it's not just police," he said.

The bodies of Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were recovered from the ocean. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

The commissioner added the case was now part of a coronial investigation and would not elaborate on any interactions Ms Wright had with police.

"That evidence [to the coroner] will include all of the activities involving Helena and her interactions with police, any other services in the days leading up to what we are now describing as a murder-suicide," he said.

UEFA member federations agreed on Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions in protest of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.

“UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions,” the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of the 55 members.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump at the World Cup final earlier this month. Getty

“Some things are simply too important to sell,” UEFA said in a statement. “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

The strategy meeting was called to counter FIFA president Infantino’s offer of $US20 million ($28.5 million) to each of its 211 global members that has to be accepted by mid-September.

World.title: The 39 minutes that showed why the Cats have the wood over the Pies
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The 39 minutes that showed why the Cats have the wood over the Pies Peter Ryan July 31, 2026 — 1:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

This was a start with a difference. The coin toss happened indoors an hour before the game. Theme songs were replaced with nightclub jams to accompany the players running out. Smoke poured into the ether, lights flashed and spectators cringed. Nick Daicos was under pressure all game. AFL Photos



But then Oisin Mullin found Nick Daicos, Ed Allan stood next to Bailey Smith and Mark O’Connor went to Jordan De Goey and when the ball was thrown in the air, everyone realised that for all the hype nothing much had changed at all. Related Article AFL 2026 Bobby Hill targeted in vile racist rant as Geelong hold off surging Pies in MCG blockbuster Geelong, who have beaten every team above them this season bar Hawthorn, were too good for Collingwood, who have a draw against the Hawks and a win against the Crows to show for their 11 matches against teams in the top eight. The Magpies may have sat above Geelong on the ladder, but their form line was worse. That reality revealed itself when the game was up for grabs early. Geelong dominated, kicking a goal within the first two minutes via a big mark from Shannon Neale. After 39 minutes, Geelong had a 48-point lead after kicking nine of the first 10 goals.



The Cats played fast and wide, spreading the ball to the extremities of the MCG where they found time and space. They knew that Collingwood could repel attacks if they were slow, so they resolved to go hard and fast. If they turned the ball over, they counter-attacked at speed, creative players such as Gryan Miers and Shaun Mannagh happy to make things up as they went. There were pre-game fireworks for Collingwood’s clash with Geelong. Getty Images Ollie Dempsey, shining like a dashboard on a late-night drive, kicked two goals in the opening quarter as Geelong dominated Collingwood in the air and on the ground. Former Magpie Ollie Henry and Neale were a handful for their opponents, with Collingwood veteran Jeremy Howe the only player looking likely to counter their aerial exploits. Mullin stifled Daicos, who could not find room to explode from contests and break open the Cats’ defence, which can be vulnerable if the ball moves without pressure. It was a great battle, with Daicos and Mullin both refusing to wilt. Geelong survived a furious charge from the Pies to win their MCG blockbuster. Getty Images



“It’s a mental battle, really, to see who’s going to give in first. So it’s just [about] kind of being stubborn,” Mullin told Fox Footy. Even without Max Holmes, the Cats’ midfield of Smith, Mullin, Tom Atkins and James Worpel looked stronger than the combination of Daicos, Allan, Ned Long and De Goey. Related Article AFL 2026 AFL round 21 teams and expert tips: Pies, Cats both lose crucial stars for MCG blockbuster However, Collingwood under Craig McRae don’t give up. If they couldn’t move the ball easily, they would make it hard for the opposition. So they threw themselves at the Cats, tackling them hard and forcing the ball loose through pressure. They scrubbed five goals in a row and put roadblocks on Geelong’s attacking avenues. For 40 minutes they chipped away at the lead, but it was hard work. McRae said their effort made him proud, but he knew in his heart of hearts he was scrambling when he kept telling players on the bench how good coming from eight goals down to win was going to be if they could make it happen.



They narrowed the margin to 16 points, forcing Worpel into action around stoppage. The ex-Hawk, who battled to get a game until the Cats lost five in a row, stood up at crucial stoppages and reclaimed territory for the Cats. He showed himself to be more than a depth-adding free agent, muscling a stoppage win that ended up with the ball reaching another former free-agent signing Jack Martin inside 50. Martin broke the goal-drought with a steadier. Craig McRae looks on as the Magpies leave the ground. Getty Images It was crucial because Collingwood had already lost Harry Perryman to a hamstring injury and needed everything to go right to pull off a miracle. It didn’t. Howe fractured his arm just before three-quarter-time. Suddenly, it seemed like that sort of year for Collingwood.



The Magpies did not get any closer for the rest of the night, even with Daicos occasionally finding space when Mullin left his side and handed over to Smith – a brave move if ever there was one. View post on X Dan McStay kept up his strong form with five goals. Collingwood won the free kick count handsomely, which elicited another umpiring sermon from Chris Scott, but the Magpies’ key forward had little support elsewhere. Geelong – missing Jeremy Cameron and Patrick Dangerfield – found support in all the right places, their second win over the Magpies in 2026 confirming their ranking above them on the ladder. View post on X



The Cats are now fifth and a sneaky chance to finish in the top four. Collingwood are ninth, with a buffer between them and 10th. But they will need to keep the foot down, with a trip west to play West Coast, before Hawthorn and the Brisbane Lions to finish. Their supporters will hope to hear their theme song again before the year is over because the night that started differently finished much the same: Geelong are proving too good for Collingwood in 2026. World.title: Say ciao to Delmonte, the shiny new jewel in Lygon Street’s crown
World.content:
Eating outJust open Say ciao to Delmonte, the shiny new jewel in Lygon Street’s crown The former King & Godfree site is now home to a glam Italian wine-diner, with Karen Martini calling the culinary shots. Expect a menu of Italian crowd-pleasers with flavour “taken to the brink”. Tomas Telegramma July 31, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a momentous day for Carlton’s iconic King & Godfree building. The new jewel in the crown, Italian restaurant and wine room Delmonte, has arrived. On the corner of Lygon and Faraday streets, occupying the street-level space where the historic Italian deli and grocer stood for more than a century, a new era is in full swing. Delmonte has moved into the iconic corner building formerly known as King & Godfree. Parker Blain The 160-seat Delmonte now anchors the dining and drinking precinct, which comprises new-ish pizzeria Garfield, rooftop bar Johnny’s Green Room and gelateria Pidapipo. Behind the latest addition is Jamie Valmorbida, whose family bought King & Godfree in 1955. The deli was retained in the site’s previous iteration, which reopened with the addition of casual dining in 2018, but this most recent reroute leaves it in the rear-view. “It was hard for the family to close the deli – that was a big decision,” says Valmorbida.



1 / 8 Calamarata pasta with prawn, clams, calamari and chilli at Delmonte. Parker Blain 2 / 8 Pasta fritte with parmesan fonduta and culatta (dry-cured prosciutto). Parker Blain 3 / 8 Keep a look out for Lygon Street’s new red neon sign. Parker Blain 4 / 8 There’s pasta aplenty at Delmonte. Parker Blain 5 / 8 Hanging cured meats at Delmonte. Parker Blain 6 / 8 Steak and salad at Delmonte. Parker Blain 7 / 8 Sit at the bar and sip on martinis. Parker Blair 8 / 8 Desserts include gelati from neighbouring Pidapipo. Parker Blain Previous Slide Next Slide Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up As was figuring out its replacement: “[Reimagining] the corner was a challenge because it’s got so much history and it means so much to people. Everyone wants it to work. And that was also a big part of wanting to capture the history of the deli in this concept.” There are nods to the deli in Delmonte’s design by Valmorbida collaborator Dion Hall (Garfield, Johnny’s, Supernormal). Slick terrazzo floors join overhead tube lighting and utilitarian tiling. Valmorbida is also in talks with council to install a King & Godfree plaque on the building’s exterior. The Delmonte team (L-R): Joel Penno, Jamie Valmorbida, George McCullough, Diana Desensi, Mark Glenn, Karen Martini and Dion Hall. Parker Blain The deli days might be over, “but you can still get your mozzarella, your salumi – it’s just going to be on a plate”, says Karen Martini, the precinct’s culinary director (who also has the hatted Bar Carolina).



Her kitchen team at Delmonte includes executive chef Mark Glenn and head chef Diana Desensi, who Martini worked with at St Kilda’s Saint George. Their menu is intentionally familiar and all-encompassing, but it’s attention to detail that they hope will set it apart on a strip that’s flush with family-style Italian joints. “We are doing a lot of dishes that have been served all the way up and down Lygon [Street] for years, but we’re doing them a bit differently,” says Martini. “Things are very honest, but the volume’s up ... whatever the flavour is has been taken to the brink.” The snack game is strong at Delmonte. Parker Blain Strong snacking awaits, from house-baked focaccia Genovese to house-made tuna ’nduja. Martini’s take on the trending charcuterie-loaded chips is crisp shards of gnocco fritto dough (the secret is chicken fat) draped with culatta and white anchovies. It’s what aperitivo-hour dreams are made of. Walk in, perch at the zinc bar, and order a quince-y house bellini or a chinotto spritz. Or you can do what Martini likes to call “the full catastrophe”: a multi-course feast.



Vitello tonnato is sourced from Donati’s butcher across the road. Parker Blain Valmorbida’s acquisition of legendary Carlton butcher Donati’s this year inspired the vitello tonnato. “[Founder] Leo Donati was known for his white veal,” says Desensi, who’s cooking it classically: gently poached, sliced thinly, layered with a tuna sauce. “If I did it with foams, and bells and whistles, it wouldn’t be well received,” she says. For Valmorbida, broad appeal is important. “We don’t want to be fancy or exclusive ... just somewhere everyone feels comfortable.” The warmth of the room is reminiscent of Martini’s former Melbourne Wine Room. Parker Blain



The name comes from a wine label that Valmorbida’s nonno Carlo launched in the ’60s, with the tagline “in ogni occasione”. The wine was “for all occasions”. So too is the restaurant. Pizza reigns at Garfield and Johnny’s, leaving room for Delmonte to be the pasta paradise. The offering will grow, but initially it’s simple pleasures like tagliatelle bolognese, and calamarata (the calamari-ring-shaped pasta) with prawns, vongole and calamari in a yellow passata that’s bolstered by colatura, the aged Italian fish sauce made from anchovies. Donati’s rib-eye steak on the menu at Delmonte. Parker Blain Donati’s steaks come off a wood-fired grill, ranging from single-serve bavette and eye fillet to daily specials (first up: a 900-gram salt-crusted rib-eye that’s carved to share). This is a restaurant built for conviviality. The lived-in warmth and mixed-and-matched chairs and tables have drawn comparisons with Martini’s legendary Melbourne Wine Room from the 1990s. There’s bar and banquette seating aplenty, and alfresco dining is set to take over Faraday Street. The kitchen plays a part, too.



“The whole idea was to drag the theatre – and energy – of the kitchen into the restaurant,” says Martini. Most snacks and sweets are plated in full view of diners. The dessert station is adorned with the day’s biscotti and torta (or pie, currently caramelised apple and custard); steel pozzetti are filled with Pidapipo gelato. Much has been said about declining trade and foot traffic on Lygon Street, which has seen a shift towards fast-casual openings in recent years. But if anywhere has the potential to make dining out on the street truly great again, it’s Delmonte, and this precinct, with a subterranean, late-night cocktail and music bar still to come. Delmonte opens today, Friday, July 31. It’s currently dinner-only six days a week, with Tuesday trade and weekend lunches to come. Open dinner Wed-Mon 293 Lygon Street, Carlton, delmontewine.com

World.title: Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts Matthew Knott July 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Up to 400 Defence Force personnel will be tracked during weapons training as part of a sophisticated study that follows years of growing complaints about a lack of action on alarming reports of blast injuries among military veterans. In the first-of-its-kind study, researchers will cross-reference blast pressure readings from gauges on soldiers’ helmets with blood tests and neurological data conducted within a day of exposure to blasts. Retired lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan, an advocate for action on blast injuries in defence, during his time in the army. Blood tests analysed at Monash University’s Melbourne laboratory will be used to detect tiny amounts of proteins known to be released in the bloodstream during a traumatic brain injury. The study is a response to the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which recommended the government establish a brain injury program to better understand the impact of repetitive low-level blast exposure on brain processes.



Retired army lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan has led a veterans’ push for greater action from government and the Australian Defence Force on brain injuries among current and former service personnel. “From Afghanistan, there are guys now from that who have committed suicide,” Scanlan previously told this masthead. “And not just suicides. Families are being destroyed because of the effect it’s having. I think they deserve a lot better.” Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said: “The health, safety and wellbeing of current and former serving Defence Force personnel is my highest priority. “As part of our response to the royal commission, we’ve been investing in research and monitoring to better understand the complex nature of brain injury and its causes.



“While a co-ordinated effort is under way to decrease risks where possible, in line with international research, we know we need to do more.” In a 2024 interview with this masthead, then-army chief Simon Stuart apologised to veterans suffering from potentially avoidable impacts of blast trauma. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations The blasts, the battle and at last an apology. Now it’s time for action “There have been research and trials and other work going on since 2010, so far as I can ascertain. I think what’s been missing is sort of the golden thread of logic,” he said. Previous ADF studies have recorded blast pressure via the helmet-mounted gauges, but have not cross-referenced the results with blood and neurological data to determine the actual effect of blast pressure in real time.



Professor Sandy Shultz, a principal investigator at Monash’s school of translational medicine, said: “There has been very little research on brain injury as a result of low-level blast exposure, despite this being such a common experience across the defence sector. “Exactly how and to what extent low-level and repetitive exposures to blast affects the brain is really unknown. “The knowledge gained from this research will help inform policy and guidelines around what thresholds can result in a brain injury and when ADF personnel should be removed from further exposure.” The study, which will be conducted over the next four years, will focus on how repeated, low-level blast exposures may impact brain health across a military career. More is known about high-level blast events, which can result in immediate traumatic brain injury.



The study will focus initially on the army but could later be extended to the navy and air force. “By combining blast monitoring, blood-based biomarkers and cognitive and psychometric assessments, we’re building the evidence needed to strengthen force health protection,” said army neurologist Lieutenant Colonel Antony Sutherland, a member of the study team. The royal commission, released in 2024, found that traumatic brain injuries are associated with a heightened risk of death by suicide in veteran and civilian populations. “Traumatic brain injury from blast exposure is common in active-duty military personnel,” the final report found. “Many researchers believe that the pressure wave passing through the brain significantly disrupts brain function, causing damage.”



The royal commission found current and ex-service members “reported receiving insufficient support from the ADF for brain injury and having difficulty obtaining compensation”. If you are a current or former ADF member or a relative and need counselling or support, contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046. The Roosters scored eight first-half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker’s 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at half-time with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

UEFA member federations agreed on Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions in protest of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.

“UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions,” the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of the 55 members.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump at the World Cup final earlier this month. Getty

“Some things are simply too important to sell,” UEFA said in a statement. “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

The strategy meeting was called to counter FIFA president Infantino’s offer of $US20 million ($28.5 million) to each of its 211 global members that has to be accepted by mid-September.

World.title: The 39 minutes that showed why the Cats have the wood over the Pies
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The 39 minutes that showed why the Cats have the wood over the Pies Peter Ryan July 31, 2026 — 1:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

This was a start with a difference. The coin toss happened indoors an hour before the game. Theme songs were replaced with nightclub jams to accompany the players running out. Smoke poured into the ether, lights flashed and spectators cringed. Nick Daicos was under pressure all game. AFL Photos



But then Oisin Mullin found Nick Daicos, Ed Allan stood next to Bailey Smith and Mark O’Connor went to Jordan De Goey and when the ball was thrown in the air, everyone realised that for all the hype nothing much had changed at all. Related Article AFL 2026 Bobby Hill targeted in vile racist rant as Geelong hold off surging Pies in MCG blockbuster Geelong, who have beaten every team above them this season bar Hawthorn, were too good for Collingwood, who have a draw against the Hawks and a win against the Crows to show for their 11 matches against teams in the top eight. The Magpies may have sat above Geelong on the ladder, but their form line was worse. That reality revealed itself when the game was up for grabs early. Geelong dominated, kicking a goal within the first two minutes via a big mark from Shannon Neale. After 39 minutes, Geelong had a 48-point lead after kicking nine of the first 10 goals.



The Cats played fast and wide, spreading the ball to the extremities of the MCG where they found time and space. They knew that Collingwood could repel attacks if they were slow, so they resolved to go hard and fast. If they turned the ball over, they counter-attacked at speed, creative players such as Gryan Miers and Shaun Mannagh happy to make things up as they went. There were pre-game fireworks for Collingwood’s clash with Geelong. Getty Images Ollie Dempsey, shining like a dashboard on a late-night drive, kicked two goals in the opening quarter as Geelong dominated Collingwood in the air and on the ground. Former Magpie Ollie Henry and Neale were a handful for their opponents, with Collingwood veteran Jeremy Howe the only player looking likely to counter their aerial exploits. Mullin stifled Daicos, who could not find room to explode from contests and break open the Cats’ defence, which can be vulnerable if the ball moves without pressure. It was a great battle, with Daicos and Mullin both refusing to wilt. Geelong survived a furious charge from the Pies to win their MCG blockbuster. Getty Images



“It’s a mental battle, really, to see who’s going to give in first. So it’s just [about] kind of being stubborn,” Mullin told Fox Footy. Even without Max Holmes, the Cats’ midfield of Smith, Mullin, Tom Atkins and James Worpel looked stronger than the combination of Daicos, Allan, Ned Long and De Goey. Related Article AFL 2026 AFL round 21 teams and expert tips: Pies, Cats both lose crucial stars for MCG blockbuster However, Collingwood under Craig McRae don’t give up. If they couldn’t move the ball easily, they would make it hard for the opposition. So they threw themselves at the Cats, tackling them hard and forcing the ball loose through pressure. They scrubbed five goals in a row and put roadblocks on Geelong’s attacking avenues. For 40 minutes they chipped away at the lead, but it was hard work. McRae said their effort made him proud, but he knew in his heart of hearts he was scrambling when he kept telling players on the bench how good coming from eight goals down to win was going to be if they could make it happen.



They narrowed the margin to 16 points, forcing Worpel into action around stoppage. The ex-Hawk, who battled to get a game until the Cats lost five in a row, stood up at crucial stoppages and reclaimed territory for the Cats. He showed himself to be more than a depth-adding free agent, muscling a stoppage win that ended up with the ball reaching another former free-agent signing Jack Martin inside 50. Martin broke the goal-drought with a steadier. Craig McRae looks on as the Magpies leave the ground. Getty Images It was crucial because Collingwood had already lost Harry Perryman to a hamstring injury and needed everything to go right to pull off a miracle. It didn’t. Howe fractured his arm just before three-quarter-time. Suddenly, it seemed like that sort of year for Collingwood.



The Magpies did not get any closer for the rest of the night, even with Daicos occasionally finding space when Mullin left his side and handed over to Smith – a brave move if ever there was one. View post on X Dan McStay kept up his strong form with five goals. Collingwood won the free kick count handsomely, which elicited another umpiring sermon from Chris Scott, but the Magpies’ key forward had little support elsewhere. Geelong – missing Jeremy Cameron and Patrick Dangerfield – found support in all the right places, their second win over the Magpies in 2026 confirming their ranking above them on the ladder. View post on X



The Cats are now fifth and a sneaky chance to finish in the top four. Collingwood are ninth, with a buffer between them and 10th. But they will need to keep the foot down, with a trip west to play West Coast, before Hawthorn and the Brisbane Lions to finish. Their supporters will hope to hear their theme song again before the year is over because the night that started differently finished much the same: Geelong are proving too good for Collingwood in 2026. World.title: Bobby Hill targeted in vile racist rant as Geelong hold off surging Pies in MCG blockbuster
World.content:
Collingwood coach Craig McRae threw his support behind forward Bobby Hill, who was subjected to vile racist abuse online, on a night the Magpies’ 25-point loss to Geelong was compounded by a suspected broken arm to star defender Jeremy Howe.

Hill received a horrific direct message on Instagram from a fan angry with the 2023 Norm Smith medallist’s output over the past 12 months.

The Age has chosen to blur out the worst of the language directed at Hill, who has reportedly agreed with the Magpies to part ways just three years after his starring role in the club’s last premiership.

An edited version of the horrific message Bobby Hill received. Instagram

“You have disappointed this whole club and it’s 100 thousand plus fans what you have done the last 18 months,” the account posted. “I hope nothing but the worst for you.”

World.title: Say ciao to Delmonte, the shiny new jewel in Lygon Street’s crown
World.content:
Eating outJust open Say ciao to Delmonte, the shiny new jewel in Lygon Street’s crown The former King & Godfree site is now home to a glam Italian wine-diner, with Karen Martini calling the culinary shots. Expect a menu of Italian crowd-pleasers with flavour “taken to the brink”. Tomas Telegramma July 31, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a momentous day for Carlton’s iconic King & Godfree building. The new jewel in the crown, Italian restaurant and wine room Delmonte, has arrived. On the corner of Lygon and Faraday streets, occupying the street-level space where the historic Italian deli and grocer stood for more than a century, a new era is in full swing. Delmonte has moved into the iconic corner building formerly known as King & Godfree. Parker Blain The 160-seat Delmonte now anchors the dining and drinking precinct, which comprises new-ish pizzeria Garfield, rooftop bar Johnny’s Green Room and gelateria Pidapipo. Behind the latest addition is Jamie Valmorbida, whose family bought King & Godfree in 1955. The deli was retained in the site’s previous iteration, which reopened with the addition of casual dining in 2018, but this most recent reroute leaves it in the rear-view. “It was hard for the family to close the deli – that was a big decision,” says Valmorbida.



1 / 8 Calamarata pasta with prawn, clams, calamari and chilli at Delmonte. Parker Blain 2 / 8 Pasta fritte with parmesan fonduta and culatta (dry-cured prosciutto). Parker Blain 3 / 8 Keep a look out for Lygon Street’s new red neon sign. Parker Blain 4 / 8 There’s pasta aplenty at Delmonte. Parker Blain 5 / 8 Hanging cured meats at Delmonte. Parker Blain 6 / 8 Steak and salad at Delmonte. Parker Blain 7 / 8 Sit at the bar and sip on martinis. Parker Blair 8 / 8 Desserts include gelati from neighbouring Pidapipo. Parker Blain Previous Slide Next Slide Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up As was figuring out its replacement: “[Reimagining] the corner was a challenge because it’s got so much history and it means so much to people. Everyone wants it to work. And that was also a big part of wanting to capture the history of the deli in this concept.” There are nods to the deli in Delmonte’s design by Valmorbida collaborator Dion Hall (Garfield, Johnny’s, Supernormal). Slick terrazzo floors join overhead tube lighting and utilitarian tiling. Valmorbida is also in talks with council to install a King & Godfree plaque on the building’s exterior. The Delmonte team (L-R): Joel Penno, Jamie Valmorbida, George McCullough, Diana Desensi, Mark Glenn, Karen Martini and Dion Hall. Parker Blain The deli days might be over, “but you can still get your mozzarella, your salumi – it’s just going to be on a plate”, says Karen Martini, the precinct’s culinary director (who also has the hatted Bar Carolina).



Her kitchen team at Delmonte includes executive chef Mark Glenn and head chef Diana Desensi, who Martini worked with at St Kilda’s Saint George. Their menu is intentionally familiar and all-encompassing, but it’s attention to detail that they hope will set it apart on a strip that’s flush with family-style Italian joints. “We are doing a lot of dishes that have been served all the way up and down Lygon [Street] for years, but we’re doing them a bit differently,” says Martini. “Things are very honest, but the volume’s up ... whatever the flavour is has been taken to the brink.” The snack game is strong at Delmonte. Parker Blain Strong snacking awaits, from house-baked focaccia Genovese to house-made tuna ’nduja. Martini’s take on the trending charcuterie-loaded chips is crisp shards of gnocco fritto dough (the secret is chicken fat) draped with culatta and white anchovies. It’s what aperitivo-hour dreams are made of. Walk in, perch at the zinc bar, and order a quince-y house bellini or a chinotto spritz. Or you can do what Martini likes to call “the full catastrophe”: a multi-course feast.



Vitello tonnato is sourced from Donati’s butcher across the road. Parker Blain Valmorbida’s acquisition of legendary Carlton butcher Donati’s this year inspired the vitello tonnato. “[Founder] Leo Donati was known for his white veal,” says Desensi, who’s cooking it classically: gently poached, sliced thinly, layered with a tuna sauce. “If I did it with foams, and bells and whistles, it wouldn’t be well received,” she says. For Valmorbida, broad appeal is important. “We don’t want to be fancy or exclusive ... just somewhere everyone feels comfortable.” The warmth of the room is reminiscent of Martini’s former Melbourne Wine Room. Parker Blain



The name comes from a wine label that Valmorbida’s nonno Carlo launched in the ’60s, with the tagline “in ogni occasione”. The wine was “for all occasions”. So too is the restaurant. Pizza reigns at Garfield and Johnny’s, leaving room for Delmonte to be the pasta paradise. The offering will grow, but initially it’s simple pleasures like tagliatelle bolognese, and calamarata (the calamari-ring-shaped pasta) with prawns, vongole and calamari in a yellow passata that’s bolstered by colatura, the aged Italian fish sauce made from anchovies. Donati’s rib-eye steak on the menu at Delmonte. Parker Blain Donati’s steaks come off a wood-fired grill, ranging from single-serve bavette and eye fillet to daily specials (first up: a 900-gram salt-crusted rib-eye that’s carved to share). This is a restaurant built for conviviality. The lived-in warmth and mixed-and-matched chairs and tables have drawn comparisons with Martini’s legendary Melbourne Wine Room from the 1990s. There’s bar and banquette seating aplenty, and alfresco dining is set to take over Faraday Street. The kitchen plays a part, too.



“The whole idea was to drag the theatre – and energy – of the kitchen into the restaurant,” says Martini. Most snacks and sweets are plated in full view of diners. The dessert station is adorned with the day’s biscotti and torta (or pie, currently caramelised apple and custard); steel pozzetti are filled with Pidapipo gelato. Much has been said about declining trade and foot traffic on Lygon Street, which has seen a shift towards fast-casual openings in recent years. But if anywhere has the potential to make dining out on the street truly great again, it’s Delmonte, and this precinct, with a subterranean, late-night cocktail and music bar still to come. Delmonte opens today, Friday, July 31. It’s currently dinner-only six days a week, with Tuesday trade and weekend lunches to come. Open dinner Wed-Mon 293 Lygon Street, Carlton, delmontewine.com

World.title: Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence Army to use blood tests to detect brain injuries from weapon blasts Matthew Knott July 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Up to 400 Defence Force personnel will be tracked during weapons training as part of a sophisticated study that follows years of growing complaints about a lack of action on alarming reports of blast injuries among military veterans. In the first-of-its-kind study, researchers will cross-reference blast pressure readings from gauges on soldiers’ helmets with blood tests and neurological data conducted within a day of exposure to blasts. Retired lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan, an advocate for action on blast injuries in defence, during his time in the army. Blood tests analysed at Monash University’s Melbourne laboratory will be used to detect tiny amounts of proteins known to be released in the bloodstream during a traumatic brain injury. The study is a response to the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which recommended the government establish a brain injury program to better understand the impact of repetitive low-level blast exposure on brain processes.



Retired army lieutenant colonel Paul Scanlan has led a veterans’ push for greater action from government and the Australian Defence Force on brain injuries among current and former service personnel. “From Afghanistan, there are guys now from that who have committed suicide,” Scanlan previously told this masthead. “And not just suicides. Families are being destroyed because of the effect it’s having. I think they deserve a lot better.” Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said: “The health, safety and wellbeing of current and former serving Defence Force personnel is my highest priority. “As part of our response to the royal commission, we’ve been investing in research and monitoring to better understand the complex nature of brain injury and its causes.



“While a co-ordinated effort is under way to decrease risks where possible, in line with international research, we know we need to do more.” In a 2024 interview with this masthead, then-army chief Simon Stuart apologised to veterans suffering from potentially avoidable impacts of blast trauma. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations The blasts, the battle and at last an apology. Now it’s time for action “There have been research and trials and other work going on since 2010, so far as I can ascertain. I think what’s been missing is sort of the golden thread of logic,” he said. Previous ADF studies have recorded blast pressure via the helmet-mounted gauges, but have not cross-referenced the results with blood and neurological data to determine the actual effect of blast pressure in real time.



Professor Sandy Shultz, a principal investigator at Monash’s school of translational medicine, said: “There has been very little research on brain injury as a result of low-level blast exposure, despite this being such a common experience across the defence sector. “Exactly how and to what extent low-level and repetitive exposures to blast affects the brain is really unknown. “The knowledge gained from this research will help inform policy and guidelines around what thresholds can result in a brain injury and when ADF personnel should be removed from further exposure.” The study, which will be conducted over the next four years, will focus on how repeated, low-level blast exposures may impact brain health across a military career. More is known about high-level blast events, which can result in immediate traumatic brain injury.



The study will focus initially on the army but could later be extended to the navy and air force. “By combining blast monitoring, blood-based biomarkers and cognitive and psychometric assessments, we’re building the evidence needed to strengthen force health protection,” said army neurologist Lieutenant Colonel Antony Sutherland, a member of the study team. The royal commission, released in 2024, found that traumatic brain injuries are associated with a heightened risk of death by suicide in veteran and civilian populations. “Traumatic brain injury from blast exposure is common in active-duty military personnel,” the final report found. “Many researchers believe that the pressure wave passing through the brain significantly disrupts brain function, causing damage.”



The royal commission found current and ex-service members “reported receiving insufficient support from the ADF for brain injury and having difficulty obtaining compensation”. If you are a current or former ADF member or a relative and need counselling or support, contact the Defence All-Hours Support Line on 1800 628 036 or Open Arms on 1800 011 046. World.title: Roosters shatter NRL records in highest-scoring performance since 1935
World.content:
Sydney Roosters sent a warning to the rest of the NRL about their premiership credentials with an 82-12 whipping of North Queensland in Townsville, the most points by a winning team in 91 years.

Halfback Sam Walker, in the midst of a multi-million dollar contract negotiation, showed why Roosters supremo Nick Politis wants to keep him at the club for life in a masterclass display.

Loading

This was a muscle flex of epic proportions as the visitors scored the equal most first half points in premiership history to lead 48-6 after 40 minutes.

The Roosters scored eight first-half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker’s 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at half-time with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

Loading

The Roosters temporarily joined Penrith on 34 competition points at the top of the table in their most complete performance of the season.

It was their sixth win in a row and a sign that come September they will be in prime position to challenge their bogey team Penrith.

The Cowboys are hanging on in eighth position but will drop back to ninth if Canterbury beat Melbourne away on Friday night.

The nature of the thrashing will test Cowboys coach Todd Payten’s ability to get an appropriate response.

Captain Tedesco, fresh from a hat-trick of tries last week, started and finished the opening try and it was carnage from that moment.

Roosters forwards Naufahu Whyte and Salesi Foketi monstered the hosts early and the spine of Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Walker and Reece Robson ran riot.

Tedesco, also the NSW custodian, is making a compelling case to oust Reece Walsh from the fullback position for Australia at the World Cup later in the year.

Loading

The Cowboys levelled at six-all when halves Jake Clifford and Jaxon Purdue combined to put Braidon Burns over but that was the only moment the match was in the balance.

A brilliant interchange of passing between halfback Walker and Tedesco led to the No.7 slicing over.

Tedesco then laid on a try for centre Hugo Savala with a left-foot grubber and it was clear which way the match was heading. Walker’s left-foot step on the last tackle to score his second was elite.

The dazzling half set up runaway Foketi for a 40m rampage to the line.

The last try of the match, scored by replacement fullback Cody Ramsey, featured Walker grubbering and then kicking the ball over the head of the last dismal line of Cowboys defence.
