World.title: Stephen Fleming replaces Brendon McCullum as England Test coach
World.content:
England has named Stephen Fleming as its Men's Test head coach, replacing one New Zealander with another.

He fills the space left by Brendon McCullum, who was fired earlier this month following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents.

In an announcement on Thursday night (NZT), the England and Wales Cricket Board also named Joe Root as returning captain.

Fleming, who played 111 Tests for New Zealand between 1994 and 2008, stepped down as Chennai Super Kings (CSK) head coach earlier this month after 18 years with the Indian Premier League franchise.

"Fleming is one of the most highly regarded coaches in world cricket," the board said.

"As a player Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving (80 Tests) and most successful Test captain (28 wins). He played for Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire where also enjoyed success in captaining Notts to a drought-breaking County Championship title in 2005."

It said Fleming was chosen unanimously "following a rigorous process, which involved numerous high-quality candidates".

England's next series is against Pakistan next month. Marcus Trescothick will serve as interim head coach, with Fleming due to start in time for the winter tour to South Africa.

"This is to allow Fleming to spend time with his family in New Zealand after leaving his long-term association with CSK earlier this month. Fleming is set to fly to the UK later this summer."

Fleming said he was "incredibly excited" to be appointed to "one of the most prestigious coaching positions in world cricket".

"I am looking forward to working with the players and bedding in the gains made by Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes. Of course, the ambition is always to win now. But equally, it's about ensuring the team is well placed for the medium and long-term future. There is a lot of young talent in and around the team and our aim is to help them fulfil their potential as world-class cricketers," he said.

England’s captain Harry Brook (L) interacts with team head coach Brendon McCullum on March 4, 2026. PUNIT PARANJPE / AFP

"I'm particularly looking forward to working with Joe Root as Captain - a generational talent who has achieved so much already. There is still plenty more to come from him, and I'm excited to support him so he can enjoy and thrive in the role in what is a different context to his first stint.

"I'm also excited to work with Harry Brook. The best players are never finished products, and helping Harry continue to develop his extraordinary talent and his leadership will be an important part of this journey.

"I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll, and when that happened to me, my love for the game was rekindled by going to Notts and winning the County Championship. English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back."

McCullum, who played under Fleming in the Black Caps, will remain England's white ball coach and the pair will be required to work closely together.

World.title: Climber who survived 200m fall on Mount Aspiring should buy Lotto ticket, rescuers say
World.content:
A climber who survived a big fall down a steep, icy face on Mount Aspiring should buy a Lotto ticket, his rescuers say.

Emergency services launched a highly technical, high-altitude rescue on Tuesday night after the man's climbing companion hiked three hours to call for help, presuming his friend was dead.

The pair had summited Aspiring's south face and were descending via a steep snow and ice ridge known as The Ramp on Bonar Glacier.

Helicopters Otago chief executive Graeme Gale said climber fell just after dark at about 7pm.

"The message that I got was that he had fallen approximately 200 metres and his companion felt it was unsurvivable," he said.

The fallen climber had all of the pair's gear, including their locator beacon, Gale said.

With no way to signal for help, the second climber spent about three hours trekking back towards the summit in freezing conditions, searching for cellphone coverage.

Once the call for help came through, Gale said Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue teams met Helicopters Otago crews in Queenstown to co-ordinate a response.

"We had some pretty sketchy co-ordinates of where it was, taken from the cellphone by the police. Police did a great job co-ordinating it and then we started pulling our guys together," he said.

With the climbers at nearly 3000m, wind building and poor weather pushing in from the west, the helicopter had to be stripped and made as light as possible.

Gale said crews used night vision goggles to track down the climber who had called for help.

"We could land on the edge of the ice shelf and pick him up and so we were able to hover load - with one skid on the edge - and got him in," he said.

The crew then decided to investigate a light source they had spotted "a couple of thousand feet below".

"They thought it was possibly other climbers on the mountain but it turned out to be this guy's companion and he was actually on his feet, although he'd had injuries," he said.

"Once again, we didn't need to winch, which was great. We were able to put a skid down, just hoverload again, and one of the alpine [cliff rescue team] guys got out and escorted him back into the helicopter."

Once the call for help came through, Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue teams met Helicopters Otago crews in Queenstown to co-ordinate a response. Supplied / Screenshot

Gale was not sure the climber would have survived the night in frigid conditions if rescuers had not reached him.

He said the rescue was "the best of the best outcome" crews could have hoped for.

"It could have been catastrophic for him," Gale said.

"He was standing on a high shelf, on a slope on the mountain itself, so pretty lucky that he had gone into a crevasse and pretty lucky he hadn't had other injuries that would have been life-threatening. He was in remarkably good shape for the fall that he'd had. I reckon he should go and buy a lottery ticket for Saturday night."

Second rescue from The Ramp in a month

Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue Team co-ordinator Russ Tilsley said it followed another even more technical rescue on 30 June on the same section of Mount Aspiring.

That rescue also took place late at night and involved two climbers who had ascended the south face, he said.

"These guys had basically been out too long and I think they were very tired. They abseiled down into an area where they got stuck in and they couldn't get out," he said.

"They were frostbitten, tired and had run out of food."

While winter was typically a quiet time for the rescue team, there seemed to be more and more people undertaking winter climbing missions, Tilsley said.

Summitting Mount Aspiring from the nearest walk-in Department of Conservation hut, French Ridge Hut, was a "big thing to do in a day", he said.

"To go up, climb and come back again is probably a 24-hour mission."

Earlier Sergeant Darren Cranfield from Wānaka Police described Tuesday's rescue as a timely reminder of the risks of alpine areas.

"Conditions in the mountains can change rapidly and even experienced climbers can find themselves in dangerous situations," he said.

World.title: New $2 million blood bank opens in Wellington, major upgrade on old facilities
World.content:
The New Zealand Blood Service says the capital's new blood bank - officially opened by the Health Minister on Wednesday - couldn't come soon enough.

The service at Wellington Regional Hospital plays a critical role in delivering life-saving donor blood to patients and according to staff, the new facility is a major upgrade.

NZ Blood Service chief executive Sam Cliffe said the almost 50-year-old former laboratory was "hopelessly not fit-for-purpose".

"The light fittings were so old we couldn't get new bulbs ... it was virtually impossible to clean. The staff did an amazing job of continuing to operate a very safe and reliable service."

New 'state of the art' blood bank opens in Wellington Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

She said the new space had been a long time coming and a couple of years ago things reached a crisis point.

"It could have been quite a dangerous situation in that we could have had our accreditation removed and we wouldn't have been able to provide a full service blood bank," she said.

That didn't happen. Health New Zealand found a solution, Cliffe said and the team was "utterly delighted" with it.

She said the facility was built for under $2 million "on time and on budget".

Sam Cliffe says the old laboratory was old and not fit for purpose. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Wellington blood bank team leader Dan Gyles said he felt a mixture of relief and excitement at Wednesday's opening after pushing for a new lab for close to 16 years.

"It means everything. We now have space to do the job that we should have been doing all along. We have, despite the previous conditions, managed to maintain a safe service, but that was all it was."

He said they now had the space to implement laboratory practices around wearing gowns and protective gear, where required. "Rather than having tea breaks on our knees in the corner."

The laboratory, which includes pneumatic tubes that send and receive blood to and from the wards, multiple blood fridges, freezers storing plasma at minus 35 degrees, and room-temperature storage cabinets that keep platelets "jiggling," is three times the size of the old lab - built to meet expected future demand.

The new Wellington blood bank offices was built for $2 million and came in on time and one budget. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Gyles said the extra space also meant a second blood grouping and screening machine, which was a game changer for the dozen staff that keep the service running around the clock.

Mel Homer received multiple blood transfusions during treatment for blood cancer. Supplied

"These do our grunt work, so this is where the patient samples are loaded up and we determine their blood group ... and then we do a red cell antibody screen."

The process ensured the blood was compatible with the patient who received it, he said.

Gyles said the blood bank was the behind-the-scenes critical step between people donating blood and patients receiving a transfusion - the majority of which were cancer patients, like Mel Homer.

Homer has received multiple blood transfusions over the past year while undergoing treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia, a blood cancer.

"They basically nuke your whole system, it's like scorched earth and you have no immune system and the idea is that they also kill off the cancer cells, and hopefully they don't grow back."

She said the treatment saw her haemoglobin and white blood cell count drop and her platelets - the clotting component - tank.

"You can't function properly so you need blood transfusions to top you up to a level so you can start healing."

In addition to red blood transfusions, Homer also needed platelets to reduce the risk of brain bleeds - but there were only two donors whose platelets were compatible, she said.

"It was life-saving." She said every time she used it - which was multiple times - she would think, "I'm so grateful".

The frozen blood product has to be thawed before it can be used. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The blood bank also had to be ready for emergencies, Gyles said. Plasma was most often used for bleeding patients, patients in theatre, or trauma patients, he said.

It took about 15 minutes for the frozen blood product to thaw in a jiggling bath at 37C, he said.

"A bleeding patient - they need it quickly. So we've got some pre-thawed ahead of time."

Megan Piercy required an emergency blood transfusion after suffering from a post-partum haemorrhage. Supplied

Two years ago, Megan Piercy became a bleeding patient when she suffered a post-partum haemorrhage following the birth of her son.

"It was all kinds of bells and whistles from there. I had lost ... just over two litres at once."

She said given the emergency situation, she received blood from the universal donor type, however, samples of her blood were also sent off for testing in case she needed something more specific.

Piercy said the transfusion was crucial.

As a passionate blood donor herself, she knew the importance of it, she said. "I just never expected to be on the receiving end of it."

Michelle Sutherland, interim group director of operations for Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley, said the new blood bank was an important investment in the region's health services.

"Having this purpose-built facility on site strengthens our ability to deliver timely, safe and high-quality care for patients who need blood transfusions and other specialist services," she said.

Cliffe said patients, however, shouldn't notice the difference between Wellington's new blood bank and its predecessor.

"We've continued to maintain the same level of service delivery under incredibly trying conditions. [For] the people of Wellington this should be seamless."

Health Minister Simeon Brown cutting the ribbon to open the new Wellington Blood Bank. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

She said the new facility - in addition to future-proofing the service - provided the space for it to resume practical laboratory training for pathology professionals in the Pacific.

World.title: Police crack down on drug dealing in Wairoa
World.content:
A specialised police unit is cracking down on drug dealing in Wairoa, with six people arrested so far.

Four men and two women aged between 19 and 44 have been charged with drug dealing, firearms and dishonesty offences.

Police said eight search warrants were executed by specialist police staff and the Eastern District Gang Disruption Unit within three days.

Senior Sergeant Nathan Snell said the operation focused on the impacts of drug supply into the community.

"Police recognise the burden drug use and addiction has on the community and are committed to holding those involved in its supply to account," he said.

World.title: Defence Force training infrastructure in 'World War II era', new documents reveal
World.content:
The Defence Force is on its biggest push ever to get more combat ready and lethal at the same time its training infrastructure is in "World War II era", according to newly released documents.

Proactively released Cabinet papers from April and May outline the big deficit.

"The infrastructure to support training of recruits, in particular, is not in a position to meet existing ... demand in an effective way," said one 12-page paper that asked for, and got, a start to planning for an upgrade to how recruits are trained.

"Much of the infrastructure required to train NZDF personnel, like classrooms or rifle ranges, is World War II era, and is increasingly ineffective, and creating a potential for unsafe training environments.

"Investment is needed to avoid future failure."

The paper asked Cabinet to back a business case for fixing this, and Budget 2026 put in $23m.

However, this only funds a design phase out to 2029-30.

That means an actual fix of systems and infrastructure together appears at least three years away.

Defence Minister Chris Penk said there have been many years of under-investment into the Defence Force and this government is working to fix the consequences.

"We've begun the process of doing so to ensure training can be delivered safely, effectively and at the scale required into the future."

The Defence Capability Plan suggested investments over the next 15 years including into recruitment, retention and training, he said in a statement.

The paper said one upgraded rifle range would be added meantime, but one or two other short-term moves "to add resilience to a significantly degraded capability" were blanked out.

'Failing condition makes it difficult to train'

The deficiencies are a big hurdle to Defence's must-have in its new workforce strategy "to grow more soldiers, sailors and aviators, with urgency" and more tech-savvy ones as drone, cyber and electronic warfare take over.

Instead, "poor infrastructure in failing condition makes it difficult to train and retain people."

An example is old manual target practice ranges not suitable for modern weapons. Two other examples were blanked out.

The wider context is grim:

The state of bases and facilities was a key reason given at scrutiny week in June for the land combat readiness falling to 45 percent at the end of 2025.

Defence has admitted its training systems are degraded too much to rapidly boost battlefield adaptability and agility.

NZDF's ways of managing its existing assets do not meet Treasury standards, and it is slow to get contracts for projects signed up.

Eroded by old gear and slow take-up of new tech, 60 percent of the army's land training system had got to the end of its life, said the May Cabinet paper.

Recruits 'most pressing'

The whole system relied in the first place on recruit training but this was significantly degraded and the "most pressing" thing needing fixing.

That fix would focus on Waiouru camp and line up with Australia, which was putting almost a billion dollars into recruit training, as well as looking to the US, UK and Singapore.

The paper that Penk lodged with Cabinet showed the ministers - Judith Collins was Defence Minister at the time - walking a line between "capability and affordability", even after Defence got a $9 billion fillip in new spending over four years from 2025.

So they narrowed in on a new recruit training system and curriculum which was the "minimum viable capability needed in the short term", and would need to integrate with Australia, other partners and other government services.

"Australian designs will be used where possible" in the detailed business case that is now being worked on.

'Future growth' option not chosen

A third more ambitious option that catered for "future growth and the introduction of new and emerging ... capabilities" did not make the cut.

Budget 2026 also had funding for an undisclosed amount for a new 'virtual training' facility at Linton camp near Palmerston North.

Defence has a huge estate, huge budgets and a chequered track record running it all.

The latest available Treasury report on how NZDF was doing with its big capital investments said it was no longer reporting a significant underspend (which can indicate projects hitting delays). Its actual spend on projects at $406m, and its spending on repairs and maintenance at $193m, at that stage were only a bit behind forecast.

However, Defence spending on specialist equipment and on data/digital was running well behind forecast.

The report for the September-December 2025 quarter showed it took about a year for procurement processes to get to the point of signing contracts, among the slower on the major public agencies covered by the Treasury investment reports.

Its asset registers and asset management plans were not up to scratch according to the latest gauge in June 2025. An update for 2026 won't be publicly available for months.

Labour's defence spokesperson Damien O'Connor said it supported the direction of the Defence Capability Plan.

"Personnel is the most acute issue facing NZDF. Labour sees this as a priority and will get advice on ensuring training capacity is built when in government," he said.

World.title: Rush to desex pigs rehomed after alleged murder as boars break in
World.content:
An animal rescue charity is rushing to desex 42 female pigs due to frisky wild boars breaking through electric fencing and into their enclosure.

The 70 or so pigs were previously cared for by Coromandel farmer Stuart Edmonson, who has been charged with murdering a pig hunter and attempting to murder another in December 2024.

His pigs were taken into the care of charitable trust HUHA, whose chief executive Carolyn Press-McKenzie said the break-ins mean they're scrambling to desex 42 females at their Wellington sanctuary.

"We were never quite sure how they were getting in, we can't find any holes in the fencing, but they're very determined so they're either throwing themselves over the fencing or they're wiggling under the fencing."

Supplied/HUHA

The male pigs were desexed soon after coming into HUHA's care, so they thought they wouldn't need to do the same for the females in order to prevent any unwanted litters.

"One day we saw a skinny, wily-looking chap wandering around. It was definitely a wild boar," Press-Mckenzie said.

"We'd been really responsible desexing our boys but we hadn't factored the food and the environment attracting wild boars down."

They de-sexed the "wily-looking chap", but he was followed by two more wild boars.

"Our ones don't get out - they all stay-put because they've got everything they need. They've got like a little village, there's a lovely little stream, they have this beautiful forest with natives and some pine trees," Press-Mckenzie said.

The 70 or so pigs had gone into the care of HUHA Supplied/HUHA

"They don't really want for anything. But of course the wild boars on the outside looking in, they're desperate, they need food and they need care."

HUHA staff were able to catch and castrate two of the three wild boars.

"They're now living as part of the community so they've achieved the dream life they were after."

Stuart Edmonson, who was known internationally for the wild pigs he kept as pets, is due to stand trial next year charged with the murder of 41-year-old father-of-five Kevin Mabbott and attempting to murder another man.

Mabbott, 41, was a father-of-five and was described by his loved ones as a "loveable ratbag".

The 70 or so pigs had gone into the care of HUHA Supplied/HUHA

Carolyn Press-McKenzie said HUHA staff have managed to desex most of the female pigs with just a few more to go.

"We shouldn't be having any more piglets, and that's forever, so that's really exciting."

She said the pigs are doing very well, and are enjoying meals including malt donated by Panhead Brewery and vegetables by Pak'nSave.

World.title: Live: Aussies involved in velodrome crash, pursuit gold up for grabs
World.content:
Lots of medals up for grabs in the velodrome from 1:00am AEST this morning.

Women's Tandem B Sprint

(Getty Images)

Jess Gallagher and her pilot Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr will go for gold in the women's tandem sprint against New Zealand's Emma Foy and her guide Jessie Hodges.

This is the head-to-head part of the sprint races, a best of three battle where racing comes to the fore over brute speed.

Men's Tandem B 1,000m Time Trial

World sliver medallist in this event Kane Perris will go in this race with his pilot Luke Zaccaria.

Women's team pursuit

(Getty Images)

The greatest test of a nation's endurance program - the team pursuit.

Australia qualified fastest, just head of New Zealand for the chance to race for gold in the 4,000m team pursuit.

Australia's team will be Sophie Edwards, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden.

It should be a ripper of a battle between the trans-Tasman rivals, with the Kiwis lead by 2025 Tour of Britain winner Ally Woolaston, a two-time track world champion and silver medallist in this event at the 2024 Paris Olympics, with Bryony Botha another survivor from that team who lost to the USA.

Women's C4-C5 4,000m Individual Pursuit

(Getty Images)

Two Aussies in this one — Erin Normoyle goes for bronze against Nicole Murray of New Zealand.

Then, it's the two record-breakers, England's C5 athlete Morgan Newberry taking on Australia's C4 athlete Tara Neyland.

Both women broke their respective world records in the qualifiers, so this one could be fun too.

Men's team pursuit

Two of Australia's draught-ending Olympic champions will look to add Commonwealth Games golds to their burgeoning medal cabinets.

(Getty Images )

Oliver Bleddyn and Conor Leahy have those gold medals from Paris in their pockets and their golden bikes are a constant reminder of that. Can they add Commonwealth gold alongside fellow world championship silver medallists Blake Agnoletto and James Moriarty as they take on an England team that rather fell apart in qualifying?

Women's team sprint

The Aussie women will go up against the Scots in the bronze medal race, in what will be a raucous atmosphere on the track.

Molly McGill, Kristina Clonan and Alessia McCaig are an impressive bunch of women and would have hoped to have been contesting gold here, so will want to power past the home team to silence the crowd.

Men's team sprint

(Getty Images)

Another Ashes battle.

Yes, there's no Matt Richardson - the man who won an Olympic bronze medal in this very event in Paris for Australia, alongside Leigh Hoffman.

But reckon either of these two squads care about that?

Australia's strength is in its cohesiveness and class throughout - Hoffman's power on the second lap absolutely crucial after the inevitably lightning start from Ryan Elliot, while Dan Barber will bring them home.

World.title: Tomic continues resurgence, de Minaur sets up clash with Hewitt
World.content:
Born-again Bernard Tomic has continued his extraordinary renaissance with another stunning victory to surge into his first ATP quarterfinal in seven years.

A day after notching the fastest win on the tour all year, Tomic claimed the prized scalp of dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov in a straight-sets blitz in Mexico on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

And rounding out a banner day for Australian tennis less than a month out from the US Open, world number six Alex de Minaur has beaten his old nemesis Stefanos Tsitsipas to set up an intriguing showdown with Cruz Hewitt in Washington.

The day, though, belonged to the resurgent Tomic.

The one-time world number 17 crushed fourth-seeded Khachanov — the big-serving Russian who ousted Nick Kyrgios to reach the 2022 US Open semifinals — 6-2, 6-4 to continue his spectacular comeback from the brink of retirement.

The 33-year-old hinted he was considering hanging up his racquet before snaring the Lincoln Challenger this month.

"I'll be as honest as I can, about 10 days ago I hit a bit of a brick wall, maybe two weeks ago," Tomic said in the aftermath of his biggest breakthrough since 2018.

"I said this was going to be my last year, so I guess I have to reassess a few things now. Now that I won, I'm going to have to go back to the table. I'm probably going to play another 20 years."

Twenty more years may be a stretch, but Tomic is playing some vintage tennis.

The former teenage Wimbledon quarter-finalist only made the main draw in Mexico as a qualifying lucky loser.

Now he is three wins away from hoisting the trophy in Los Cabos, having earlier needed just 46 minutes to take down Alex Hernandez 6-1, 6-0 in the first round.

Currently ranked 171st, Tomic will climb even further and potentially to as high as number 132 if he wins a most unexpected fifth ATP title.

Next up will be either British fifth seed Cam Norrie or fellow Australian James Duckworth in Tomic's first ATP quarterfinal since losing to de Minaur in Atlanta in 2019.

De Minaur, meanwhile, is celebrating his own big victory, after downing Tsitsipas for only the second time in 14 meetings to reach the last 16 in the US capital.

The 6-4, 3-6, 6-3 win earned the top seed and defending champion a first-time encounter with 17-year-old Hewitt, de Minaur's understudy and son of Australian Davis Cup captain and mentor Lleyton.

After winning his first ATP match on Wednesday, Hewitt said it would be a "dream" to square off against de Minaur, who he likened to a big brother.

"I've known him basically my whole life," said Hewitt, who made the Wimbledon boys' final two weeks ago.

"​He's stayed with us and we have Christmas together, also. He's taught me so ​much. I think that ⁠would be a pretty cool memory for us."

AAP

World.title: Last-minute race to deliver marathon medals after shipping delays
World.content:
A last-minute logistical scramble has ensured thousands of runners at a major Queensland marathon festival will receive their medals.

A record number of more than 16,000 people will descend on the Sunshine Coast as the region hosts the event on Sunday.

But participants received an email late on Wednesday informing them they might not get a medal for crossing the line.

A medal from last year's Sunshine Coast Marathon Festival. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Event director Jason Crowther told the ABC a container full of T-shirts and medals arrived at the Port of Brisbane on Tuesday, but was stranded on the dock.

Mr Crowther said the merchandise was ordered months ago and was due to arrive on July 3, with the shipping company blaming point-of-origin delays and a typhoon for the late arrival.

"This is something you just don't want to happen," he said.

"To not get a finisher medal is not acceptable from our point of view.

"We don't take this lightly."

The Sunshine Coast Marathon Festival is a popular event, which attracts runners from around the country. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Marathon)

Port mobilises to solve crisis

When the Port of Brisbane was made aware of the issue following a media enquiry, officials rolled up their sleeves.

Executive general manager Brendan Connell said he was "really pleased" to help.

"We've been able to identify the container, get it moving and get it onto the Sunshine Coast so that all those hard-running marathoners, very worthy recipients, can get their medals on the weekend," he said.

"As soon as we found out … we wanted to do everything we could to help.

"We made a couple of phone calls, some senior people made some decisions, and in fact they disrupted their own days to ensure that we could identify this container.

"A few other things were put on the backburner to make that happen, but ultimately, everybody was able to come together and get to a really good outcome."

The event provides a much-needed tourism boost for the region over the winter months. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Marathon)

Mr Crowther said he was grateful to port officials for helping get the medals and merchandise released.

"They've moved heaven and earth to make it happen so a big thank you to them," he said.

" I've had a week of sleepless nights; it was something that was meant to arrive a long time ago. "

For anyone considering calling the port to get their parcel delivered faster, Mr Connell has bad news.

"It is a really complex series of events that moves freight around the world," he said.

"This isn't a scenario we could repeat every day, it isn't something that we can ordinarily influence.

"But certainly when there's a massive event like this going on … we wanted to make sure we could come together and do what we could to find those medals and get them on their way."

Last year, tourism officials estimated the Sunshine Coast race weekend generated about $10.5 million for the local economy.

World.title: Final frontiers drive Hazlewood in twilight years
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has more boxes to tick in a stellar career after returning to peak fitness following several injury impacted years.

The 35-year-old Australia paceman, veteran of 76 Tests, has never won a series in India or England, two classic confrontations that loom large in the 20 Tests at least the team are set to play in the next 12 months.

Australia have not won an away Ashes series since 2001, while 2004 was the last triumph in India — well before any of the current squad were playing Tests.

Australian men's Tests in 2026/27 August 12-26: Two Tests vs Bangladesh

Two Tests vs Bangladesh October 9-31: Three Tests in South Africa

Three Tests in South Africa December 9-January 7: Four Tests vs New Zealand

Four Tests vs New Zealand January 21-February 23, 2027: Five Tests in India

Five Tests in India March 11-15, 2027: One Test vs England

One Test vs England June, 2027: World Test Championship final (potential)

World Test Championship final (potential) June-July, 2027: Five Tests in England

"The big series are obviously England and India. I haven't won in South Africa either, so there are a few boxes to tick off there, not just me, but this whole playing group," Hazlewood said.

"That's been a driving factor during this prep, it is in the back of your head, and in the months leading into it. They're real big Test series, all away against tough competition. Hopefully we get the job done."

Hazlewood's most recent setback in the Test sphere came when Achilles tendon and hamstring injuries cruelled any involvement in last summer's Ashes series.

Since then he has returned to the bowling crease with a bang, helping Royal Challengers Bengaluru win back-to-back IPL titles.

Hazlewood has been preparing with other members of the Australia squad at the National Cricket Centre in Brisbane ahead of two Tests against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay next month.

He said the "big days" of training in one location and without other playing commitments had been ideal.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"Leading into other Test series and Test matches, you're playing T20, you're playing one-dayers, you're travelling, so it's tough to fit those bowling sessions in," he said.

"It's just trying to replicate a day in the field of Test cricket. It's bowling multiple spells in a day. It's bowling back-to-back days."

"This has been tailor-made for a Test match, which I think should work out well."

Hazlewood said it would be "tough" for any of the quicks in the squad to play every Test in the next year.

"Maybe a spinner," he quipped.

Hazlewood, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Scott Boland, Brendan Doggett and Michael Neser will all be vying for games.

Boland, who has been in sensational Test form, has been mostly overlooked when Hazlewood was previously available, but it need not be an either/or proposition.

"I think we've only played one game together … in England at Edgbaston, which was nice. I'd love to play more with Scotty," Hazlewood said.

"We're obviously a little bit similar, but there are still a lot of differences in our bowling. Every time he's come in, he's done unbelievably well. His career just keeps getting better and better the older he gets.

"I think there are enough opportunities in the next 12 to 18 months for us to play a lot of cricket, hopefully, together. We've got Ness (Neser) and Doggy (Doggett) there as well, so I think we'll have to lean on all six at some point in the next 18 months."

Hazlewood's most recent injuries have coincided with home Tests, but he is not sweating over what transpired in the past.

"We've got a nice lead-in this time. We've got Test matches abroad, so hopefully we hit the ground running again in Australia," he said.

"I've been lucky enough to play 70-odd Test matches now, which is quite a lot in terms of Aussie quicks. Hopefully I can tick a few more off."

AAP

World.title: People across Ireland wake up at all hours to watch AFLW
World.content:
In the middle of the night in a house in Ballinamore, in the North West of Ireland, Sharon O'Dowd wakes up to put on an Australian broadcast.

Two years ago, her young sister Eilish, who she helped raise with 12 years between them, moved from County Leitrim to Sydney to play AFLW for GWS.

Sharon and Eilish ODowd at a Gaelic game. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

When one of two of Eilish's matches haven't been available to stream across the ocean, the mother of two — her kids three and six — has put the commentary on and sat and listened instead while the rest of her house sleeps.

"I don't mind getting up this early as I love to watch her and the Giants play," Sharon told ABC Sport.

"If it's a particularly early game I usually go back to bed after it."

Sharon is one of many families across Ireland who wake up at all hours to watch GAA-turned-AFLW stars.

There are 47 Irish players in the AFL women's competition, many of whom will be on show in this weekend's inaugural AFLW Australia v Ireland clash in Sydney.

Their feats regularly make headlines back home.

Eilish with the first touch of her ball for GWS scored the fastest opening goal in AFLW history. The clip — in which she won the tap in the ruck and bolted straight through the corridor to score within 15 seconds — made the national news.

Sharon and EIlish O'Dowd. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

As it was her first game, Sharon was still getting familiar with the stream and watched, stunned, from her phone.

"I was in shock when she scored because I just couldn't believe what had happened," Sharon said.

"Everyone else in my house was asleep so I couldn't even celebrate with them. I knew my parents were watching the game in their house so I texted them.

"But it had happened so quickly they didn't even see it because they hadn't got logged into their streaming account fast enough."

Luckily, they have since watched the video of the replay multiple times.

Vikki Wall is a two-time premiership player with North Melbourne. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Over in Dunboyne, a town of less than 10,000 people in County Meath, the Wall family regularly pack their house for North Melbourne games.

Tom and Caroline Wall's daughter, Vikki Wall, is a star sportswoman from the Eastern Coast.

She twice led County Meath to historic All-Ireland Senior Championship titles in 2021 and 2022 before being signed as an international rookie by North Melbourne and playing all 13 games of her 2022 debut season.

Vikki Wall is a star player in Ireland. (Supplied: Caroline Wall)

She missed the 2023 AFLW season to play rugby sevens for Ireland ahead of the Paris Olympics and returned to Arden Street to win premierships in 2024 and 2025.

"We've had events in our house where 30-plus people come and have breakfast and cheer on the teams," Tom told ABC Sport.

"We try to watch all of Vikki's matches but it can be difficult to access the games online sometimes, so we listen to the match commentaries on the radio, if necessary."

Like Sharon, this means getting up before the sun. "But it's worth it," said Tom.

Dublin, Ireland, August 15, 2021: Vikki Wall of Meath is congratulated by family following the TG4 All-Ireland Senior Ladies Football Championship Semi-Final match between Cork and Meath at Croke Park. (Getty: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

Vikki's younger sister Sarah was drafted to the Kangaroos last year. Thankfully for Tom and Caroline, this means still just the one early alarm.

Similarly, Collingwood's Sarah Rowe is a cross-code athlete, whose dad has followed her career across the globe.

Sarah represented County Mayo across all age groups from under-12 to the senior team before she moved to Australia.

There, she became a fan favourite for the Magpies after debuting in 2019 and won an A-League Women's championship with the Central Coast Mariners in 2025.

Her father Alan hasn't missed a game.

"My passion for the AFLW is total," Rowe told ABC Sport.

Sarah Rowe with her dad Alan after winning the A-League Women championship. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

"I originally had not a clue about the rules, regulations or how to play the game but over a period of time, I've got to understand everything about it, I've seen the great players grow and understood the game passionately and very deeply, to now [to be able to] say that's it's one of the great games that I love watching."

Rowe has made the trip over to Sydney for the first AFLW Australia v Ireland representative game, as he does for all her big games: her 50th, 75th and Collingwood's 2022 semi-final against Adelaide.

"It's a great honour to represent the country at the highest level and I will be there with great pride and for the family and for the town of Ballina," Rowe said.

Alan Rowe hasn't missed a single game of his daughter's, Collingwood star Sarah Rowe. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

Back in Ballina, Sarah's mother Grainne will be watching the match with "everybody within our family," Rowe said, including aunties, uncles and cousins.

"It's one of the big days of sporting life within the Irish calendar.

" And it'll be one that everyone will be so much looking forward to watching and very proud to be a part of. "

Sharon said it gets hard being away from Eilish, but she's happy players like her sister can give their all to the game overseas.

"When she has had a great game I would just love to be there to be able to tell her how amazing she is, and also when she is having a hard time or she gets injured I would love to be able to make sure she is ok. We do video calls all the time though so that helps," Sharon said.

The AFLW Australia v Ireland Cup and Best on Ground medal ahead of the inaugural clash. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

She's hoping it'll be a very happy FaceTime after Saturday's game against Australia at North Sydney Oval.

"It is an incredibly proud moment for all our family to see Eilish wear an Irish jersey and represent her country. There is no higher honour in sport in my opinion," she said.

"I'd imagine for this game the whole family will get up early to see her. We will have our Irish flags out and cheer the whole team on."

World.title: Storm coach responds to Munster's PNG ultimatum
World.content:
A part of Craig Bellamy would love it if he and Cameron Munster could bow out of Melbourne together.

But as the pair consider their NRL futures, Bellamy remains committed to supporting Munster whether or not he signs with expansion franchise PNG.

Storm veteran Munster turned the heat on Bellamy on Wednesday by claiming he would reject interest from the Chiefs for 2028 if Bellamy remained Melbourne's coach for that season.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Bellamy re-signed with the Storm through 2028 in February, but the master mentor's diagnosis with a neurodegenerative condition has since cast doubt over his future.

On Thursday, Bellamy reiterated "the next year or two I'll be finishing up" but did not say whether his health would permit coaching on as late as 2028.

Bellamy handed Munster his NRL debut in 2014 and coached him in two premiership triumphs, with the 31-year-old now the Storm's longest-serving active player.

For Bellamy, the chance to bow out together would be fitting, but Munster indicated on Wednesday he may not be able to wait for the coach to make his own decision.

"I'd love to go right through my coaching career with him, ending about the same time," Bellamy said.

"[But] he's got a decision to make. He'll make the right decision for what's right for his family. He's got the right to do that.

"I'll back 'Mun' up, whatever he wants to do."

Munster remains sidelined with a knee injury for Friday's clash with resurgent Canterbury and is now joined on the pine by captain and hooker Harry Grant.

In a season of injury carnage, Bellamy said Grant's hamstring problem was another big blow for the 12th-placed Storm.

"Any team losing their captain, that's a big loss, but Harry especially," Bellamy said.

"He's always in the middle of the play whether it be with the ball or without the ball."

Injuries, roster turnover and a seven-game losing streak early in the season have all left the Storm's finals hopes hanging by a thread ahead of round 22.

A loss to the Bulldogs would ensure they miss the top eight for only the second time under Bellamy, and first since mass salary cap breaches consigned them to the wooden spoon in 2010.

It would also mark a 12th loss of the year — the most the Storm would have suffered in any of their 24 seasons under Bellamy.

"We know it's going to be a tough ask tomorrow night, but we've had a good week's preparation with the guys we've had," Bellamy said.

AAP

World.title: Cricketer dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' suspended as stats show unusual trend
World.content:
The club at the centre of the "Clicky Ponting" scandal in English amateur cricket has suspended its player over the matter.

Saltburn Cricket Club said Brian Devine had been suspended for the rest of the season after several videos were posted online with claims Devine was clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat to mimic the sound of an edge.

The club has forfeited its next match in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League.

"We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the league's investigation," a statement read.

"We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us.

"The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation."

Devine is yet to comment on the matter and an investigation into the claims has yet to be completed, with the allegations so far unproven.

However, an amateur data analyst on social media platform X said they had trawled all scorecards from Saltburn games and found wicketkeeper catches dramatically increased when Devine was playing.

"Been requested to split it by the matches where Devine (the slip clicker) played, and it's even more stark," X account @maxtempers, which usually posts about British politics, wrote.

"39 keeper catches in 13 matches with Devine. 5 keeper catches in 7 without."

The post followed an original analysis that found wicketkeeper catches increased four-fold when the particular keeper standing alongside Devine in the alleged clicking footage was playing, including eight catches in one innings.

The record at Test level is seven catches in one innings, shared by five players.

"The league has received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25 July, 2026," a league statement read when the controversy came to light.

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made."

Australian cricket podcasters The Grade Cricketer have offered to provide financial support to Devine and Saltburn.

World.title: Broncos premiership prop announces medical retirement due to blood clots
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos premiership prop Corey Jensen has announced his medical retirement from the NRL after ongoing problems.

Jensen, who played 95 games for Brisbane including last year's grand final win over Melbourne Storm, also played 58 games in five seasons for North Queensland.

After becoming unwell during round seven, Jensen was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs).

"After receiving medical advice and speaking to specialists, it's clear that it's no longer safe for me to play rugby league," he told reporters.

Jensen said he had been told he would have to take blood thinners for the rest of his life.

Big Ben heading to NFL The Brisbane Broncos are releasing forward Ben Te Kura from the rest of his NRL contract to allow him to pursue his dream of playing in the NFL.

"Since [the diagnosis] I've been able to train properly again, it's been like a mini pre-season, and I can do everything other than the contact, which is the frustrating part.

"Overall, my health's pretty good, I can continue training in the future and it's not going to affect me in any way."

The Broncos had confirmed he had another incident with deep vein thrombosis in his calf a year earlier, with both incidents considered unprovoked, meaning there was no obvious trigger such as a long-haul flight or injury.

"I leave with absolutely no regrets," he said, thanking his teammates for being part of the premiership win with them.

"I never chased individual recognition, but being part of a team, seeing people grow and knowing that in some way I may have contributed."

Corey Jensen played 95 games for the Broncos after joining the Brisbane side for the 2022 season. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Jensen teared up, thanking his wife Shannen for all her support and the sacrifices she had made.

"People see the player, but they don't always see what partners give up behind the scenes," he said.

Jensen is a qualified sports scientist, having completed a Bachelor of Sport and Exercise Science at James Cook University, and will have a bright future in that space if he chooses to pursue it.

Jensen was not a star as a youth but, through hard work, turned himself into a weapon after debuting for the Cowboys in 2017 and playing in the grand final.

"The late Paul Green gave me my debut back then.

"I was a bit of a late bloomer, so I'm grateful they took a punt on me, and I have to acknowledge how much the Cowboys did for my career," Jensen said.

"Coming down here was kind of a kind of a new lease on life. The Broncos gave me the opportunity, and I'm eternally grateful for what this club's done for me both on and off the field."

ABC/AAP

Tech.title: Razer’s new keyboards drop the price on powerful gaming features
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Razer has insisted that optical keyboard switches are the best choice for competitive esports stars and the sweatiest of try-hards, but it’s now relenting slightly by offering cheaper keyboards with magnetic switches and a similar array of gaming features. The $120 Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini and $140 Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless, both launching today, are the company’s first keyboards to use Hall effect switches. They’re wired-only boards loaded with gaming-first features, and I’ve had a brief chance to test both and take them for a spin.

The new Huntsman boards offer the hallmarks found in many other Hall effect mechanical keyboards, like programmable actuation points, faster key releases with Rapid Trigger, and an 8KHz polling rate. Their linear switches have an average latency of 0.6ms, which is of course very fast but ever-so-slightly slower than the 0.48ms of optical Huntsman boards like the V3 Pro. Razer can stand by its claim that optical analog boards are faster, but we’re really splitting hairs here.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Full name: Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless 8kHz.

The new magnetic models offer plenty of speed at significantly lower prices, as the optical Huntsman Pro boards start at $220, and they have Razer’s full arsenal of deeply customizable gaming features. This includes things like Snap Tap, which prioritizes your last movement input on the A or W keys and makes for easier counter-strafing (considered cheating by some and banned by Valve); Snap Flex, for setting up keys to trigger specific actions upon release; and Dual-Keypress Priority, preventing an accidental movement input from interrupting two previously held keys (like diagonal movement). Those last two features are also available on the mid-range optical Huntsman V3 Tenkeyless 8KHz, and coming to the higher-end Huntsman V3 Pros via firmware update.

Do these all sound like pretty niche features for specialized use cases? They are. While these cheaper keyboards are designed to appeal to a wider audience, these kinds of features are designed for the most competitive of online shooters — specifically, games with nuances to their movement techniques, like Counter-Strike 2. Razer is primarily competing with Wooting, Asus, and SteelSeries in this space, going feature-for-feature to cater to this hardcore subset of gamers. Wooting’s 80HE and 60HE v2 are some of the most praised gaming keyboards around, but Razer’s new HE boards undercut them by about $60.

Previous Next









1 / 6 They look like Razer keyboards. The floating key design also feels a little dated these days, but the company is sticking to its guns.

I spent some time testing both the 65-percent and TKL versions of the new HE Huntsman pair, and since my Counter-Strike days are long behind me, these keyboards feel more than fast enough for any speedy inputs my aging fingers can muster. There is obviously not much reason to buy either of these boards unless you primarily care about their deep-in-the-weeds gaming features and making detailed customizations in Razer’s software (especially since entry-level mechanicals have gotten so good). The Razer Synapse app is as burdensome as ever, but you can also use a web version if you don’t need to make frequent changes or just don’t want to deal with it constantly running.

Razer’s doubleshot PBT keycaps have a nicely textured feel that’s more coarse than typical keycaps, but boy, do I dislike these shine-through legends. Some lettering and symbols are oddly proportioned and ugly, making an otherwise simple-looking floating keycap design look basic. The plastic base sitting beneath the aluminum top case makes these keyboards pretty light and portable, but the combination feels a bit cheap compared to full-metal keyboards. And there are no added conveniences like a volume knob, included wrist rest, or status screen like on the Huntsman Pro models.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Snap Tap on.

But the magnetic Huntsman pair both sound much better to my ears than Razer’s pricier models. The new HE keyboards create a nice clacky tone, while the Huntsman V3 Pro is louder and clunkier sounding. (I’ve got a high tolerance for noisy keyboards, but the latter can get on my nerves after typing for a while.) Preferred typing sounds are pretty subjective, but as improved as Razer’s new HE boards are in the sound department, I’ve tested other 8K wired Hall effect keyboards that are much more pleasing to the ears.

For the same price of Huntsman V3 HE, you can get more unique looking and nicer sounding keyboards, but if your sole focus is competitive gaming, these new models are a good value compared to other popular (and pricier) boards. Enjoy your speedy keys and all the RGB lighting your heart desires. Just don’t get banned.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Tech.title: Zoox can now charge for rides in its steering-wheel-free robotaxis
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Zoox just got permission to charge for robotaxi rides in its boxy, steering-wheel-less vehicles. On Thursday, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced it has granted the Amazon-owned Zoox a temporary exemption, allowing it to deploy up to 2,500 vehicles annually over the next two years, as reported earlier by Reuters.

The NHTSA’s decision exempts Zoox from rules requiring vehicles to have traditional controls, like a steering wheel, pedals, windshield defrosting, and mirrors. Zoox’s vehicles are built with passengers in mind, rather than drivers, featuring an interior with two bench seats and sliding doors. Until now, Zoox had been providing free rides to people in San Francisco and Las Vegas under a “demonstration exemption.” It had been waiting on approval for paid rides from the NHTSA, which has taken steps in recent months to streamline approvals for autonomous vehicles.

The move will allow Zoox to compete against Google’s Waymo and Elon Musk’s Tesla robotaxi service, both of which have been expanding their services across the US. Zoox will begin charging fares in Las Vegas next month, according to a press release. The company plans to bring its service to Miami and Austin as well.

In its decision, the NHTSA says it determined that Zoox robotaxis “have an equivalent or greater level of motor vehicle safety” compared to vehicles compliant with federal vehicle safety standards. Under the exemption, Zoox will be subject to “an enhanced oversight condition” that “may update and expand” as the company’s self-driving technology evolves. Zoox issued a software recall for its vehicles earlier this month over concerns that they may not detect smoke.

Tech.title: Spotify Running Mode helps match tunes to tempo
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Spotify has introduced a new Running Mode feature that makes it easier to curate playlists around your workout goals, music tastes, and desired beats per minute (BPM). The aim is to help you “spend less time hunting for the right music and more time moving,” according to Spotify’s announcement, providing customizable running presets and optional coaching features.

The feature looks similar to the regular Spotify mobile app UI, but with some additional running-focused information and customization options. Image: Spotify

Running Mode is an AI-powered experience that builds on personalization capabilities that were introduced with Prompted Playlists last year, with Spotify finding that fitness-based prompts have been some of the most popular uses for that feature. It requires a Premium subscription and can be found under the Fitness hub that Spotify launched in April. It’s available starting today on Spotify’s iOS app, but only for users in the US, UK, Canada, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, and Sweden for now.

There are 25 curated running playlist presets to choose from, which can be further customized around your preferred music genres, workout duration, BPM, and training method — including interval, steady, and pyramid. Running Mode also includes optional audio prompts in English that provide “timely cues and motivation without getting in the way of your music,” according to Spotify.

This isn’t the first experience that Spotify has made specifically for runners. It launched a Spotify Running feature in 2015 that was also designed to help you match music to your running pace, before retiring it in 2018. There is a notable distinction between that and the new Running Mode, however — Spotify Running used your phone hardware to automatically detect your pace and react by playing music that synchronizes with it, whereas Running Mode needs you to proactively define your own workout playlist requirements from the start.

Tech.title: Amazon’s short story collections are one of the best reasons to own a Kindle
Tech.content:
Over the last few years, I’ve gradually shifted away from ebooks. It’s been part of a general return to physical media, an attempt to create a deeper sense of ownership over the art I love and collect. A Kindle is obviously more convenient than a paperback: It’s tiny, holds a huge library, and you can purchase new books instantly. But, much like with retro game cartridges, I find there’s a deeper connection formed with a book dug out of a stack in a used book shop versus simply choosing the next thing in a series from a menu on an e-reader. But I haven’t completely given up on my Kindle, and there’s one big reason — actually, there are lots of smaller reasons why.

Amazon’s Original Stories publishing imprint has steadily curated a huge collection of short story collections, which often feature big-name authors and are particularly great if you’re a fan of genre fiction. The most recent, which came out this week, is called “Magic and Mystery,” and it gathers a bunch of fantasy authors together and has them tackle puzzle box mystery stories, most of which involve a murder of some sort.

Like past collections — which have explored everything from the vast expanse of space to straight-up horror — the stories here are incredibly varied, and explore the theme in different and often clever ways. Travis Baldree’s Miss Gentle and the Case of the Very Flat Monk, for instance, introduces a detective character that I absolutely need to see solve other mysteries: an old woman who wears a full suit of armor covered in enchanted human appendages, and who never shows her face. Robert Jackson Bennett’s The Lion’s Tusk, meanwhile, involves a gruesome murder at a royal wedding, and features a clever and incredibly bizarre murder weapon unlike anything I’ve ever seen or read before.

Image: Amazon

Some of the most impressive stories manage to cram a whole bunch of worldbuilding into a short you can finish in one sitting. Heather Fawcett’s A Labyrinth of Honeybees introduces a fantasy realm rich with a long history of gods and competing religions, while The Wizard Who Kept Himself Suspicious by Scott Lynch convincingly presents an ancient order of magic users who have been friends for centuries, and meet up every 13 years to hang out and show off their skills.

There are two great things about these collections. One, obviously, is the stories themselves. I’d recommend all seven shorts in “Magic and Mystery,” and some of my favorite authors have contributed to collections in the past. That includes the likes of Min Jin Lee (Pachinko), Lauren Beukes (The Shining Girls), N. K. Jemisin (The Inheritance Trilogy), and Jeff VanderMeer (the Southern Reach series). There’s even an original six-part story from Guillermo del Toro and Chuck Hogan that Netflix is turning into a movie. Short stories are an oft-neglected form that both let you discover new authors and give established writers a space to get weird and experimental. Often, this results in some of an author’s most memorable work. Arthur C. Clarke published a lot of novels, but nothing has stuck with me quite like the haunting short The Star.

But what’s also great about these series from Amazon is the freedom they offer. Historically, short stories have been available either in magazines or as part of large collections. But on a digital platform like the Kindle, you have more choice for how you engage with the stories. While I think each story in “Magic and Mystery” is worth checking out, you don’t have to buy the whole thing at once. Each short is available individually, giving the collection a sort of episodic feel. It’s like watching an anthology like Black Mirror, where as soon as one episode is done, you can decide where you want to go next, or if you want to continue at all. The stories are also cheap enough — usually running a buck or two — that they stray easily into impulse purchase territory.

The drawback is that these shorts are largely exclusive to Amazon. There’s at least one exception — del Toro’s The Boy in the Iron Box is getting a physical release — but otherwise digging into these collections necessitates owning a Kindle, or reading through the app on your phone. For me at least, that’s been reason enough to keep my e-reader charged even as my shelves become stuffed with physical books.

Tech.title: A second lens makes DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4P my new favorite video camera
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4P is a pretty simple proposition: an Osmo Pocket 4 with a second camera lens slapped inside. But is that extra lens worth the added size, weight, and cost relative to the regular Pocket 4? And how does it compare to the only rival on the market, Insta360’s dual-lens Luna Ultra?

It depends on what you’re filming. But I think most prospective buyers would get plenty of use out of the 4P’s 3x telephoto lens, and its quality is certainly impressive. Meanwhile, DJI has managed to undercut Insta360 on price while at least matching it on quality. For most, this will be the better buy, though the Luna Ultra has one major advantage: You can actually buy it in the US.

DJI’s travails in the US continue, and it won’t be releasing the Pocket 4P in the country, despite launches elsewhere. In Europe, it costs £529 / €599 (about $680) for the Standard Combo set, which includes a fill light, carry pouch, and a handle with a tripod thread. For many, it’ll be worth spending extra to get the £605 / €689 ($785) Vlog Combo, which also bundles in a larger carry case, a compact tripod, a DJI Mic Mini 2, and the FrameTap remote.

There had been hope that something remarkably like the Pocket 4P might emerge from Xtra, a company which popped up in the wake of DJI’s ban from the US, selling suspiciously similar products. That now looks unlikely: Xtra has delisted its Muse 2 Pro, halted preorders, and refunded deposits, while the FCC works to crack down on alleged DJI front companies. In short, don’t hold your breath for a US version of the Pocket 4P unless the FCC begins to lose its game of whack-a-mole.

If you are in a country where the Pocket 4P is on sale, what you’re getting really is a sibling to the Pocket 4, which I reviewed in April. It has the exact same body and controls, including an identical flip-out touchscreen, apart from minor cosmetic differences. It has an almost identical main camera, though there are some key differences I’ll get to in a minute. The software, stabilization, recording options, and in-built storage are all either identical, or close enough to count.

The two lenses are stacked, making for a bulky camera module. Tracking is mostly the same as before except for this new multi-person mode. As for the controls, they’re unchanged from the Pocket 4.

Almost every change is a ripple effect from the major new addition: a second lens. This 3x telephoto (or 60mm equivalent) sits above the default camera and is a remarkably close match in specs. It uses a slightly smaller sensor, a 1/1.28-inch-type, rather than 1-inch, but makes up for that with a faster f/1.8 aperture, instead of f/2.0. It supports in the same resolutions (4K landscape or 3K portrait), shoots similar 37-megapixel stills, and can be used in low-light, slow-motion, and timelapse modes. About the only place you can’t use it is panoramas.

The quality of the telephoto is impressive. Details are crisp, helped by the same impressive gimbal stabilization that keeps the main lens steady — I recorded some astonishingly stable footage from a small boat trip on a blustery day in the North Sea. I worried the larger camera might make stabilization trickier, but I needn’t have — if anything, my footage from the 4P feels more stable than from the 4.

The Pocket 4P is capable of recording 4K footage at up to 12x zoom, but beyond 6x you will see the quality begin to drop off. At 12x footage feels a little soft, details lost and text blurry, and I wouldn’t recommend zooming that far unless you really have to.

It’s better up close. The wide f/1.8 aperture creates a relatively tight depth of field with a compressed background, meaning beautiful optical bokeh. That’s ideal for me — this is an excellent camera for shooting products — but also makes it a great camera for portrait video or filming pets.

There’s a slight, short judder in footage when you switch between lenses while recording. Occasionally I’ve noticed a shift in color at the same time, though for the most part, footage from the two cameras looks similar.

The difference is at least in part because the main camera has superior dynamic range, up to 17 stops, along with supporting DJI’s new 10-bit D Log 2 color profile. Those are the chief upgrades that the Pocket 4P’s main camera has over the Pocket 4’s — this is a new sensor, but in the same size and resolution as before, and with the same aperture lens. In most lighting, the upgrades are slight, only coming to the fore in trickier conditions, though the camera still shows some obvious limits when shooting in the dark.

Welcome as the telephoto is, it does come with downsides. Size is the obvious one. At 230g, the Pocket 4P is about 40g heavier than its little sibling. And while the body of each camera is identical, the gimbal and lens apparatus here is about twice the size, making this taller and wider overall. This is still a remarkably compact, lightweight camera, and the extra weight isn’t enough to make it uncomfortable to use. But it does feel just a little less pocketable than before, which might be a limitation if you primarily want this for travel.

The new design makes me a little worried about durability too. When the camera is off, the two lenses now face forwards, rather than sideways into the gimbal arm, meaning they’re completely exposed. That’s made worse since DJI no longer offers a gimbal clamp for the camera, a protective measure I miss. Instead, the lenses are slightly recessed. That offers a little protection from scuffs and scratches, but makes it easier for dust to collect inside. You’ll want to keep a cleaning cloth to hand, and the camera might need more babying than previous generations.

You can zoom using the touchscreen, zoom button, or joystick.

DJI says the Pocket 4P will last for 210 minutes of use, half an hour less than the Pocket 4. That’s still plenty for me though. Charging is the same, with a full charge in 32 minutes, and storage is unchanged too: 107GB built-in, with support for 1TB microSD cards.

The software experience is broadly similar too. There are three buttons and a joystick on the device, with most of the settings accessed by swiping one way or another on the flip-out 2-inch touchscreen. It’s occasionally fiddly given the size, and I still swipe the wrong way more often than I’d care to admit, but it mostly works. The major new addition to the 4P is a new multi-person tracking option, which can detect multiple subjects while following the person in the center.

More exciting is support for DJI’s FrameTap, a small wireless touchscreen that lets you control the Pocket 4P from a distance. The FrameTap was introduced in April with the larger Osmo Mobile 8P gimbal, but this is the first Pocket device to support it. You can start recording, use the joystick to turn the gimbal or zoom in and out, and access a few basic controls along with playback. You can’t access every setting however, and you’re oddly unable to change resolution or frame rate from the FrameTap.

The FrameTap is definitely the most exciting of the optional accessories. The Vlog Combo also bundles in a Mic Mini 2, with one spare face plate. The fill light is even included in the Standard Combo. And there’s the usual tripod, though you need the handle attachment to mount it.

FrameTap support is pretty transparently a response to Insta360’s Luna Ultra, which launched earlier this year with its own dual stabilized cameras in a similar design. The Luna Ultra’s unique feature is letting you pull off the whole front panel to use as a remote; DJI’s FrameTap is a simpler solution to the same problem, with the downside that there’s no way to attach the remote to the camera when it’s not in use.

The two cameras are otherwise remarkably similar in specs. The Insta360 has the advantage of offering 8K recording from the main camera, but the new DJI has better battery life, wider dynamic range, superior slow motion, and double the built-in storage. All that, and it’s £150 / €130 ($150) cheaper in Europe, making this a pretty unequivocal winner. The biggest thing the Luna Ultra has going for it is that it’s actually on sale in the US, for $769.99.

It’s a Pocket 4 with a little bit more.

Taken together, the Osmo Pocket 4P is an almost unqualified success. It combines slight improvements to the Pocket 4’s main camera with a whole new telephoto that delivers great performance in its own right, including really attractive bokeh. There are small downsides to portability and battery life, which are good reasons to prefer the Pocket 4 if you don’t expect to make full use of the telephoto here. But otherwise the Pocket 4P is better than both its DJI stablemate and its Insta360 rival, and is undoubtedly the version of this form factor I’m most tempted to buy for myself.
